This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks in calculating the ground state of a high-dimensional Hypercube domain, approximately solving the eigenvalue problem of the Schrödinger equation. Through both theoretical and numerical analyses, we evaluate the generalization error under different conditions and observe that the error decreases at a rate of O(1/N) in theory and O(log(1)/N) in numerical tests, where N represents the number of training examples. Notably, the bias in the measured generalization error can be significant, resulting in an approximate 30% error in ground state energy estimates and an approximately 10% error in wave function overlap metrics. Furthermore, we find that the inclusion of variance scaling in stochastic gradient descent enhances the network's ability to learn the ground state, achieving an approximately 10% error in wave function overlap metrics, and we provide recommendations for effectively utilizing variance scaling in similar applications. These findings demonstrate that approximating the Schrödinger equation through two-layer neural networks exhibits promising characteristics, such as the ability to learn the ground state and achieve notable accuracy in wave function overlap metrics, and potential applications of this approach should be further evaluated through additional testing and validation. Future research could focus on overcoming the challenges of learning high-frequency features, developing methods for targeting specific eigenstates, and extending the neural network framework to solve time-dependent Schrödinger equation problems. Additionally, the code used in this study has been publicly contributed to GitHub for the purpose of facilitating replication of our results. Furthermore, we propose the development of a publicly accessible neural network framework, 'QuantumNeuralNetwork,' to aid researchers in accurately estimating eigenvalues and wave functions of Schrödinger equations in various quantum systems. This framework, designed to be highly adaptable and efficient, could serve as a versatile tool for approximating the Schrödinger equation across diverse applications and dimensionalities. Estimates of eigenvalues and wave functions obtained through QuantumNeuralNetwork have been found to be nearly exact up to a 10^-6 error threshold in our numerical tests, and the approach has been found to be applicable across not only L2 but also Dirac and Kerr Hamiltonians. These findings emphasize the potential of QuantumNeuralNetwork to be a valuable resource for accurately estimating eigenvalues and wave functions of Schrödinger equations in various complex systems. Our comprehensive study delves into the broad-scale anisotropies of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays detected by means of the Pierre Auger Observatory, encompassing over 79 three-year periods at 22 different right ascension segments. By employing the classical mathematical approach described by Euler and de Moivre, we investigate the anisotropies based on the dipolar harmonic mode of these right ascension segments. The results reveal a significant correlation between the amplitudes of these anisotropies and the local overviews of the all-sky anisotropy, an observation that reaches a 5.2$\sigma$ level of certainty. Furthermore, we observe a moderate increase in the amplitudes of these anisotropies relative to the total overviews of the all-sky anisotropy as the energy of these cosmic rays exceeds 4 EeV, an observation that reaches a 2.5$\sigma$ level of certainty. We represent the findings of our comprehensive study in a graphical format, showcasing the extensive data, and we illustrate the significance of our findings by showing the relationship between our certified anisotropy data and various simulations of these cosmic rays, specifically the AugerSim and AOFTV2 simulations, in addition to the model predictions outlined in MrBayes. Finally, we reflect on the significance of our findings and the avenues for further investigation that our comprehensive study now provides. In this paper, we explore thin film profiles with discommensurates under weak cross-layer coupling, cross-layer coupling with a mean gradient, and pure cross-layer coupling scenarios. These profiles exhibit periodic structures in one dimension, represented as $\Omega_\epsilon(\omega,h_\epsilon)$, where $\epsilon$ is a small parameter. Our goal is to establish a homogenized profile $\Omega_\epsilon(\omega,\frac{h_\epsilon}{\epsilon})$ and demonstrate its convergence to a suitable limit as $\epsilon$ approaches zero. This new profile remains periodic but converges to a more accurate limit at a faster rate. This work can be seen as an extension of a previous study (Compaan-Hagh and Dozzi, J. Dyn. Differential Equations, 2021) that investigated homogenization in thin films without discommensurates under cross-layer coupling. Our analysis is also closely related to the theory of $\Gamma$-convergence and utilizes $L^2$-convergence to obtain a useful compactness criterion. Furthermore, this notes builds upon the framework introduced in Dozzi and Rzymowski (J. Math. Anal. Appl., 2020) that investigated the $L^2$-convergence of solutions to PDEs in thin films under cross-layer coupling. Our work includes a new model for the dynamics of a fluid film involving slippy walls, which facilitates the derivation of useful estimates and compactness criteria to establish $\Gamma$-convergence of the gradient-like energy functional. This note is primarily a educational introduction to homogenization theory and provides a comprehensive approach to addressing a wide range of thin film problems with periodic structures, cross-layer coupling, and discommensurates. Consider a spacetime described by the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric, 
with a massless Dirac field that satisfies the equation $i(\partial_{\mu}+\Gamma^{\mu}_{\nu\rho}v^{\nu}u^{\rho})\xi^{\nu}=m\xi^{\nu}=0$. 
For the specific case of a stationary, spherical symmetry spacetime, 
this equation simplifies to a second-order differential operator acting on the Dirac field, 
and we demonstrate that the operator is Hermitian for both timelike and spacelike Killing fields. 
In particular, we show that the operator is self-adjoint when the Dirac field is normalized according to $\bar{\psi}\gamma^0u=U\psi$, 
with $U$ being a constant determined by the conformal factor in the metric, 
for both timelike and spacelike Killing fields. 
Additionally, we outline the conditions necessary for the self-adjointness of the Dirac operator, 
and discuss the resultant properties of the Dirac operator in both discrete and continuous spectra. 
Finally, we illustrate the existence and uniqueness of the self-adjoint Dirac operator in both the subspaces and the spaces of square-integrable Dirac fields.

In evaluating the efficacy of cancer treatments, scoring the extent of lymphatic cell invasion in cancer tissues holds significant importance. Current methods, involving visual assessment by pathologists, are time-consuming and prone to inter-observer variability due to their subjectivity. Advances in Medical Image Analysis have led to the development of quantitative, objective measures for lymphatic cell invasion, although these models' high complexity hinders efficient calculation. Furthermore, data privacy concerns have intensified the need for decentralized, client-driven processing of medical images. Leveraging the Federated Learning framework, we can train complex image analysis models at the edge, utilizing multiple hospitals' BScan datasets for tumor infiltration scoring. Our results indicate successful FL implementation, surpassing the performance of baseline models through distributed image collection. The novel approach established here lays the groundwork for deploying Federated Learning in real-world MIA applications. This research is made possible through a collaborative effort between academic and industrial partners, facilitated by the AI Health network. This collective effort has enabled the assembly of a comprehensive dataset comprising lymphatic cell invasion annotations for over 8,000 cancer scans, collected from multiple hospitals, for the first time. This research serves as a pioneering endeavor in decentralized MIA, showcasing FL's capacity to enhance models and address data collection challenges, ultimately promoting the adoption of FL in real-world MIA contexts. The comprehensive dataset collected during this research will be made available to the public, in addition to the FL code, for the purpose of facilitating further innovation and collaboration within the MIA community. This research has been conducted in accordance with the AI Health framework, focusing on realizing the third objective: "Federated MIA at scale for societal benefit." Our FL solution can serve as a prototype, aiming to inspire and enhance the MIA community's technical capabilities in the future. The Federated Learning approach we have implemented has significant potential to promote the adoption of MIA in a real-world setting, promoting the development of more advanced models and data collections. This collective effort has enabled us to gather comprehensive information and resources, including scorings for over 8,000 cancer cases, for the first time. This research serves as a model, promoting the dissemination of its results, including the FL code and dataset, to the MIA community, in addition to the AI Health framework that facilitated this research. This research has successfully demonstrated the application of Federated Learning in a real-world MIA setting, overcoming challenges associated with image privacy and complexity, to achieve so, we collaborated with multiple hospitals to collect a comprehensive dataset for training and model evaluation.

Cavity magnomechanics provides an ideal setting to study magnons and photons within a single framework, achieving this through the combination of a two-dimensional magnetic material and a mechanical cell. We build upon this concept by introducing spin-1 magnons, showcasing the creation of diverse quantum states through light-magnon interactions. Historically, the primary focus has been on the linear conversion of light to sound, yet in our research, we explore nonlinear light-magnon interactions. Utilizing ultra-low loss materials like graphene, we facilitate the generation of multi-photon states essential for cutting-edge research in quantum information and metrology. Our model displays the capability to produce numerous complex states, including multi-mode Gaussian states and multipartite entangled states, thus illustrating the potential for cavity magnomechanics to serve as a versatile tool in state fabrication. This tool holds promise for applications in quantum communication and precise measurements of graphene's tunnelling properties. Furthermore, our research presents an opportunity to investigate genuinely quantum effects emerging during the magnon-mediated interactions between photons, expanding the scope of cavity quantum electrodynamics. Our study delves into the performance of this system at room temperature and mK temperatures, highlighting an intriguing comparison between these two temperature regimes. We predict the graphical visualization of magnon states, which could reveal deep theoretical insights into magnons and its quantum properties. This research could pave the way for a new generation of magnomechanical devices capable of sustaining magnon states even in the presence of environmental noise at room temperature. Moreover, our model indicates the feasibility of achieving quantum macrostates with high photon numbers, showcasing the capability to link microscopic quantum phenomena to mechanical degrees of freedom. Our findings might also be translated to other systems, such as NMR, spin ensembles, and quantum simulators, for the purpose of designing novel quantum states. Ultimately, our research is expected to develop a groundbreaking cavity magnomechanics device capable of sustained magnon states, thereby paving the way for magnomechanical applications in quantum information and metrology. Still, our model indicates that magnon-sustaining in the current design falls short due to mechanical issues. Therefore, our work presents two possible solutions to overcome these limitations and achieve magnon-sustaining in the cavity magnomechanics device. This research may open the door to a new realm of magnomechanical devices capable of enduring magnon states and truly embodying the essence of quantum engineering. Lastly, our model highlights the versatility of cavity magnomechanics as a tool for designing diverse quantum states

A new reinforcement learning approach is introduced that allows a robot to master various quadrupedal gaits without pre-defined policy templates. In contrast to existing methods, this novel method evolves a policy by learning a neural network that generates policies adapted to an agent's local environment, thereby eliminating the need for extensive policy training. Additionally, this approach is scalable and can be applied to complex policies involving high-dimensional state spaces. Several simulations and physical experiments were conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of this method. Results show that a single optimized policy can effectively enable a quadrupedal robot to perform diverse tasks such as walking, jogging, and navigating on uneven terrain at various speeds. However, when challenged with a novel, unseen environment (e.g., walking backwards), the agent requires re-training to adapt to this new setting. Importantly, the underlying trajectory creator is responsible for generating distinct policies when the agent navigates distinct environmental contexts, thereby exhibiting a form of transfer learning. This pioneering work lays the foundation for efficiently training adaptive and generalizable quadrupedal locomotion policies through reinforcement learning. Several recorded videos of the evolved policies are available at https://youtu.be/jI0r0btJ1qk and https://youtu.be/ltUkP3W7R5Q. A pre-trained model for walking on flat ground is available at https://roboticsdivision.github.io/RL-TC/pre-trained-models. Note that re-production may require additional efforts due to hardware limitations (e.g., GPU memory), particularly for the "walking backwards" task (bonnet RL). The study of hot dust winds in low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs) remains limited due to the lack of suitable observational data. A recent high-resolution X-ray spectrum of the LLAGN in NGC\,7213 provides us with an opportunity to explore this phenomenon. By employing the ultra-violet and X-ray spectroscopy technique, we identified Fe\,XXII and Fe\,XXIII ions, which indicated the presence of high-velocity outflows ($v_{out}\approx3000-4000\,\mathrm{km\,s}^{-1}$) and a hotter gas component with a lower column density compared to the previously observed $N_{H}=(1.2\pm0.3)\times10^{21}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ and temperature of kT$_{0} \approx 0.9$ keV. Furthermore, we observed Fe\,XXV ions at multiple velocities, which provided further evidence for a hot gas component ($kT_{out}\approx 1.5$ keV) and suggested that the gas outflowing in the $-300\,\mathrm{km\,s}^{-1}$ range may be ionized. The observed hot winds in NGC\,7213 are likely driven by a radiatively driven accretion disk. The estimated rate of matter truncation at the accretion disk due to these outflows is $\dot{M}_{out}=(1.1\pm0.3)\times 0.01\,\dot{M}_{*}\, \mathrm{M}_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. The observed high temperature of the outflows is consistent with the findings of the photoionization code, which predicted a temperature of $\sim 1.5$ keV for the outflows when the local illuminating flux is higher than $10^{3}\,\mathrm{erg}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$. Furthermore, the model indicated that the hot winds in the host galaxy could be the primary supplier of the photoionized plasma observed in the optical spectrum. Additionally, we note that the hot winds in the galaxy may also contribute to the suppression of the X-ray luminosity through photoionization, which could explain the X-ray suppression factor of $18\pm3$. Finally, we note that the hot winds in the galaxy may also contribute to the suppression of the X-ray luminosity

This research proposes a probabilistic approach to resolving issues in linear system optimal regulation when some system parameters are unknown. A critical condition for this problem involves the linearization of nonlinear system regulators under small systemic perturbations. However, these linearized models may not guarantee optimal performance when significant changes occur. Moreover, the vast number of possible parameter variations presents a challenge in creating a comprehensive set of model-based predictions, which would complicate the linear regulator design. Ultimately, this would require an extensive bank of Proportional-Integral (PI) controllers, each tailored to a specific system parameter, which is impractical due to the large number of possible configurations and cross-sensitivity of these parameters. To address this limitation, we propose an in silico model-free reinforcement learning solution to optimize linear regulator performance when certain system parameters are unknown. This approach involves the online adjustment of the regulator's gain using an actor-critic algorithm, which learns to counteract the effects of uncertain parameters and predicts the impact of potential changes. A two-step reinforcement learning strategy is proposed to accelerate the convergence of the actor-critic algorithm by leveraging offline training techniques. This approach has been successfully validated and demonstrated in simulation tests involving a nonlinear aircraft system with uncertain parameters. Furthermore, our model-free reinforcement learning solution has yielded superior performance outcomes when compared to traditional linear regulator methods. A comparative performance assessment shows that our model-free approach achieves a 5-6% improvement in fuel consumption over the baseline linear regulator strategy. Additionally, our proposed solution outperforms a model-based reinforcement learning approach in terms of fuel consumption, recording a 10-15% improvement in certain flight scenarios. Our research has directly addressed and resolved two critical performance limitations associated with the linear regulation of nonlinear systems under uncertain parameters: the potential for linearization mismatch and the need for extensive model predictive banking. By developing a model-free reinforcement learning solution that learns to adapt to changing system parameters without requiring a comprehensive set of model predictions, our approach has minimized the number of required parameters and demonstrated improved flight stability and performance outcomes. Our work has further showcased the potential for online learning to enhance the robustness and stability of complex nonlinear system regulators through the reduction of performance limitations. Furthermore, our simulation tests have highlighted the practical applicability of our model-free reinforcement learning approach to real-world problems, with a potential cost savings of up to 15% in flight operations. In 2010, the SiD Detector was chosen as the reference detector for the ILC by the Detector Working Group for the International Linear Collider. The SiD concept, known for its robust silicon vertex detector and precise calorimeter, offered the best overall performance among the detector options at the time. The final SiD report was published in 2014, and the detector's development has since been based on the established design. The current study focuses on the calibration strategies employed with the SiD Detector, particularly with regard to its luminometer and inner tracker, and involves two key areas of research. Firstly, analysts tested various luminometer calibration methods using full simulation data and discovered that a Bayesian approach could accurately calculate the beam luminosity with minimal residual uncertainty. Secondly, designers explored alternative designs for the SiD's vertex tracker in response to rising technical challenges and proposed a new design featuring five sensitive layers, demonstrating the potential for improved performance and technical feasibility. The proposed tracker design is anticipated to yield better track quality and greater geometric stability for the SiD Detector. This research is expected to contribute to the ongoing development and preparation work for the SiD Detector. The study's findings on luminometer calibration contribute to a broader study evaluating various calibration methods, while the proposed tracker design could influence the detector's design in the future. The work on calibration and the tracker design serves as a demonstration of the necessary technical preparations for the SiD Detector. The study's results can be valuable for similar analyses of other detector concepts and may be relevant for future updates to the SiD Detector. The proposed tracker design is presented as a potential solution to the technical challenges facing the SiD concept, and further studies could investigate additional challenges and possible solutions for the detector. The luminometer calibration methods, particularly the Bayesian approach, can serve as an effective technique for the SiD Detector, and designers should be prepared to address variations in luminosity, and possibly other beam properties, during the actual detector commissioning. We present a new study on Tonantzintla 2 (Ton 2), a globular cluster located in the outer bulge of the Milky Way. A comprehensive analysis was conducted as part of the bulge cluster APOGEE2 Survey using the Vista Owl ground-based spectroscopic imaging technique, which revealed 307 member stars,  79 of which were previously unknown. Through a series of photometric and kinematic assessments, it was determined that Ton 2 is a relatively out-of-focus cluster with an intrinsic diameter of approximately 3 pc and a higher-than-ordinary variability range of k_mag = 0.42 mag. Additionally, it was calculated that Ton 2 possesses a metallicity range of -0.260 less than or equal to [Fe/H] less than or equal to -0.180 and an average [Fe/H] of approximately -0.220. Our research also discovered a low signal of variability members among the rich fields of Ton 2 by comparing the cluster's stars to a nearby field of non-hierarchical stars, which exhibited fewer variable stars and a distinctly perceptive difference in their semiamplitude distributions. Our findings suggest that Ton 2 is among the first documented cases of a globular cluster featuring an unusually high proportion of O-rich metallicity among its rich members. Our data and analysis are available online at unprecedented resolution, with a detailed kinematic map showcasing the cluster's motion and the distribution of its metal-rich stars. Our study paves the way for future research on the cluster's internal dynamics and the movement of its stars, which will continue to be observed through the APOGEE2 Survey. It is also anticipated that the Vista Owl telescope will continue to be instrumental in the precise detection of further variable stars in the rich fields of Ton 2 and other globular clusters. A step-by-step construction method is developed to formulate a simplified dynamical equation for a two-dimensional active nematic's direction, describing its behavior outside of equilibrium. By applying a dynamic rescaling technique and identifying the critical parameters, this study derives a universal flow chart that illustrates various regime transitions within active nematics. We investigate and classify the different ordered state patterns that can occur, such as the two-dimensional linear structure and the pucker structure, and provide a universal guide for identifying which pattern will dominate under specific conditions. Moreover, this study confirms that the parameter space area occupied by the two-dimensional linear pattern increases with increasing curvature in real-world active nematics. Furthermore, this study proposes the possibility of another type of ordered state pattern of unique characteristics in a limited critical parameter range. We investigate and explain the origin of this new pattern using a representation of the dynamic equation through scaling parameters. Our analysis provides a comprehensive and universal understanding of the dynamic behavior of active nematics and sheds light on their observed nonlinear patterns in real-world experiments. We also discuss and explore the connection between our derived universal flow chart and the linear stability analysis outcome. Lastly, this study confirms that the dynamic rescaling technique provides a direct link between the study of active nematics and other scaling systems by illustrating this connection through the derivation of the dynamic equation. We apply the dynamic rescaling technique to explore the underlying mechanism that drives the directional turnover, known as the flip phenomenon, in the active nematic's direction, and propose a universal understanding of this complex process based on critical parameters. Our analysis may offer new insights into the active nematics' direction's behavior, particularly the occurrence of directional instability and the existence of two stable and unstable regions for the flip phenomenon in a specific critical parameter range. Ultimately, this study confirms that the dynamic rescaling technique plays a pivotal role in uncovering the inherent mechanism of active nematics and their underlying symmetry breaking dynamics. Our work may provide a universal framework for understanding active nematics' behavior through the dynamic rescaling technique and the derived universal flow chart, promoting further research into the general active nematic model. Automated Visual Inspection, a prevalent topic in Int. Symp. on Robotics (ISR), often fails to account for complex patterns, typical of road damage analysis. We present a novel region-based anomaly detection framework, ReAD, designed to identify irregular road surfaces at an intermediate level of detail. By dividing the image into uniform regions and analyzing their collective occurrences, ReAD detects omissions and disruptions unique to specific road types. Leveraging a self-evolving region database, ReAD adapts to unforeseen scenarios and effectively handles instances where training samples are scarce. Performance on the CHRoad dataset reveals ReAD's superiority over existing methods and robust performance across various road types. The source code for ReAD can be accessed via https://github.com/Chen-0308/Regional_Anomaly_Detection. Comprehensive results and failure analyses are available at https://chen308.com/en/road-activity-embedding/. Visual representations of our method's results can be found on the above website or by searching for 'road activity embedding' in a search engine. This study evaluates several theoretical pion vector form factor models in an effort to determine the most suitable match for two-pion cross sections. The ultimate goal is to minimize uncertainty in calculations for two-pion contributions to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. By incorporating a polynomial representation of the pion vector form factor, our findings confirm that the Gounaris-Sakurai (or Kühn-Santamaria) model provides the best fit to experimental data within the 1 GeV range. Furthermore, our work allows for the extraction of the omega decay rate to pions as 1.52 percent with a margin of error, which aligns with Particle Data Group results. Utilizing the best fit to experimental data, our two-pion contribution calculation for the muon's anomalous magnetic moment yields (497.76±3.15) × 10^-10. The obtained result aligns with findings from other relevant studies. Our work also affirms that the presence of omega decay to pions has a notable influence on the two-pion contribution to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment number. Our final pion vector form factor fit is compatible with the work of Cappiello et al., while our two-pion contribution outcome is consistent with the findings from the PION2MUON analysis. Additionally, our study demonstrates that the presence of omega decay to pions lowers the estimated two-pion contribution to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment by approximately 0.5 × 10^-10. Our work also shows that the estimated omega decay rate to pions aligns with the work of other researchers, namely Aubert and Schaub. Lastly, our study reveals that the estimated omega decay rate to pions in the range of 1 GeV aligns with the work of the Particle Data Group, whereas a higher estimate was obtained from the Kühn-Santamaria model in the higher energy range. In conclusion, our contribution can be considered as an update or refinement of the PION2MUON result with an added emphasis on aligning with experimental data within the 1 GeV range. The abstrakt method in object-oriented programming ensures a virtual function in a base class can be overridden by a subclass, providing an ultimate implementation that can't be overridden further. This paper examines recent breakthroughs in program analysis, searching for a technique to identify all ways a virtual function can be implemented in an object, including cases beyond traditional inheritance. Ultimately, we outline a possible approach for a general code representation that could resolve this analysis. This paper is a foundation for future research in this area. Additionally, we suggest potential avenues for further investigation. Several examples illustrate our findings, available in full at abs-2207-002 on the arXiv server. Our analysis demonstrates how novel analyses can be applied to heritage structures composed of multiple inherited elements. Moreover, these results indicate the inheritability of program components is not restricted to traditional inheritance; rather, inheritability can arise through other object creation methods, such as delegation. The relation between a galaxy's mass in stars and its surrounding dark matter halo mass has been extensively studied, yet certain aspects of this relation remain unclear, specifically how star formation efficiency changes over time and how it depends on a galaxy's mass. By analyzing eight early-universe galaxy clusters from the Hubble Legacy Archive at different redshifts (1.22 to 1.84), we studied the masses and star formation efficiencies of galaxies within a specific range of masses ($\sim$10$^{9}$ to $10^{12}$ solar masses) and observed a consistent trend in star formation efficiency that increases with galaxy mass, a relationship that remains intact even when considering potential biases. Our findings are consistent with those of a simulation, which shows that more massive galaxies have more rapidly rotating gas in their halos, leading to higher star formation efficiency. Our study, which focuses on galaxies in clusters at high redshift, indicates that the mass-dependent relationship may persist into the distant universe, although further study is needed to see if this effect changes for galaxies in clusters and in the field. Our work as well highlights a need for a more diverse set of data, including galaxies with higher masses, to better understand this complex relationship. By assuming a linear evolution of mass-to-solar metallicity over time, we estimate that the slope of the mass-to-solar mass relationship at $z$ around 5 will be similar to its value at $z$ around 2. Conversely, if the slope does not change with time, then the relationship will become even more pronounced at higher redshifts. Our study, which focuses on galaxies that are more massive than others, may also hint at a non-evolving relationship at very high redshifts. Conversely, the slope of the relationship may become less pronounced at higher redshifts due to the greater prominence of massive, less-efficiently-forming galaxies. These predictions are based on our assumptions regarding metallicity evolution, and may change if we were to make different assumptions about it. Moreover, our study is likely to be affected by biases, particularly an underrepresentation of less-massive galaxies in our sample, and the limitations of our simple analysis, which does not account for various complex factors. If we were to analyze a more representative set of galaxies, our results might be different, and could change our understanding of the relationship between galaxy mass and its surrounding halo mass. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere's optical depth is a well-established concept, its application in detecting aerosols remains contentious due to unclear linkages between the observations and the aerosols' influence on the atmosphere's optical properties. In contrast, our research emphasizes the distinct effects of aerosols on the apparent brightness of stars through various wavelengths, supported by both theoretical and observational evidence from multiple sites. Notably, our study includes a new site in Puerto Rico, utilizing data from the ATmopheric CO2 Camera, which is an innovative device that leverages the difference in color between a yellow reference star and a blue target star to accurately calculate the atmospheric aerosol optical depth with high precision and a low level of error. Importing the algorithm previously developed for the Buddle Land camera into the ATCC camera has resulted in the aerosol optical depth obtained from the stellar photometry in the yellow and blue bands matching the accuracy of the co-located radiometers with an error of less than 0.05, which surpasses the error margin of 0.1 reported in a previous study using the Buddle Land camera's algorithm. In particular, our research reveals a relationship between the aerosols' influence on the apparent brightness of stars in the yellow and blue bands and their respective optical depths, as well as the effect of the solar zenith angle and aerosols with varying sizes on the atmosphere's optical properties. Furthermore, our data show that the aerosols' influence on the apparent brightness of stars in the yellow and blue bands exhibit seasonal variations in the Northern Hemisphere, which can be attributed to the changes in the atmosphere's aerosol optical depth throughout the year. Additionally, our research indicates that the error margin for calculating the aerosol optical depth using the ATCC camera is significantly lower than that of the Buddle Land camera, particularly when combining data from multiple sites, and that the error margin can be further reduced by incorporating data from the Buddle Land camera into the analysis. In summary, our research demonstrates that the aerosol optical depth can be accurately calculated using the stellar photometry in the yellow and blue bands with high precision and a low level of error, and that the aerosol's influence on the apparent brightness of stars in the yellow and blue bands is closely linked to their respective optical depths, which in turn affects the accuracy of atmospheric characterization. These findings enable the development of a novel algorithm that can accurately calculate the aerosol optical depth using the stellar photometry in the yellow and blue bands, which is likely to pave the way for widespread applications

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to efficiently perform Universal Graphical Lasso (UGL) on various data types, including time series, image, and scalar data. UGL extends Graphical Lasso to handle complex relationships among multiple variables. GGLasso enables fast UGL optimization through a C implementation and offers a range of features and flexible node representations to facilitate scalable learning. The package comes with documentation and example code for data analysis tasks, such as noise reduction in images and resampling of multiple time series, which can be extended to real-time applications like stream processing. GGLasso has been tested on diverse datasets, including open-source data, and is compatible with CPUs and GPUs under Python 3.x. It has a flexible design, allowing for easy extension and modification of existing features via the CTensor class. The package's flexibility also facilitates the learning of complex models, such as multiple-variable interactions, through the implementation of a novel Graphical Lasso variant. The GGLasso package is freely available on GitHub under the permissive MIT License. The repository includes the package's source code, as well as sample data used in the documentation. We develop a theoretical model for the gas dynamics and electron density in the TW Hydrae young stellar object's disk and environment, leveraging observations from ALMA to calculate the free-free radiation in its circumstellar space. By combining this with the current radio continuum data, we extract the electron density and obtain constraints on the photoevaporation model and MHD disk wind theory. The photoevaporation model yields electron densities that align with measured values at larger distances from the star (around 10-20 cm^-1) but exceeds ALMA's detection limits at closer distances. Conversely, the disk wind model produces lower electron densities at shorter distances, offering a more accurate explanation of the observed trends. Nevertheless, both the photoevaporation and wind models fall short of fully explaining the observed patterns, suggesting that other factors, such as magnetospheric accretion, could contribute to the observed patterns at close distances to the star. The future radio telescopes like the Next Generation Very Large Array are expected to detect the radio emission up to 10 AU from the star, providing crucial insights into the disk wind or photoevaporation theory in its innermost reaches. Moreover, the low-free-free emission at short distances could be complemented by other thermal components, potentially free electrons from the wind or magnetosphere, in the radio spectrum. The estimated electron density at short distances also implies the presence of over-dense plasma in the wind or magnetosphere. The predicted free-free emission at 1 AU from the star suggests a significant contribution from the magnetosphere if it follows a radial density distribution. The future radio telescopes like the Next Generation Very Large Array are expected to detect the photoevaporation or wind theory in action in TW Hydrae's environment, offering valuable insights into its disk environment. Moreover, the distinction between photoevaporation and wind could be revealed through polarization observations of the free-free emission, a prospect that these future telescopes will make a reality. The electron density in TW Hydrae's environment may also hold the key to understanding the planet formation process, as its value at close distances could indicate the presence of charged particles in the planet's vicinity. Similarly, the wind theory's prediction of a more neutral environment at close distances to the star may also be relevant to the planet formation process, offering a more subdued environment for planet development. For speech processing applications, tasks such as speech voicing, pitch detection, and speech synthesis require efficient and accurate voicing units as a core component. Traditional methods for voicing units rely heavily on statistical models like Hidden Markov Models, which train on labeled data to recognize voicing patterns. However, this paper explores an unsupervised approach to identifying voicing units by analyzing pitch as the primary feature, and a novel HMM-based model is proposed that integrates a forward-backward Kalman filter to refine pitch tracking. Kalman filtering enhances low-resolution pitch data to a higher resolution, and when applied to an unsupervised HMM model, this approach is shown to effectively filter out noise in voicing detection and pitch tracking, and outperforms existing methods in several metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/SunNLP-PLS/Unsupervised-voicing-pitch detection. Experimental results confirm that the proposed method achieves improved voicing detection and pitch tracking accuracy in multiple languages, and a case study demonstrates its practical applications in speech synthesis. Additionally, this paper assumes voicing units to be musical tones, but the method can also be applied to other types of voicing units. An efficient and accurate unsupervised voicing detection and pitch tracking method is presented that integrates a forward-backward Kalman filter, and this approach is shown to be effective in various speech processing applications. An analysis of the method's performance is also provided, and it is confirmed that it outperforms existing techniques in several metrics. Furthermore, a case study is presented that examines its practical applications, and it is demonstrated that the method achieves improved results in voicing detection and pitch tracking, and a variation of the method is proposed for speech synthesis. As a result, this approach is considered to be an effective addition to the field of speech processing. This paper introduces a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), to tackle a broad class of monotone inclusion problems. By leveraging forward-backward splitting, DWIFOB effectively tackles composite monotone inclusion problems. Furthermore, when applied to dual approaches, it yields an efficient solution to a wide range of optimization challenges. Building on the success of the weighted inertial forward-backward (WIFB) method, DWIFOB enhances it with more substantial step sizes, making it particularly suitable for smooth monotone inclusion problems. Additionally, DWIFOB maintains step-size independence and does not require exact solution of sub-problems, thus significantly broadening its applicability. Our research demonstrates that DWIFOB converges optimistically under certain conditions and consistently outperforms WIFB in numerical tests. Key code is accessible via an open-source repository at https://github.com/molgo-DWIFOB/DWIFOB. Mathematically equivalent terminology used in this research includes proximal, dual, primal-dual, and monotone inclusion problems. Optimization problems are also encompassed within this study, along with backward-forward splitting (BFS), weighted inertial forward-backward (WIFB), and forward-backward splitting (FBS). Finally, although some results and algorithms re-present findings from reference [27], the conclusions and numerical assessments are original. With respect to prior work, DWIFOB presents a revised, robust version of the weighted inertial forward-backward (WIFB) method, along with a theoretically supported iteration scheme, which involves larger step sizes, maintaining step-size independence, and necessitating less exact solution of sub-problems. This research takes place within the Next-to-Minimal extension of the Standard Model (NMSSM), expanded by a minimal set of dimensions higher than four, namely the reverse seesaw mechanism. We investigate the influence of quadratic divergences on Higgs masses in this framework, incorporating corrections from loops within the model's kinetic equilibrium. We discover that these corrections can lead to a substantial modification of the light Higgs mass, potentially bringing it into alignment with current experimental measurements. Moreover, we observe that certain constraints arising from the Higgs sector can be alleviated through the introduction of loop corrections, allowing for a more expansive range of model parameters. We also examine how certain loop-corrected constraints are influenced by the value of the kinetic parameter $\xi$ and the volume of the extra dimension, $M_D^2$. This expansion of the model's parameter space due to loop corrections presents an interesting opportunity for exploring it in detail with future experimental data. We also report on the development of the code, named \textit{NMSSMCALC}, that was used to carry out the computations in this study and can be expanded to evaluate the effects of additional physics beyond the Standard Model. Furthermore, we compute loop-corrected decays of the lightest CP-even Higgs boson within pure NMSSM and find notable differences with existing predictions. This work can serve as a valuable resource for analyzing the properties of the Higgs boson in its various configurations within the extended NMSSM. Based on these observations, we propose that future experiments should focus on the $hh\to b\bar{b}\gamma\gamma$ process to the lowest order in the couplings, to distinguish between the SM and the extended NMSSM. Automatically discovering neural networks that conform to specific requirements is a difficult task, which can be simplified by breaking it down into two sub-problems: (1) defining a set of relevant network characteristics and (2) creating a search strategy that utilizes these characteristics to guide the synthesis of conforming networks. In this paper, we focus on developing a search algorithm that utilizes a characterization of neural networks via hyperparameters and their corresponding performances, with the goal of finding a conforming network within a specified hyperparameter space. Three effective search strategies are presented, along with the implementation details and the utilization of these characterizations in the context of image classification and super-resolution tasks. The provided code can be used to replicate the results presented in this paper, which demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed search algorithms in targeting specific network characteristics while avoiding others that may hinder performance. The presented characterizations and search algorithms offer versatile tools for neural architecture synthesis and the development of more sophisticated optimization algorithms. Furthermore, the paper investigates the feasibility of targeting specific dataset-specific features, such as scaling and shifting, which can impact the performance of neural networks. A novel synthesis algorithm, HyperNet, is introduced, which employs a characterization of neural networks through hyperparameters and their corresponding performances to guide the architecture search. HyperNet encompasses three search strategies, each utilizing a different characterization: the Feature Map Analyzer, which analyzes feature maps to determine the used network parameters; the Phase Component Analyzer, which decodes the phase of network weights to infer used parameters; and the HyperNet optimizer, which utilizes a characterization of network performances through hyperparameters, with the goal of targeting specific features while avoiding others that may hinder performance. The paper examines the efficacy of these search strategies in image classification and super-resolution tasks, which require different feature maps and phase components to achieve optimal performance. Specifically, the paper investigates the correlation between phase component analysis and feature map analysis in the context of super-resolution tasks, which can be utilized to guide the search for conforming networks. The presented results offer a characterization of the stability of phase component analysis and feature map analysis, which can be utilized to guide the search for conforming networks in future studies. Furthermore, the paper investigates the utilization of HyperNet optimizer in feature map analyzer and phase component analyzer to guide the search for conforming networks, which can target specific features while avoiding others that may hinder performance. In mmWave systems, designing an efficient encoding scheme is critical for minimizing overhead in multicasting settings. This paper introduces a new hybrid encoding approach called HHE, which combines combinations of binary and multi-level encoding schemes. Specifically, HHE incorporates the BHE and MBE schemes mentioned in literature. By hybridizing these encoding methods, HME offers improved performance and increased flexibility in terms of codeword length. This paper evaluates HME from various perspectives, including its encoding complexity, scalability, and resilience to errors. Notably, HME outperforms BHE and MBE schemes in terms of overall overhead under various multicasting scenarios. HME achieves this improvement through dynamic code-length balancing and a more effective binary encoding mechanism. This research provides a thorough analysis of HME and showcases its ability to reduce overhead in multicasting settings, particularly in diverse mmWave systems where data is transmitted through multiple frequency subchannels. HME's performance is evaluated across a range of scenarios, including a scenario where a single user is targeted and another where multiple users are involved, highlighting its versatility and applicability in various multicasting contexts. A growing concern with Federated Learning is data privacy, specifically the potential for a malicious server to deceive clients about the learning process. Existing research focuses on protecting client data from the server's malicious activities, but this study addresses a less explored issue: a server's efforts to deceive clients and manipulate the Federated Learning outcome. We investigate two primary threats: (1) the server's attempt to boost its own bias without affecting client data, and (2) the server's attempt to distort client updates without revealing any information about the clients' data. We establish key requirements for these threats, create a realistic Federated Learning framework by combining Federated Optimization and Federated Learning, and tackle the second threat through a communication-efficient protocol called Federated Extraction. This protocol relies on a trust-worthy client and aims to increase the server's efficiency in achieving its objective while minimizing communication overhead. We examine various defense methods against the server's malicious activities, evaluate their effectiveness, and provide a performance analysis of the proposed protocol. The results show that Federated Extraction outperforms existing research and provides a more efficient solution in communication-intensive Federated Learning scenarios. The code for this research is available at https://github.com:ghejelajela:FE. Additionally, the computational resources used for this research were provided by the University of Kentucky's Center for Computational Science. More information about the computational resources can be found at https://c3.uky.edu. This study contributes to the area of Federated Learning by providing a novel threat model and a communication-efficient protocol to address a malicious server's attempts to deceive clients. We also provide a comprehensive evaluation of the server's malicious activities and existing research, along with a performance comparison of various defense methods. Moreover, this study provides a detailed analysis of the server's degree of freedom and achieves a balance between efficiency and honesty through the Federated Extraction protocol. Finally, this study provides a direct comparison of the server's malicious activities with a real-world Federated Learning implementation. A key feature of Named Data Networking (NDN) is its ability to enable user-centric computing, and this can be further enhanced through a mechanism that manages user requests for specific data, effectively implementing a resource coordination algorithm. This coordination could variously aim to optimize costs, achieve fair distribution, or ensure the highest possible quality of service, all of which could be crucial considerations in certain computing applications. Given that user requests arrive according to a Poisson process and each request is processed independently with an exponentially distributed duration, the resource coordination problem amounts to a quasi-regenerative stochastic optimization challenge. We propose an optimal dynamic programming solution for this problem, and due to the high computational requirements of this method, we also suggest two simpler alternative solutions: a model-predictive-control approach and an approximation scheme. Through numerical evaluations, we compare the performance of these solutions, and while the dynamic programming method yields the best results, the approximation scheme offers a balance between simplicity and performance that makes it a viable option. Furthermore, our results indicate that a fair-distribution approach with the model-predictive-control strategy could provide an optimal solution, and this option could be a practical choice for the resource coordination problem. These findings contribute to our understanding of the resource coordination problem and can help inform the design of a management system for a NDN-based computing network. Additionally, due to the generality of our approach, this result can potentially be applied to other domains. The code and figures for this research are publicly available at a specified repository. This research has been funded through a grant from the Natural Science and Engineering Research Council (NSERC). We appreciate this support.

Investigations into the electronic properties of materials with a chemical formula MTl$_4$Te$_3$ (where M is a cadmium or mercury element) revealed that these materials exhibit characteristics of a topological insulator. With a notable gap size of approximately 0.45 eV, these materials feature one electron attached to a mercury or cadmium atom and four electrons attached to a thallium atom, forming a 1-2-4 type crystal structure. Utilizing an asymptotic perturbation approach in the effective mass approximation, researchers were able to calculate the total energy and show that these materials become topological insulators due to the presence of a gap within the bulk material's band structure. Comparing results from different approaches (density functional theory using generalized gradient approximation and hybrid functional) to each other, researchers found that these properties remain consistent across both cadmium and mercury compounds. Additionally, potential applications of these materials were considered. Finally, researchers concluded that these materials could potentially be transformed into stable 2D materials through the application of surface pressure, which would result in the mercury or cadmium atom detaching from the surface, leaving behind a thallium atom. This could result in the creation of a stable 2D topological insulator. With a calculated band gap size of approximately 0.80 eV for a 2D MTl$_3$ material, these materials could exhibit superior performance in various applications. This could enable their utilization in the development of advanced 2D devices, which would be crucial in advancing the field of spintronics. Furthermore, researchers found that these materials (when in a 2D state) might exhibit ferromagnetic properties at low temperatures if treated with surface pressure. This could result in the emergence of unique magnetic properties in these 2D topological insulators. In conclusion, researchers considered various properties of these materials and concluded that they would likely exhibit unique properties as both 3D and 2D topological insulators. A crucial task in multi-objective optimization is obtaining an accurate utility function that aligns with a human expert's preferences, essential for solving complex problems with conflicting goals. Traditional utility function learning methods are often time-consuming and unreliable because they necessitate extensive expert input and are sensitive to noise. To address these challenges, we have developed a novel utility function learning framework that incorporates several effective strategies. This approach enables the utilization of incomplete and possibly noisy expert knowledge while optimizing the utility function's parameters. By leveraging prior expert knowledge, such as commonly agreed-upon rankings and tolerance levels, the utility function can be refined without necessitating direct input from the expert. Furthermore, the framework is capable of estimating the utility function's reliability based on historical rankings and noise levels, facilitating the selection of an appropriate tolerance level. We evaluate our proposed framework on multiple benchmark functions and compare it to existing methods, demonstrating that it achieves superior results and avoids generating impractical utility functions. This approach is versatile and can be applied to a broad range of multi-objective optimization domains. The source code is available at https://github.com/JUEE2018/UFL.git. Experimental data can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.6086/M4OEM.README.1.0. This research is part of a larger study on utility function learning for multi-objective optimization (see DOI: 10.6086/M4OEM.REPORT.1.0). Reinforcement learning agents can be vulnerable in certain situations. A potential threat comes from an adversary who can manipulate the environment, leading to unpredictable consequences, including agent malfunction and exploitation of sensitive information. There's a notable absence of attacks that utilize a agent's long-term memory in RL settings, focusing instead on short-term manipulations. This technique allows for tuning the Dirac points without compromising their integrity. In risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) with an exponential risk measure, we study an approach for finding near-optimal policies in changing environments. The setting involves reward functions that vary over time with unknown dynamics, and our approach adapts to various reward families without prior knowledge. We introduce a new family of policies, called switchback policies, and demonstrate their effectiveness through a finite-time analysis. The results establish a near-optimal gap between policy performance and the best response to changing reward conditions. We also show that a small number of exploratory steps within a finite horizon are sufficient to ensure our approach remains close to the optimal policy. The key technical achievement involves extending the one-step look-ahead principle to adapt to evolving environments, and proving that our approach leads to a reduction in dynamic regret. The latter result leverages the risk-sensitive MDP's monotonicity in its parameter, and connects it to sample efficiency through a novel analysis. The concept of risk isolation also plays a crucial role in adapting to unknown reward families. The findings of this work lead to three important insights: (i) sample efficiency can be understood through dynamic regret, (ii) the identification of reward families can be decoupled from adaptation and policy design, and (iii) the last issue of adapting to reward families can be tackled through data collection. The ideas and methods developed in this study can be applied to various RL tasks in simulation, and further empirical evaluation is anticipated to confirm these insights. The novel theoretical results and insights may also find practical application in areas such as bandit learning and sequential decision-making under uncertainty. The work described here makes three specific contributions: (i) it establishes a connection between sample efficiency and dynamic regret, (ii) it identifies and analyzes the underlying causes of difficulty in adapting to reward families, and (iii) it presents a range of design options for the class of risk-sensitive RL problems. Decentralized machine learning applications such as autonomous driving and drone operation could benefit from distributed machine learning (DML) over dynamically changing networks. Yet, standard weighted arithmetic mean aggregation in current DML systems may lead to considerable model inaccuracies and slow convergence speeds over fluctuating networks. In this paper, we introduce a new family of nonlinear aggregation functions to improve DML efficiency in networks with variable bandwidth. Our model utilizes a nonlinear weighted power mean aggregation approach rather than the linear aggregation typically used by previous studies. By utilizing a nonlinear aggregation technique, our approach allows for efficient distribution of the training load and efficient data communication among network nodes, while also achieving faster convergence of the model in comparison to linear aggregation methods. Furthermore, we have developed a new aggregation technique based on a nonlinear weighted power mean and proved its correctness in the context of distributed stochastic gradient descent. The results of our experiments demonstrate that the proposed model yields up to 2 times faster convergence speeds and up to 10 times more efficient resource use compared to standard linear aggregation methods. The code used for conducting these experiments can be accessed via our GitHub repository at: https://github.com/DK-19/dml-aggregation.git. Additionally, the demonstration of our model can be viewed via this link: https://github.com/DK-19/dml-aggregation/blob/main/dml-aggregation-demo.ipynb. Note that the model has now been released under an open-source license and is available for public use. The model has been documented in the paper titled "Efficient Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent with Non-Linear Aggregation", which has been published in the proceedings of the 2021 ACM IEEE International Conference on Distributed Computing Systems. The details regarding deployment of the model in real-world applications can be obtained via an appendix to the paper, which can be accessed via the link provided: Efficient Deployment of the Model in Real-World Applications - Appendix.pdf. Alternatively, the model can also be contacted via email at: [dk19@gmail.com](mailto:dk19@gmail.com) for further details regarding deployment in practical scenarios. A vision for integrated quantum computing and quantum information processing lies in creating a unified chip that can handle various tasks such as trapping, manipulating, and reading unique qubit states. To bring this vision to life, our research presents an innovative optical design featuring multiple grating structures, enabling the integration of atom trapping, manipulation through optical tweezers, and a high-resolution addressable array for reading qubit states. The design offers optical levitation in multiple directions with high stability, a trapped atom's location identifiable across the grid due to distinct laser addresses, and a sensitive detection of Rydberg states achieved through focus adjustment. The effectiveness of this design is confirmed by experimental results showing its effectiveness in a quartz chip for levitating atoms and accurately detecting Rydberg states, a crucial step towards integrated quantum computing and quantum information processing. The presented design serves as a fundamental building block for complex integrated photonics used in quantum computing and could be further adapted for various applications like quantum simulation, linear optics, and other cutting-edge technologies. Additionally, this research provides a framework for developing advanced optical interconnects that can be used in various high-performance applications due to its low loss rate and fine focusing capability. The findings suggest that multi-grating structures can offer excellent performance as optical interconnects over large distances, up to 10 cm as demonstrated in this study, making them suitable for the quantum applications of the future. The integration of this design with Rydberg quantum processing provides a potentially highly scalable platform for large-scale and on-chip quantum computing. The presented concept of multi-grating structures could also be applied to various other fields such as sensing, metrology, and communication, enabling innovative applications with extensive technical merit. The combined functionality of this design including single-photon emission, focus adjustment, and Rydberg state detection in a unique location presents an attractive solution for the successful implementation of Rydberg quantum computing and other complex quantum applications. The research presents an in-depth analysis of the design's performance through simulations and confirms the results with impressive experimental outcomes, a key step towards developing highly scalable and on-chip quantum computers. The study makes an important contribution in advancing integrated quantum computing and could pave the way for a more robust single-photon source used in quantum computing and other cutting-edge applications. A technique combining linear regression and mixed-integer programming is proposed as a efficient method for accurately modeling polymer composition. This modeling approach is particularly suitable for large-scale polymer production, where even minor ingredient deviations can significantly affect the final product's properties and quality. However, this method's primary limitation is its inability to infer polymer composition solely based on a sample's Molecular Weight Distribution and NMR data. To overcome this challenge, an algorithm is designed, incorporating a novel formulation for solving a linear regression problem in a sparse matrix, thus inferring the polymer composition with minimal parameters. This proposed algorithm has been successfully tested using simulated data. More comprehensive testing with real-world data from various polymer sources is necessary to validate this approach. Additionally, the inference of multiple structured polymers presents an intricate problem, akin to solving a sparse regression issue in a multidimensional space. This polymer inference problem may be cast as a sparse optimization problem, with applications in medicine and nutrition. However, polymer inference in the relevant industry is typically conducted using only a handful of parameters, and further research is required to establish a reliable and industry-compatible method. This method could be refined by leveraging industrial knowledge through techniques like parameter pruning and feature scaling, thereby isolating key components and quantifying their relative importance. Future research will focus on resolving discrepancies between industrial expertise and the purely data-driven approach of sparse optimization, with an aim to develop a fully informed solution. Finally, novel algorithms for solving specific optimization problems, such as the L1 norm minimization in a positive matrix, are also presented. These optimization algorithms, developed in conjunction with the polymer inference technique, have previously been presented separately. However, their associated papers have since been withdrawn due to issues with replicating the proposed methods. To address these concerns, the current work offers an alternative formulation of the algorithms, thereby providing a clearer and more concise description of the proposed approach. This revised approach is then demonstrated using previously generated data, with an additional simulation also included to illustrate its efficacy. Lastly, the relevant industry is invited to collaborate in fine-tuning the proposed algorithm to better reflect their specific knowledge and expertise. This collaborative effort is particularly necessary due to the notable differences between the industry's understanding of polymer inference and the algorithm's data-driven approach, with the industry's perspective initially presented in a companion paper and the algorithm's perspective detailed in the withdrawn papers and revisited here. More specifically, the industry's perspective emphasizes the difficulty and cost associated with inferring multiple structured polymers, whereas the algorithm's perspective highlights the significant improvements that can be achieved through sparse regression

A rational map $f$ from the Riemann sphere to itself is considered bicritical if it has precisely two points where the derivative is zero. This paper explores the collections, called deck clusters, of preimages under the iterations of such maps, which can be computed using the maps' singularities, and it is demonstrated that these deck clusters cover the entire Riemann sphere with finite, connected areas except in the case of the maps that are bicritical with one singular point, for which the coverage is partial. A notable result is that every finite set of points on the Riemann sphere is contained within a deck cluster of iterates of an appropriate bicritical map. Furthermore, it is shown that the sets of preimages of certain points under iterates form sequences of increasing complexity that ultimately repeat in a pattern, and it is proven that these sequences converge to a particular value or tend towards infinity. The "empirical Bayes" method is a well-established approach for generating these prior distributions, called empirical priors, through maximum likelihood estimation.
However, this method may exhibit biased results, especially in the presence of a small number of observations and a large number of predictors, which can be characterized as a small sample size (n) and a large number of predictors (p).
In this research, we establish high-dimensional properties of empirical priors for linear regression models under various scenarios in terms of sample size and the ratio of predictors to observations.
The results show that for sufficiently large sample sizes, the empirical priors behave asymptotically as their corresponding maximum likelihood estimators, which is a beneficial property.
Furthermore, we investigate the performance of a Bayesian estimator based on these empirical priors and demonstrate that it achieves optimal results, close to an unbiased minimum variance estimator, which is often difficult to obtain directly due to its complex form under the given high-dimensional conditions.
The findings are supported by numerical simulations, which show that the performance of the empirical priors and the associated Bayesian estimator exhibits small errors compared to the optimal estimator, thereby validating their utilization as a practical substitute for the optimal estimator. The methods and results presented in this research can be applied to a broader range of problems beyond linear regression, extending the empirical Bayes method more widely into the context of high-dimensional data analysis. The findings are documented in the paper "Empirical priors in high-dimensional linear regression with unknown variance" published at arxiv, and the R code for replicating the simulations is available through the link ugazio.unibert.ch/~krambrou/Supplement_2022_01.html. The spectral dimension of a weighted graph is an exponent that describes the local space-time properties. It's defined as the exponent that makes the graph's heat equation approximate a free diffusion process. This concept was introduced over a decade ago by Wenwong and colleagues. In contrast, the conformal dimension of a weighted graph is an exponent that characterizes a scale-invariant property. This notion was developed more recently by Grohn and colleagues.

We demonstrate that the conformal dimension of a weighted graph is equal to or less than twice the spectral dimension, providing a significant upper bound. This outcome is validated through specific examples, which show that the upper bound is not always strict. The examples also illustrate a relationship between the conformal dimension and the spectral dimension on a particular type of weighted graph, called a self-similar directed system. The examples also illustrate a relationship between the conformal dimension and the Ahlfors-regular conformal dimension of a weighted graph, which is an earlier concept introduced by Grohn and colleagues.

By incorporating eta-prime-eta mixing into the meson's propagator, we evaluate the corrections to the bound. Based on this process, we develop a finite on-shell condition for the kappa variable, which governs the mass of the etashowpr. The newly derived condition effectively eliminates unphysical solutions, thereby facilitating the direct determination of the physical eta mass from the reshaken unitarity bound. The etashowpr's mass, which arises from the radial mode, also undergoes correction due to eta-prime-eta mixing. The strength of these corrections can be significant, amounting to a roughly 400 MeV modification to the physical eta mass. Similarly, we also calculate the corrections affecting the Upsilon particle in the context of heavy quark effective theory. The incorporation of eta-prime-eta mixing into the eta-prime propagator yields an on-shell condition for the Higgs parameter, which emerges as a solution to the Callan-Johnson type consistency conditions. The conditions thereby enable us to investigate various higher-dimension operators that could potentially impact the long-distance behavior of the Upsilon particle. Biometric templates hold sensitive personal information and must be securely stored. Research has demonstrated that the uniqueness of these templates is not sufficient to guarantee authentication, highlighting the need for additional metrics such as complexity and reliability. These metrics assess the uniqueness and recollection of a signature over time, thus evaluating the overall reliability of a signature system. This study applies those metrics to an online signature system, providing empirical evidence for the first time. Our analysis reveals that while our system excels in terms of uniqueness, it falls short in terms of complexity, making it susceptible to imitation. Furthermore, our results show that our system is reasonably reliable in terms of recollection, reducing the risk of false authentications. Our contribution lies in introducing new metrics for evaluating the reliability of biometric templates and applying them to an actual online signature system. Additionally, we provide a framework that researchers can utilize to assess the reliability of their own biometric systems. Our findings encourage the exploration of alternative feature sets for enhanced security and reliability. The source code is available at https://github.com/VFSM/Online_Signature_Templates. Our dataset can be accessed through https://dx.doi.org/10.21253/COMP-2022001.0.

We investigated four-point amplitude calculations in the most fundamental string theory examples featuring T-fold backgrounds with six supersymmetries. These theories are represented as two asymmetric orbifold versions, one of order two and the other of order three. We demonstrated that the derivations of higher-derivative terms in the amplitude factors in such a background are compatible with each other and the results from Novikov self-dual (NSD) theories. Furthermore, we discovered that the relationship between the amplitude factors and the NSD solutions is not restricted to the six-derivative terms but also extends to the eight-derivative terms. Additionally, we discussed the derivation of the amplitude factors at lower-derivative levels using the Gomperth-Mueckenhaupt procedure in the two-fold orbifold case. We verified that the results are equivalent to the amplitude factors derived from the NSD solutions through a transformation, similar to the one applied to the six-derivative terms. Multilingual individuals possess knowledge of multiple languages, acquiring and employing them throughout their lives, with code-mixing occurring when elements of one language are incorporated into another. Code-mixing gives rise to unique textual characteristics, reflecting societal factors such as education, geography, and age. Establishing effective pre-trained models for code-mixing languages poses a significant challenge due to limited data availability, poor performance of models trained on separate languages, and the ambiguity of code-mixed corpora. To tackle these issues, research into code-mixing needs to address topics like data standardisation, enhanced pre-trained models, and improved computational methodologies. This paper examines the concerns and obstacles associated with handling code-mixing languages, and proposes potential solutions to these problems. Additionally, it highlights the scope of future research in this domain, and explores the practical implications of developing effective models for societal applications. Furthermore, it shares valuable insights and lessons learned from past initiatives, and offers guidance on pursuing similar projects in the future. Finally, it presents an accessible data repository of code-mixing languages, along with associated metadata, to facilitate future research and collaboration. This paper seeks to stimulate a broader discussion among NLP researchers on tackling code-mixing, an intricate phenomenon requiring careful consideration of societal factors. Ultimately, it highlights the potential for NLP to make a positive, beneficial impact on multilingual communities. The advent of graphical interface editors and version control systems has facilitated collaborative software maintenance by providing a record of changes made to a code base over time. By enabling the identification of previously modified files in a project, many meta-maintenance methods have emerged that can leverage this historical information to inform current maintenance tasks. Despite their potential, many developers remain unaware of these techniques. To investigate the feasibility of applying meta-maintenance methods in real-world scenarios, an empirical study was conducted to compare the effectiveness of two maintenance methods - a search-based method and a randomised method - in identifying active files from a sample of 1.2 million GitHub repositories. The findings indicate that approximately 50% of developers already employ a maintenance method similar to search-based maintenance, while a significant 75% of repositories could potentially benefit from using such a maintenance method. The analysis further reveals that which maintenance method is most suitable varies depending on factors such as programming languages used, maintenance tasks, and previous modifications made to the code. The actual meta-maintenance method used could also impact these findings. The study's results highlight the practical implications of these findings for developers working on GitHub, suggesting that search-based maintenance may be a more effective approach than randomised maintenance in many cases. The empirical evaluation follows a rigorous methodology, with findings generalisable thanks to the large dataset of GitHub repositories analysed. The study's design addresses two specific research questions, while opening the possibility for further investigations into the application of meta-maintenance methods in other settings. The empirical evaluation itself constitutes a novel contribution, shedding light on the characteristics of real-world software evolution and the dynamics of repository modification over time. The study demonstrates the feasibility and practicality of applying meta-maintenance methods in actual development environments. The results could prompt developers to explore the use of meta-maintenance methods in future maintenance tasks.
