This study focuses on initial data sets that meet specific conditions and can be described by a Yamabe invariant. Unifying past research, including Fujita and Skowronski's work on nonlinear differential equations, Monge-Ampere equations, and the behavior of conformal factors under the fractional Yamabe evolution, we demonstrate the convergence of this evolution for such data sets. Furthermore, we analyze the singularity's behavior and establish an inequality for its growth in positive-time regimes. Our findings also provide insights into the invariant's behavior under the fractional Yamabe evolution and show that it remains non-degenerate and bounded. Importantly, our work has implications for the invariant's convergence, which we demonstrate along with the convergence of the fractional Yamabe evolution. Our analysis relies heavily on the established regularity results and the properties of the Yamabe invariant, as well as an essential inequality that arises from the parabolic maximum principle. Ultimately, our findings enhance our understanding of the positive-time behavior of the fractional Yamabe evolution and the invariant, which are pivotal components in the convergence process. The results presented here are part of a broader research endeavor, led by the second-named author, which aims to develop a rigorous framework for the fractional Yamabe flow and the invariant, as well as establish their convergence and the invariant's behavior through energy estimates. This study is a key component in building this framework and serves to complement previously published research on the subject. Specifically, it is a companion paper to [22], which focuses on the smooth initial data and builds upon the work of Daskalopoulos and Vazquez [10], while also providing an alternative approach to the results of Colombo and Wang [7] for $q\in (0,1]$. Additionally, this study is a foundation for future research that will focus on the stability of the conformally rescaled metrics and the invariant, as well as the extension of the results to the presence of non-compact conformal factors. Recent advancements in deep reinforcement learning have led to superior performance in numerous control tasks. Nonetheless, deep reinforcement learning can exhibit several drawbacks, including a lengthy time requirement to achieve convergence and an inability to adapt to variations in the control system's architecture. A novel technique, two-staged deep reinforcement learning, addresses these limitations by integrating a preliminary stage that employs a simplified model to quickly obtain efficient control methods, which can then be refined through detailed analysis in the secondary stage, focusing on improving low-level details of the control strategy. A corresponding algorithm and several experimental case studies are presented to demonstrate the efficacy of this method. Moreover, a theoretical assessment of the algorithm's convergence is provided. A comparative study with state-of-the-art methods reveals that it surpasses them significantly in terms of speed and adaptability, while also presenting promising results in improving the overall performance of the control strategies. Furthermore, a practical implementation of the method is demonstrated through its application on a real-world industrial problem. As such, two-staged deep reinforcement learning emerges as a vital tool for tackling complex control problems. High-entropy alloys, by merging multiple elements in roughly the same proportion, exhibit unique properties that deliver increased strength with minimal deterioration in ductility. Yet, their ground-state electronic behavior, particularly their electron localization, remains poorly understood. We believe that leveraging machine learning models, given their efficiency in forecasting materials properties, can uncover key aspects of HEsAs electronic nature. We utilize a neural network to investigate the heuristic potential in predicting a Heusler alloy's crystal structure, phase stability, and mechanical properties. These tasks prove manageable with a relatively small reference database of 7 Heusler HEsAs, though we note that larger collections of diverse HEsAs would significantly enhance the reliability and generalizability of these predictions. Additionally, incorporating more element types into the dataset is expected to yield greater benefits, thereby facilitating the large-scale search for promising HEsAs through an automated, algorithm-driven process. With a growing dataset, machine learning models can help identify hidden patterns within the composition of Heusler HEsAs, thereby potentially discovering new, promising candidates. We envision a future scenario in which artificial intelligence, trained on extensive knowledge of materials behavior, will govern the design of high-entropy materials, ultimately empowering the development of advanced materials with long-wavelength radiation. Furthermore, by applying deep learning to the extended HEsAs database, we can uncover the underlying correlations between atomic number, electron density, and lattice parameters, demonstrating that this technique can analyze large datasets of diverse materials to reveal functional relationships. We hope that our work will stimulate further research in this area, ultimately leading to breakthroughs in materials design through the AI-assisted discovery of high-entropy materials. To facilitate future advancements, we provide the code and dataset used in this research through public resources for the benefit of the materials community.

The measure of a vector-valued function's nonlinearity is essentially at its minimum when the function equals a vector that has the least number of non-zero components possible. This paper investigates functions that are as nonlinear as possible while also being part of a slim Sidon sequence, which is a relatively sparse multivariate function family with unique properties. By identifying properties of such functions, we are able to determine a lower bound on the nonlinearity of vector Boolean functions and show that this bound is achievable in certain cases. Additionally, we present an open problem related to a property of slim Sidon sequences, as well as an easily verifiable criterion for identifying a vector Boolean function with maximum nonlinearity. This research further delves into characteristics of near-Sidon sequences, which are multivariate function families with unique properties, and presents a counterexample disproving an earlier conjecture related to vector Boolean functions' nonlinearity. This work is based on the author's doctoral dissertation. 

Keywords: Slim Sidon sets, nonlinearity of vector Boolean functions, characteristics of power functions, necessary conditions for near-Sidon sequences.

Binary matrix sampling is employed in multiple machine learning and computer vision applications as a technique for regularization and Bayesian model interpretation. The most common method for generating sampled matrices is one that utilizes a chain Monte Carlo algorithm, specifically designed for binary matrices. However, this approach can result in biased samples when working with large datasets, as discrepancies in binary label distributions can lead to varying levels of useful information within the sampled matrices. For instance, some datasets may contain clear class divisions, whereas others may not, resulting in difficulty in selecting an optimal sample size that effectively showcases relevant features. Furthermore, the previously employed algorithms often require users to specify both a sample size and a matrix format, introducing an additional challenge. Quantization has emerged as a feasible method for reducing the computational burden and memory requirements of deep neural networks during deployment. Nonetheless, the positive effect of quantization on model generalization remains an area of curiosity. In this study, we demonstrate that the binary weight neural network's success can be attributed to the quasi-orthogonality of its layer-wise neural network's Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK). We also find that the binary weight quantization achieves the maximum degree of neural tangent kernel's orthogonality, resulting in an optimal regularization effect on the model. Furthermore, we derive the expression for the binary weight neural network's NTK and establish its asymptotic property as the network depth increases. Moreover, we provide a proof that the binary weight neural network's generalization error is ultimately determined by its training error, analogous to the finding by Lee et al. for the neural tangent kernel model, thereby paving the way for future investigation into the optimization theory of binary weight neural networks. We examine how the properties of a point spread function (PSF) in a combined image change when the contributions of individual measurements with varying signal strengths and positions are recalculated. Recalculating the PSF in a new combined image using data from all measurements yields the best fit, resulting in the most accurate PSF properties. However, this recalculation can be cumbersome, especially in 3D data sets, due to the need to adjust the image coordinates. An alternative, simpler approach for fitting a Gaussian PSF to 2D data is also presented. This approach involves calculating the mean and standard deviation of signals within a specified boundary from the target pixel using a weighted average, considering the actual pixel positions of the measurements, and accounting for any outlying pixels that may skew the fit. We demonstrate that this method produces reliable results for our test data, including accurate assessments of the stellar crowding, signal-to-noise ratio, and PSF ellipticity. Additionally, we find that our method is resistant to biases triggered by varying signal strengths and positions of the measurements, and it provides a practical solution for astronomers to use efficiently in their future research. An implementation of this simpler approach is available through our pointspread package on GitHub, including features to plot the PSF, demonstrate the reliable recovery of low signal-to-noise ratio stars, and visualize the contributions of individual measurements to a combined image, including the option to recalculate the PSF using a machine learning algorithm. This pointspread package can be utilized in conjunction with other popular imaging packages, including numpy, astropy, scipy, matplotlib, and seaborn, to provide a comprehensive toolkit for the accurate analysis of 2D and 3D image data. An integration of our simpler approach into the astropy library is currently under consideration. We also show that our method can be extended to fit a Gaussian PSF to 3D data, and we provide a companion paper that explores the application of our simpler approach to the analysis of 3D data, along with the necessary code to reproduce our results. This companion paper is available through arXiv, doi: 10.11664/ires.2001.021.001.20220403.

The behavior of a cell is influenced by its shape, which is regulated by specific molecular processes. Due to the intricate structure of cells, developing a method to generate synthetic cell shapes realistically is crucial for simulating cellular activity in artificial environments. Current approaches using implicit surfaces have shown potential, but face challenges in accurately representing closed shapes with complex geometries. In this research, we explore the effectiveness of implicit neural representations in modeling cell shapes through a two-part process. First, we develop an neural network-based method that generates novel, diverse cell shapes while maintaining the input's topological properties. Second, we train the network to produce output shapes topologically equivalent to the input, which we validate on microorganism datasets and compare favorably to previous studies. The advantages of our approach include its ability to generate precise, closed shapes with detailed geometry and novel, diverse outputs inspired by real-world cell forms. The method holds promise for simulating cellular activity in artificial environments in a more realistic way. Concurrent transmission in multi-access wireless systems enables coexistence with minimal interference, by allowing multiple nodes to transmit simultaneously on the same frequency. This principle underlies systems that exploit diversity, offer same-level transmission opportunities, or create dependent relationships among transmitted information bits. Our discussion begins by explaining the underlying theory of superposition, transmission, and detection, before delving into the design goals and approaches of these systems. We then gather existing research on categories of concurrent transmission, covering transmission models, reliable data transmission, transmission in noisy environments, transmission for specific purposes, and transmission supported by auxiliary information. Furthermore, we outline promising areas for future research and provide practical examples to illustrate the usage of concurrent transmission in real-world applications. Lastly, we summarize the main findings and reflect on the development of concurrent transmission in wireless systems.

Recent findings from the search for massive black holes at the centers of dwarf galaxies reveal a dramatic disparity between expected rates and observed frequencies. To better comprehend this enigma, we develop three distinct massive black hole formation pathways, all of which could account for the observed black hole masses and local abundance. Pathway A suggests a massive black hole emerges from the collapse of a dense star cluster, while Pathway B proposes a massive black hole forms through the merger of stars and star clusters within a dark matter halo. Finally, Pathway C involves a massive black hole formed within a stellar feedback-dominated structure before being captured by a dark matter halo. We analyze the X-ray and radio emissions from the central regions of dwarf galaxies, predicting their spectral properties under each scenario. Our models indicate that the star formation history and subsequent mass buildup surrounding a massive black hole influence a galaxy's ability to produce observable emissions. Despite Pathway B following closely to the observed emissions from the nearby galaxy, Leo I, in terms of radio luminosity, we find it struggles to replicate Leo I's X-ray spectrum. Conversely, Pathway C appears to successfully explain both Leo I's X-ray and radio emissions, suggesting the galaxy, Leo I, may serve as a validating example for this massive black hole formation pathway. However, further data is needed to discern between the three possible massive black hole formation pathways, with future observations potentially preferring Pathway C due to its ability to reproduce Leo I's observable emissions. In addition, our study reveals that massive black holes in their growth phase may not always be actively accreting; rather, they could be generating emissions from the decay of surrounding star clusters, challenging current massive black hole accretion models. Finally, our study indicates that the proton conduction in the hot gas surrounding a massive black hole may provide a more favorable environment for hisonic emission to occur, thus broadening the possible parameter space for producing observable emissions during the massive black hole growth phase. To verify our predictions, space-based telescopes such as the Nancy Grace Roman Telescope or Chandra X-ray Observatory would need to observe more galaxies like Leo I due to their low luminosity. Moreover, the serendipitous discovery of a new dwarf galaxy acting as an intense X-ray and radio source could provide further insight into the properties of its central massive black hole and, potentially, its emission-producing mechanism. As such, our study emphasizes the significance of further observational research into the central, emission-producing phase of massive black holes, necessitating more powerful and flexible telescopes in the future. At the atomic level, in certain lattice structures like kagome, flat bands arise due to symmetry protections, resulting in unconventional electronic behavior when flat bands overlap with normal bands.  Researchers at to be named institution, in collaboration with a team at to be named institution, have developed a model based on a kagome lattice with transition metals substituted with different elements, demonstrating how a nearby flat band can cause a significant decrease in electrical resistance in response to an external magnetic field.  Computational data showed that this decrease in electrical resistance is more pronounced at higher temperatures in systems featuring multiple atomic layers, whereas a simpler one-atomic layer version displayed the opposite effect.  Through detailed analysis, it was determined that a previously unknown flat band-induced effect was responsible for this phenomenon, and that achieving superconductivity might be more feasible in such multi-atomic layer structures.  It is anticipated that further study of such flat band-induced mechanisms will reveal new, unexpected properties of materials.

To study the inherent complexity of small hydrogen-like atoms in confined environments, we examine information entropies in helium-like atoms with varying Coulomb correlations. Based on the Calogero conjecture, we modify the Hamiltonian to generate an effective electron-electron interaction, obtaining a soft pairing gap from the Klein-Gordon momentum distribution. This pairing effect increases the entropy of each proton, especially in situations of tight confinement. Our findings indicate that Coulomb correlations elevate entropy in confined, hydrogen-like atoms, with the extent of this effect being contingent upon the tightness of the confinement. Consequently, this principle could be observed in the entropy of positive muonic hydrogen and could also influence the properties of impositively charged hydrogen-like ions. Additionally, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the fundamental, confined hydrogen-like atom dynamics crucial to the development of quantum technologies based on trapped electrons. To achieve further progress in this field, we propose an approach that incorporates the wavenumber of the paired electrons, yielding an enhanced, effective electron-electron interaction. This approach enables a more in-depth analysis of the role of confinement and Coulomb correlations in the dynamics of hydrogen-like atoms, with potential applications in the design of positron-emitting sources and other quantum devices. Furthermore, our research offers a ground-level understanding of the behavior of hydrogen-like atoms in the vicinity of atomic nuclei, with implications for research in nuclear physics and astrophysics. Finally, we demonstrate how our proposed methodology can be utilized to study other complex many-body systems, such as those found in the cores of atoms, where the dynamics of hydrogen-like atoms and Coulomb correlations give rise to a wide range of phenomena observable in the visible spectrum. Identifying gravitational anomalies in astronomical data can serve as a means of determining whether deviations from Newton's law of gravity can be observed. A particularly effective technique for doing so involves utilizing wide binary systems that are in a state of equilibrium, as their orbital characteristics are expected to be well-predicted by theoretical models, and thus, any discrepancies may indicate a deviation from the predicted gravitational norms. Nevertheless, we contend that binary orbital data alone is insufficient for this purpose, and that parallax data, which describes the angular widening of binary orbits over time, is also required in order to effectively test for gravitational anomalies. In this study, we demonstrate that a large binary catalog used for such purposes does not exhibit any clear evidence of such anomalies, and we suggest that any purported findings based only on orbital data are susceptible to interpretations that do not necessarily imply a gravitational anomaly. Furthermore, we propose that any analysis seeking to detect gravitational anomalies in binary data should utilize the complete set of observable binary characteristics - including those facilitated by the South Pole Telescope's observations of the Galactic plane - in order to effectively do so. Such an approach, we believe, would serve as a more reliable means of testing for gravitational anomalies and would enable us to better understand the anomalies that have already been detected at approximately $k\sim 0.1$ Mpc in scale. Lastly, we note that such a detection does not necessarily align with the predictions of alternative theories of gravity. In particular, we demonstrate that the anomalies previously reported for the binary system of J1124-364, which is located at a distance of approximately 27 kpc from us, can be fully accounted for by a standard model that incorporates dark matter, and thus, any deviations from the predicted gravitational norms may indicate the presence of dark matter or any other unsolved astronomical enigma. Finally, we remind readers that any analysis seeking to detect gravitational anomalies must prioritize accuracy and robustness in order to effectively do so, and that the anomalies that are ultimately observed should be consistent with the predictions of standard gravitational theory. To each multiplicative linear logic proof structure, we relate a cut-free version through a process involving substructures, cuts, and contraction elimination. This method mirrors the tactics of subproof elimination and cut-elimination that are commonly employed in proof theory. We demonstrate that our method for modifying proof structures can be translated into a transformation of proofs, and that it adheres to a key invariant; consequently, this result can also provide a new explanation for a known theorem stating that an original proof implies a cut-free version. Our approach can be extended to obtain a new proof of the latter theorem as well as a generalisation of the theorem to the broader context of proof nets. Furthermore, our method allows us to identify the specific type of units that are involved in the cut-elimination process, and to establish a new unit composition theorem for proof nets that takes into account cuts of any degree. Finally, our method can be used to derive a version of the cut-elimination theorem for proof nets that incorporates a contraction elimination process, and to establish a connection between proof nets and the abstract machine that is commonly used as the target of transformation in proof normalization. This finding can also be viewed as a normalisation procedure that does not alter the truth of a proof net. The key tool that enables our method is a novel application of the concept of unit composition that does not rely on the traditional notion of congruence to compose units, but instead uses a different type of unit composition that we call weak unit composition, and can be obtained through a process of substructure contraction. To investigate the impact of momentum on the electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions, we analyzed the symmetry-allowed and momentum-dependent electron-phonon and spin-phonon coupling components using a general tight-binding model and numerical data from graphene and MoS2. Our analysis reveals that momentum significantly influences the amplitude of these interactions, with the electron-phonon coupling generally increasing linearly with it and the spin-phonon coupling increasing quadratically. This understanding can facilitate the calculation of electron-phonon and spin-phonon coupling tensors for materials exhibiting five-atom hexagonal rings, including carbon nanotubes and transition metal dichalcogenides. Our findings also demonstrate that momentum-dependent electron-phonon interactions can contribute substantially to electron effective mass, transport, and lattice heating. Ultimately, we anticipate that our work will facilitate the accurate prediction of electron-phonon and spin-phonon coupling components for any tight-binding model or hexagonal material, enabling the widespread application of these interactions in phonon-electron effective mass, transport simulations, and device design. Additionally, these results can be scaled to account for effects seen in moire systems. Our code for generating these results is available at https://github.com/stevefong12/epb_coupling.git. This technical report expands upon a previously submitted paper, exploring the concept of information systems through case-based reasoning. A case model is defined as a data structure comprising instances, associated with process models, enabling the analysis of system behavior via instance projections. Three case model variants emerge when considering attribute occurrences in processes: occurrence-aware, single, and multiple instances, with cardinality constraints adding additional complexity to the former. Although occurrence-aware case models seem advantageous, their practical application is complicated by the requirement for attribute occurrences, ultimately making the three variants incompatible. To address this limitation, this technical report provides a method to augment occurrence-aware case models with cardinality constraints, effectively merging the behavior of the three variants into a single representation. It also introduces the concept of instance regions, defined by process models, and demonstrates how case models with cardinality constraints can facilitate the analysis of system behavior via instance projections, ultimately leading to the specification of reachable instance regions. This idea is further exemplified in a system analysis, showcasing the differentiation in reaching capabilities between two occurrence-aware case models with cardinality constraints when compared to their respective single and multiple instance counterparts. Finally, this technical report is complemented by a prototype implementation in the form of a UML tool model, available for public download, which reinforces the conceptual foundations of case models with cardinality constraints and their practical application in system analysis. This technical report is a extension of the paper titled "Enhancing Case Models with Cardinality Constraints", originally submitted to the 20th International Conference on Theory and Application of Graphs in June 2022. Wildfires disrupting solar energy significantly through atmospheric aerosols,
resulting from diminished solar radiation reaching Earth, can be monitored by
Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) data streams retrieved from geostationary satellites.
However, identifying AOD's physical relationship with wildfires is complicated
due to inconsistent satellite data across different regions and conflicting prior
information. This research presents an innovative approach that utilizes physics-
informed statistical modeling to map AOD's geospatial relationship with wildfires
from diverse satellite data streams. By integrating physics principles to align
disparate data scales and correct biases, this method enables accurate AOD
estimations and downstream applications such as wildfire detection and solar
radiation forecasting. The procedure's effectiveness is validated through cross-
validation and comparison with nominal AOD values derived from co-located in-
situ measurements, and the model's capability to detect wildfires and solar
reductions is demonstrated. Furthermore, different proxy models derived from
the physics-informed analysis exhibit superior performance compared to models
without such analysis, and the impact of satellite data differences is examined.

Recent research has indicated that positional encoding can play a crucial role in the effectiveness of sequence-to-sequence models. Nevertheless, the standard method of positional encoding is entirely position-based, which may not adequately capture the characteristics of code-mixed texts, where words with similar positions may possess distinct positional information. In order to address this limitation, we present an innovative, adaptive positional encoding solution called PESTO, which incorporates switching, relative, and position-based techniques. Empirical evidence demonstrates that PESTO significantly enhances the accuracy of word-level sentiment prediction in code-mixed social media text, surpassing a benchmark by approximately 6.3%, and its development marks a significant advancement in the field of adaptive encoding for mixed-language datasets. Furthermore, PESTO serves as an effective means of incorporating positional awareness into adaptive encoding methods, and its designed features serve as a valuable resource for researchers working on tasks involving code-mixed text. Additionally, we introduce a word-level sentiment classification dataset known as ISNT-SE, which comprises 29,337 sentences comprising of ISNT-SE_train, ISNT-SE_val, and ISNT-SE_test with 18,011, 3,072, and 3,274 sentences respectively. This dataset is based on Instagram captions that are part of the Instagram Sentiment Neural Toolkit (#ISNT). It is designed to aid researchers and knowledge seekers in their efforts to analyze the sentiment patterns of individual words within code-mixed text, which is an area of limited study despite its importance for comprehensive understanding. In particular, we delve into topics such as the most prevalent sentiment labels for each language, words that consistently convey a strong sentiment in a single language, and certain words that are likely to convey a strong sentiment only when used in a specific language. These findings could yield valuable insights for multiple areas of study, including natural language understanding, sentiment analysis, and cognitive psychology. The #ISNT project also includes a host of additional tools that enable researchers to easily obtain additional datasets based on Instagram posts, along with support for multiple languages such as Hindi, English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Arabic. Federated learning has a limitation known as model ambiguity that arises from aggregating different user model parameters. This issue becomes more pronounced in certain scenarios, such as when working with small datasets or semi-supervised learning setups. The latter scenario involves a global model that incorporates both labeled and unlabeled data, but the model's variability can hinder performance by causing excessive feature activation. The current approaches to reducing model ambiguity are either too restrictive, limiting a model's capacity, or too loosely bound, enabling excessive model divergence. In response to this challenge, we introduce a novel objective function that strikes an optimal balance between reducing model ambiguity and allowing a reasonable model size. Furthermore, we develop a protocol that enables decentralized computation of proximal operators without requiring users to share their data. Finally, we present comprehensive experimental results that confirm our approach outperforms existing methods on various federated learning use cases, particularly in personalized semi-supervised learning scenarios. The developed code is publicly available at https://github.com/nanduelamanussov/personalized-federated-ssl. Our work is facilitated by a mathematical framework that generalizes existing model ambiguity approaches, thereby enabling seamless integration of other objective functions into our proposed framework, as demonstrated by the appendix. This integration can be found at https://nanduelamanussov.github.io/ambiguous-federated-learning/. In essence, our objective function leverages the model's Jacobian to regularize against excessive variability, but other dimensions of the model's parameter space can also be employed, depending on the specific problem at hand. The key to our approach is the proximal monster, a mathematical concept that decentralizes the computation of optimal models, thereby aligning with the distributed architecture of federated learning. The model's size is carefully calibrated such that it consumes minimal resources while effectively regulating model ambiguity, according to our proposed objective function. Emergency department wait times can be modeled as a network with nodes representing events such as check-in and treatment completion, and edges with associated time values indicating processing intervals.  The average reaction curve for treatment time - a vital metric in managing emergency department capacity - can be calculated by considering the waiting distribution of patients. This involves applying the law of iterated expectations to a conditional average, ultimately resulting in a computationally efficient formula. Specifically, the average reaction curve for treatment time can be expressed as the sum of an implicit constant, the mean processing time of the final operation, and the product of the mean waiting time and the standard deviation of processing times for that operation, and further modified by the impact of initial node wait times. By applying this formula in conjunction with a reduced Markov chain representation of the emergency department process, we are able to calculate the average reaction curve for treatment time with minimal computational requirements. The accuracy of this approach is confirmed through comparison with simulation data. Furthermore, the theoretical framework has been validated through application to actual data from a hospital in the United States. The results provide insights into the dynamics of the emergency department, and allow for the application of stochastic processes in managing patient flows. Ultimately, the model presents a dynamic averaging approach that can be applied across a range of operations management contexts. Machine learning (ML) based detection of network attacks has shown effectiveness when tailored to a single organisation, but combining data from multiple sources is challenging due to data format inconsistencies and privacy concerns. To address this issue, a collaborative federated learning (FL) framework is proposed for developing an effective intrusion detection system (IDS) that can analyse labelled network data from multiple organisations without compromising privacy. This novel approach allows multiple organisations to share cyber threat intelligence while maintaining the security of their individual datasets. A key feature of the framework is its ability to form a federated graph across multiple organisations, enabling the development of a unified ML model for detecting novel attacks. To test the framework's efficacy, experiments were conducted using data from the NIST dataset, and results indicate that an FL-based ML model can achieve high accuracy in detecting both known and unknown attacks. Furthermore, the framework's ability to combine data from multiple organisations enhances its overall performance, and the use of FL enables the development of a robust model in a distributed environment. The proposed FL framework provides a viable solution for organisations to collaborate in developing effective IDS models while addressing privacy and format inconsistencies through a unified ML solution. The implementation details, including the federated learning architecture and the intrusion detection process, are documented to enable straightforward integration into existing cyber security systems. Finally, the proposed framework's flexibility allows it to be adapted for various cyber security applications beyond traditional IDS. The source code of the proposed FL framework is publicly available on GitHub for easy reproduction of the experimental results. A possible future direction for the research is exploring the use of FL for detecting and mitigating emerging threats in real-time. Additionally, the novel FL-based IDA algorithm proposed in this study can be further developed by incorporating novel intrusion detection techniques for enhancing its performance. The integration of FL and IDA could provide a collaborative advantage in detecting attacks and detecting and mitigating emerging threats efficiently. The FL framework's capability of developing a long-term and robust attack detection model can be leveraged by combining it with the real-time emerging threat detection capabilities of IDA for a more comprehensive cyber security outcome. The integration of these two techniques would offer a collaborative cyber security solution for effectively detecting novel attacks, emerging threats, and continuously improving the cyber security posture of organisations through a collaborative and robust cyber threat intelligence sharing mechanism. The performance of the interface between semiconductors and barriers is a crucial factor in producing reliable spin-transistors. This research investigates the characteristics of undoped Si substrates fabricated using a full 300mm CMOS process, focusing on both undoped Si with a SiGe buffer and undoped Si without a SiGe buffer. By leveraging a full CMOS process, we were able to produce SiMOSFETs exhibiting exceptional mobility - up to 15,000 cm^2/Vs for Ge MOSFETs and 13,000 cm^2/Vs for conventional MOSFETs, surpassing previously reported values from 300mm CMOS processes. By understanding and controlling the residual dopant levels, we were able to produce SiMOSFETs with residual dopant concentrations as low as 1e13 cm^-2, leading to significant enhancements in mobility, from 5,000 to 15,000 cm^2/Vs for Ge MOSFETs and from 3,000 to 13,000 cm^2/Vs for conventional MOSFETs. This level of mobility is now comparable to that found in Germanium MOSFet technology and in III-V-on-insulator CMOS, making it an attractive option for integrating CMOS and quantum electronics. As a result, high-mobility SiMOSFETs can now be produced using full 300mm CMOS processes, paving the way for reliable high-mobility spin-transistors. We propose the concept of group harmony, which refers to members' shared extrinsic values and intrinsic personal characteristics. Our findings reveal that group harmony enhances performance, whereas task-related alignment remains essential for surviving parameter mismatches and maintaining a stable performance level within a group. A practical application of these findings could involve incorporating a performance-enhancing strategy, such as hiring team members with similar cultural backgrounds or providing them with team-building activities to foster a sense of community. Pseudo-labeling is a popular technique in supervised learning that overrides model probabilities with confidence-based class predictions as fake labels to accelerate training.  However, due to the low quality of these fake labels, the typical pseudo-labeling approach is only suitable in the initial stages of training.  In order to expand the effectiveness of pseudo-labeling across the entire training process, we propose using a strategy called informative pseudo-tagging (IPT), which incorporates a query network to filter out unreliable pseudo-labels and instead uses a sampling strategy to select a specified number of high-confidence training data fake labels.  Through this mechanism, a double filter is applied to pseudo-labels: first, a high-confidence filter is applied to exclude low-confidence pseudo-labels, and then a sampling filter is applied to reduce the number of pseudo-labels derived from easy data, which effectively prevents overfitting.  Experimental results on multiple graph classification and link prediction tasks demonstrate IPT to be a robust method for training graph neural networks with a limited number of labels.  Additionally, IPT has been found to enhance the performance of current state-of-the-art baselines based on pseudo-labeling, and its code and data have been publicly released at https://github.com/keunhee/Informative-Pseudo Tagging.  It has been proven that IPT is compatible with a variety of models, including SGC, GNN-LP, GraphSAGE, GraphAttention, and GAT, and can be applied to a wide range of machine learning problems.  Furthermore, the methodology is generalizable and can be applied to problems beyond the graph neural networks.  A major potential drawback is the additional computational overhead required by IPT, which may be mitigated through the use of modern high-performance computing hardware.  A detailed analysis of the theoretical performance was provided in the paper, and it was found that IPT can provide a performance boost of up to 6.01% relative to the baseline methods.  A comprehensive evaluation was also conducted to validate the robustness of IPT, which was found to be superior to the baseline methods in multiple robustness metrics. In video processing tasks, rapid movement creates problems for models trying to improve inference speed by exploiting spatial redundancies. We develop PatchNet, a neural network designed to quickly identify useful static features in video patterns and apply them to challenging motion cases. By matching known features to unknown areas, PatchNet improves the accuracy of video inference models on a range of tasks, from 2D to 5D, and surpasses the performance of existing methods on high-reiteration videos. Furthermore, PatchNet facilitates the creation of compact, efficient models that can effectively handle a wide range of video patterns. We showcase the effectiveness of PatchNet in various applications, such as the creation of a high-speed semantic segmentation model and a high-quality video interpolation tool. By automatically detecting feature patterns and matching them across frames, PatchNet enables video processing models to achieve both higher performance and more efficient inference. The code for PatchNet is publicly available at https://github.com/zhangyang24/PatchNet. Experimental results can be found at https://yangzhang18.github.io/PatchNet.

We examine the one-dimensional discrete-time asymmetric exclusion process with a cyclic system boundary, using a system that includes a large number of particles.  A set of discrete time, cyclic TASEP multipoint distributions are developed, which satisfy the AEP's commutativity and uniformity conditions.  These distributions are shown to be unique and finite for any number of particles and any set of evaluation points.  They reduce to known solutions for specific situations: the stationary state for an ordinary cyclic TASEP process, and the current-coupling technique's distribution for an asymmetric exclusion process.  A proposed method for obtaining the discrete time, periodic TASEP multipoint distributions is supported through explicit computation of the distributions for two and three particles.  A conjecture is presented that these discrete time, periodic TASEP multipoint distributions are a special case of the TASEP process's distribution, parameterised over the Martin-Sweet basis.  A key tool in these investigations is a graph representation, based on 'bricks', that allows for the decoupling of the graph's vertices, and a related 'unfrozen' process, introduced for the first time.  These novel techniques are shown to be effective through the derivation of specific equations for the discrete time, periodic TASEP process's distribution, and the obtainment of exact expressions for two and three particles.  A further conjecture presents a possible further simplification of these discrete time, periodic TASEP process equations, obtained by re-expressing them in terms of the Martin-Sweet basis.  A related claim is also presented that similar graph representation and 'unfrozen' process techniques can be applied to obtain exact expressions for the discrete-time, multi-branching TASEP process.  These conjectures are marked as open problems.  A further related field of study, the periodic TASEP process with a generally distributed initial condition, is also explored. A new method of wireless communication, SWIPT, utilizes the same transmission signal in two distinct ways, for receiving both information bits and electrical energy that can be stored in a capacitive bank and used later. This study focuses on optimizing energy distribution within a SWIPT system, serving multiple users who require information from the same message, in real-time. Utilizing a generalized DSR approach, we modified the standard power splitting policy to accommodate multi-service applications, actively adjusting energy allocation between users and information streams. Mathematically converting this optimization challenge into a standard convex DSR problem, we were able to derive computationally efficient solutions: closed-form solutions for users with identical capabilities and approximate solutions for users with varying capabilities, both obtaining a low level of error. Our proposed solutions were tested in scenarios with either one to multiple users or multiple users with varying requirements, demonstrating significant improvements over traditional power splitting methods. These improvements led to increased energy efficiency for each user when compared to a splitting method designed for information-only optimization. Furthermore, when comparing SWIPT to a non-energy-efficient information-only approach, we found that SWIPT achieves a balance between energy efficiency and information reliability, outperforming the non-energy-efficient approach but falling short of an ideal, all-energy-dedicated approach. These observations highlight the ability of SWIPT to effectively mitigate a transmitter's power limitations, at the cost of slightly reduced information reliability when energy allocation is split between information bits and electrical energy. In a multi-service application, we found that information bits from one message can be used to supply energy for another, with some level of energy distribution still possible, even when each user requires information from a separate message. These insights will contribute to the development of practical SWIPT systems, helping to bridge the theoretical performance and realistic performance gaps. Ultimately, this study provides approaches for optimizing energy distribution in real-time, within a SWIPT system, facilitating a clearer understanding of the underlying mathematics of energy efficiency in wireless communication. The derived solutions can be applied directly in practical systems, enhancing their performance. Additionally, the analytical methods employed in this study may be extended to address other optimization challenges in wireless communication, beyond energy distribution. Furthermore, these analytical methods provide valuable insights into the underlying mathematics of resource allocation in multi-service wireless communication, which may be useful in future research on related topics. This study investigates how mobile robots navigate around an obstructing wall in an area with randomly distributed obstacles. The robots adhere to a wall-follower strategy that utilizes a narrow corridor for navigation, and their movement is controlled by a simple policy that relies on local sensor data. This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, building upon a previously published study.  It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are embedded in the full theory's algebra.  It also establishes that the construction of these subalgebras is Cauchy surface-independent and yields a well-defined covariant theory on the space of null geodesics.  This new theory represents a chiral 2dcft, which can be extended to include multiple null geodesics, effectively describing a (1,1)dcft.  This approach can be extended to other chiral aspects in 2dcft.  An example is considered where this method is applied to a spin-1 field under the influence of a gravitational field, where the concept of chiral aspects is reinforced.  The study concludes by relating the observed phenomena to the behavior of chiral fields in quantum field theory.

We investigate this method's effectiveness for estimating a symmetric tensor when only a single entry is known.
Our contribution lies at the intersection of information theory and high-dimensional statistics, particularly in understanding how non-negative distributions in a tensor context convey information, which is typically overlooked in existing studies.
We demonstrate that the known-entry-first (KEF) prior remains stable and computationally efficient, even in extremely high-dimensional scenarios, and is characterized by a straightforward formula involving the gamma function.
Our analysis showcases the versatility of the KEF prior, revealing its capability to achieve optimal results in a wide range of scenarios, and even allowing for the estimation of a tensor with tens of billions of dimensions when only a single entry is known.
Our findings also enable the development of an unbiased estimator for the kest tensor entry, which we call KEST, and show that it outperforms existing methods on both theoretical and practical grounds. 
Our experiments reveal that KEST provides the most accurate results when estimating a kest tensor entry with a specific value as part of a symmetric multi-response tensor. 
Our study provides a framework for designing robust and efficient priors, which is crucial for applying Bayesian techniques in high-dimensional scenarios, and also opens up new avenues for a wide range of estimation tasks. 
Furthermore, our results have significant practical implications and can be used to tackle various challenges in data-driven tensor estimation. 
Our code is publicly available for testing and validation purposes.

A cost-effective and pervasive solution, UWB-based location tracking, holds significant value across various industries. Despite its advantages, UWB signals are susceptible to interference from wireless telecommunication bands. In this research, an enhanced algorithm is introduced to mitigate the impact of interference by leveraging machine learning and adaptive filtering. Initially, a non-orthogonal sparse mutli-conjugate adaptive filter is developed to counteract LoS and NLOS signal distortions, followed by a non-linear transformation to compensate for remaining distortions. Subsequently, a message transmission-based adaptive filter is designed to optimize performance in the presence of channel impairments and real-time location estimation errors. This proposed method significantly outperforms existing approaches by achieving lower location error standards without compromising its real-time and data-driven efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this algorithm, yielding a 60% reduction in location error relative to a baseline UWB-based tracking method. Furthermore, the algorithm maintains low computational complexity, facilitating its practical implementation in mobile device localization and tracking applications. Experimental findings validate the algorithm's effectiveness in diverse environments, surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art deep learning-based and conventional filtering methods. In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, speeding up convergence often involves developing tailored preconditioners for the solver. Since progress in both areas is interconnected, it's beneficial to establish a common indicator of convergence for both the IPM and the solver. This can be done by monitoring how quickly the residual of the linear system diminishes in relation to an orthogonal basis generated during solution processing. However, this requirement may appear unrealistic at first because the residual's direction is constantly changing. Nonetheless, by periodically re-orthonormalizing the generated basis and taking'snapshots' of the residual at these intervals, a consistent standard of comparison for convergence can be maintained. Furthermore, this approach allows the interior-point method to determine when the linear system has been solved accurately enough, thereby autonomously controlling the computational expense. Our method was tested by comparing it to existing solutions for a range of problems drawn from the COCO collection, which includes various problem sets derived from diverse applications. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this novel criterion in autonomously controlling the computational expense of IPMs, thereby facilitating more efficient convergence. Moreover, our approach is now openly accessible on the GitHub platform under the name 'AutoIPS'. Moreover, our approach is versatile and can be used with various interior-point algorithms as well as diverse solver solvers. Our findings also uncover additional research questions that we intend to explore further. Firstly, our strategy may offer a fresh perspective for developing preconditioners that are oblivious to the system's physical structure. Secondly, we aim to expand our method to address other key challenges encountered in interior-point simulations, such as efficiently handling out-of-memory data. To address this gap, our solution integrates KPI and model-driven process monitoring by leveraging process models with defined performance indicators. To enable monitoring, we represent KPI constraints as temporal logic specifications and apply model checking to define valid time windows for them. These time windows serve as the basis for a metric that measures process performance, enabling the identification of conforming processes. These changes are performed in a way that the process remains consistent with the modified model, effectively resolving conflicts between performance and process validity requirements. Ultimately, our solution identifies the optimal balance between performance and conformity, demonstrating the applicability of model checking techniques to real-world process monitoring scenarios. Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to create continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By applying graph abstraction, sequences with no linear connection are grouped and eliminated, then the genome is partitioned to ensure equal workloads among nodes. Through reassignment and subgraph computation, sequences are optimally distributed among nodes. Finally, sequences within each partition are concatenated to produce the complete genome, achieving up to 80% efficiency across 128 nodes. This optimized assembly approach significantly streamlines the genome construction process and demonstrates promising results in terms of accuracy and computational speed, paving the way for low-host-complexity assembly methods. Furthermore, the code has been successfully tested on multiple configurations, including 40-node IBM LS42 and a dual-socket AMD Rome system with 56 cores. In recent years, research in lattice field theories has expanded rapidly, 
with advancements in computational technologies and standardization tools. 
To accelerate progress, the Lattice QCD community has sought to 
standardize methods and tools, just as the particle physics field has done 
in the past. We aim to facilitate this process through a series of 
pedagogical introductions to cutting-edge techniques, marked with 'LFU'. 
This particular contribution provides an overarching framework for future 
lectures and serves as an introductory guide to the field, connecting 
research trends to their underlying historical developments. Future 
introductions ('LFU' follow-ups) will delve into specific topics, 
highlights, and breakthroughs within lattice field theories. We also outline 
plans for a series of comprehensive reviews ('LFU' legacy) that will 
summarize the state-of-the-art in relevant sub-fields, shedding light on 
the evolution of research over the course of the lattice community's 
entire history. 

\textit{Note: } This paper is primarily aimed at students and non-experts 
in the field of lattice field theories. We hope it serves as a valuable 
resource for those seeking an overview of the research landscape, along 
with a concise historical context. We chose to publish it as an e-Print, 
hoping to reach an even broader audience. We welcome feedback and 
suggestions for improvement.

The proposed technique finds applications in text analysis, particularly when dealing with formatted documents, domain-specific lexicons, or known formats like driver's license numbers and medicinal prescription terminology. The TOTEM experiment's measurement of total pp, p-Pb, and Pb-Pb cross-sections at 13 TeV has been utilized to derive the cross-section for top quark production in proton-lead collisions at the same energy. By applying the theoretical expectations for top quark pair production in collective motion environments and correcting for biases, the cross-section has been found to be $16.4 \pm 5.6 (stat.) \pm 2.4 (syst.)$ nanobarns. Furthermore, the experiment has measured the total cross-section for lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV, yielding $\sigma_{\rm T} = 2046.9 \pm 35.6 (stat.) \pm 114.3 (syst.)$ millibarns, in substantial agreement with Monte Carlo simulations based on the next-to-leading order QCD model. By incorporating these measured cross-sections into the TotEM FELICE detector model, the necessary luminosity for top quark pair production cross-section determination has been calculated as $\mathcal{L} \approx 2.6 \times 10^{32}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$. The cross-section for bottom quark production in proton-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV has also been derived as $\sigma_{\rm T} = 181.2 \pm 16.2 (stat.) \pm 13.1 (syst.)$ nanobarns. Additionally, the total pp cross-section at 13 TeV for high mass states has been measured as $\sigma_{\rm T} = 105.8 \pm 3.0 (stat.) \pm 6.3 (syst.)$ millibarns. Additionally, our framework accounts for the uncertainty inherent in these factors, allowing for varying levels of confidence in social interactions and personal beliefs to influence opinion shifts. We discovered that extreme personal beliefs can either stabilize or disrupt opinion dynamics, depending on the associated confidence levels, which in turn affects the structure of social networks as revealed through a balance theory. Our findings also reveal that higher confidence levels in social interactions are required to maintain a balanced social network, whereas increased confidence in personal beliefs may suffice in certain cases. These outcomes emerge from a combination of the exploration of a complex opinion dynamics model and a balanced social network, which can be applied to various scenarios including the spread of misinformation. Ultimately, our study provides insight into the relationship between opinion dynamics, social network structure, and the role of confidence levels in shaping both individual beliefs and the overall structure of a social network. Crucially, our work highlights the potential for a delicate balance between social interactions and personal beliefs to avert the polarization of opinions and maintain a balanced social network. Furthermore, it reveals the utility of modeling opinion dynamics as a robust tool for understanding and approaching the spread of misinformation. Lastly, our research underscores the importance of incorporating the notion of confidence levels in studies of opinion dynamics.

A linear complementary pair of group codes $(C, D)$ is formed when the direct sum of $C$ and $D$ results in the entire group algebra $R[G]$, given a finite ring $R$ and a finite group $G$. We identify a required and confirming criterion for pairs of group codes $(C, D)$ in group algebra $R[G]$ to be a linear complementary pair, subsequently proving the equivalence in terms of permutations between codes $C$ and the dual code $D^{\perp}$. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that if a pair $(C, D)$ satisfies the condition $C \subseteq D^{\perp}$, then $(C, D)$ is indeed a linear complementary pair. Furthermore, our research showcases instances of linear complementary pairs of group codes that do not adhere to the hypothesis of code equality, $C \cong D^{\perp}$. Finally, our investigative work focuses on exploring linear complementary pairs of group codes originating from cyclic codes, along with examining instances of linear complementary pairs of group codes derived from diplotropic codes. Our findings also reveal that if a pair $(C, D)$ is comprised of cyclic codes, then the index of code $D$ in group algebra $R[G]$ is equal to the code dimension of $C$. Lastly, our research showcases instances of linear complementary pairs of group codes derived from semigroup codes. These instances serve as novel contributions to existing literature and provide valuable insights for future research.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional and academic settings is particularly understudied is the retrieval of scientific knowledge. Many assume that Web search results are objective, but studies have shown that personalised search can distort users' understanding of existing information. 
For instance, in the fields of medicine and law, there's a concern that personalised search may lead to biased professional judgments. A key challenge in measuring the full extent of Web search personalisation's impact is identifying all the relevant sources of information. 
To address this issue, we designed an experiment where participants conducted keyword-based searches on Google's personalised results page using two scientific topics. The selected keywords ensured a high level of personalised search influence, and participants were unaware that their searches were being personalised. 
The key findings of our experiment highlight the significant under-recovery of relevant information that occurs in the range of up to 20% when using Google's personalised search results. 
Notably, the results also show that the number of unique Web pages retrieved in the experiment's first result page varies greatly between the two search keywords, emphasizing the potential for a high degree of personalised search variability in scientific knowledge retrieval. 
These findings have important implications for scientists and researchers who rely on Web search as an information retrieval method, suggesting a need for greater awareness about the personalisation effect and its potential to skew retrieval results. 
The experiment's outcomes may also be applied to other areas beyond scientific knowledge retrieval and could have practical applications in fields like medicine, where the accuracy of diagnosis or treatment may depend on comprehensive search results that personalised search may fail to provide. 
To enhance transparency and reduce the influence of Web search personalisation, we propose a set of practical solutions, including displaying results from various search engines and warning users about the personalisation effect. 
Ultimately, our experiment highlights the need for further research into the full range of Web search personalisation's effect on the retrieval of scientific knowledge and related fields, as well as its potential consequences and benefits. 
To meet this goal, we've made the data collected during the experiment available for download on GitHub and CERL ARCHIVE for the benefit of the academic community. 
The data includes information about all the relevant sources of information, search keywords, and pages that were not retrieved due to Web search personalisation, as well as the number of unique Web pages that were and were not retrieved. 
The experiment's data can serve as a valuable resource for future research into the personalisation effect and its applications in various fields.

These structural elements like nodes, edges and hierarchies are essential components in program flow charts that need to be addressed. This paper proposes an novel approach called GRCNN, a graph recognition convolutional neural network, to effectively utilize this information and generate code from flow charts. GRCNN leverages a custom-designed graph representation and employs a novel feature extraction method that incorporates both node and edge features. It also includes a hierarchical recognition module that optimizes node and edge assignment during program synthesis. GRCNN's effectiveness is validated by comparing its performance with state-of-the-art models that only focus on visual or structural elements. Experimental results demonstrate that GRCNN can generate highly accurate programs from flow charts with minimal human intervention. For instance, its error rate is 11.2% compared to 31.3% for the visual-only model and 18.9% for the structural-only model in recognizing 10 program nodes. Additionally, its error rate in synthesizing 10 programs is significantly lower at 4.9% compared to 24.1% for the visual-only model and 12.8% for the structural-only model. These substantial performance enhancements indicate that GRCNN effectively utilizes the available structural elements to achieve better results. The developed model and associated software frameworks, as well as the used dataset, are made available for public use. The used dataset is based on C and comprises over 1.4 million distinct programs, 380 concept tokens and 3000 flow chart templates. A combination of multiple neural networks is utilized to analyze the anatomical relationships among organs and create a precise segmentation mask. However, the previous method we developed relied on a pre-defined segmentation mask, which was obtained through manual annotation of a limited number of training images. Consequently, the model was susceptible to the effects of limited training data, resulting in decreased accuracy. In an effort to overcome this limitation, we developed a new fully automated approach, which applies a neural network to analyze a CT scan without requiring any pre-defined masks or input parameters. This novel method consists of a regional segmentation network and a spatial relationship analysis module, both of which utilize anatomical information extracted from the scan. In our experiments, this fully automated approach demonstrated accurate segmentation of the gastrointestinal tract, with results comparable to those achieved with the previous, semi-automatic method. The segmentation quality was assessed using several metrics, including the Dice score, sensitivity, specificity, and the Hausdorff distance. Our findings indicate that the fully automated approach achieved a Dice score of 0.874, sensitivity of 0.923, specificity of 0.942, and Hausdorff distance of 0.074 for gastrointestinal tract segmentation, outperforming a semi-automatic approach in multiple evaluations. Furthermore, our method preserved the internal structure of the gastrointestinal tract with greater detail, as evidenced by the lower Hausdorff distance. We believe this fully automated approach holds great promise for clinical practice, eliminating the need for manual segmentation and potentially enhancing the accuracy of medical assessments. We investigate the possibility of compressing dark matter particles into a small, dense area, taking into account their Yukawa interaction with standard model particles.  In particular, we focus on the behavior of bosonic dark matter particles that form a condensate due to their Yukawa interaction, resulting in an extremely dense state.  Utilizing the Schwinger mechanism, we determine the rate at which dark matter particles undergo decay, as well as the reaction rate resulting from interactions between dark matter particles and those of the standard model, for both a zero-temperature and a temperature-dependent environment.  Our analysis indicates that in a dense, compact object such as a neutron star, the breakdown of symmetry in the dark matter fluid may lead to an exponential decay of the star.  Furthermore, we consider the impact of a dark matter particle's mass variation on the star's structure, employing a modified equation of state for the dark matter fluid and calculating the star's mass-radius radius relation.  Based on this analysis, we determine whether a neutron star or other compact object could potentially be a dark matter bomb.  Additionally, we discuss the possibility of a dark matter particle's spin polarization as a result of its Yukawa interaction, particularly in the presence of a magnetic field, and outline the implications of this polarization for astrophysical phenomena involving neutron stars, such as their rotational slowing down and heat emission.  Finally, we explore the possibility of a dark matter particle's spatial polarization due to its Yukawa interaction, particularly in the presence of a dense, gradient-filled environment, and outline the consequences of this polarization for the structure of neutron stars and other compact objects.  These considerations expand our understanding of the complex, non-relativistic behavior of a dark matter particle, exemplified by its behavior in a neutron star and other dense environments.  In particular, we discuss the phenomenon of a dark matter particle's freezing into a configuration that cannot be undone, particularly in the context of a neutron star composed of both neutrons and dark matter particles.  This consideration expands our understanding of the phenomenon of freeze-in, particularly in the context of a neutrally charged dark matter particle.  Furthermore, we discuss the possibility of a dark matter particle's decay being prevented, yet its energy being converted into standard model particles, particularly in the context of a neutron star composed of both neutrons and dark matter particles.  This consideration expands our understanding of the phenomenon of dark matter being invisible to detection, particularly in the context of a neutron star composed of both neutrons and dark matter particles.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and selection capabilities, characteristics inherent to cognitive processes in humans and animals. Notably, cognitive biologies often employ sparsification to moderate interneural interaction; this study demonstrates that introducing fixed, projective noise into RNNs yields a faster convergence to optimal solutions for a wide range of cognitive tasks. Comparing the performance of traditional and sparse RNNs on cognitive benchmarks, the latter achieved significant speedup advantages, with improvements ranging from modest factors to substantial factor-of-10 increases in efficiency. The advantage of sparse RNNs became more pronounced as the task complexity increased, showcasing their potential as more robust and efficient cognitive models than their dense counterparts. The source code for the experiments is publicly accessible on GitHub, enabling replication of the results. Furthermore, an open-source library called the Cognitive Benchmark Library (CBL) has been developed to standardise the evaluation of cognitive tasks and facilitate universal assessments of cognitive models. It is also possible to replicate the results on the Empirical Brain Project website, a comprehensive collection of cognitive tasks and models. The Empirical Brain Project aims to create a unified platform for cognitive research, featuring a comprehensive library of tasks and models derived from various public sources, as well as an interactive interface for demonstrating their functionality and dynamic behaviour. In addition to the code, the EBP website provides a permanent reference to the study's results, guaranteeing long-term accessibility to the information. The observation that fixed, projective noise can improve the efficiency of RNNs, despite being non-adaptive, offers an unexpected insight. It also presents an unexpected analogy with the biological cognitive systems, challenging the conventional assumption that adaptive mechanisms are necessary for modelling them effectively. Moreover, the study's results highlight sparse RNNs as an overlooked solution with superior cognitive performance, warranting further research into their intricate dynamics and potential connections to the complex cognitive processes they resemble. The findings also raise possibilities for applications in areas such as smart robotics and drug discovery, where systems with extensive state spaces and limited computational resources come into play. Ultimately, the study contributes to a broader goal of developing and evaluating cognitive models that can efficiently process and generate information, enabling them to mimic biological brains more accurately. The study also seeks to promote reproducibility in research through transparent and accessible experimentation, replicable results, and a permanent record of the findings, as well as sparking further discussion and investigation into the sparse RNNs' dynamics and their potential as superior cognitive models. Our research reveals the primary component of this binary to be a white dwarf star, supported by various characteristics of the system. Our examination of the system's behavior over time, utilizing data from multiple bands (UV, blue, and red), allows us to derive the system's overall size and offer a fresh perspective on its features. Our estimates for the system's dimensions are further validated by comparing them with previously obtained periods. We propose that the system's distortions are a result of the presence of a second white dwarf component rather than other possible explanations. Our calculation of the system's mass ratio supports this hypothesis, indicating that the secondary component is most likely smaller than the primary but still substantial enough to cause noticeable distortions in the system's overall shape. An alternative theory exists, which suggests the system's mass ratio might be closer to equal but requires further confirmation due to uncertainties associated with the system's observation challenges. Our study enhances the understanding of this binary star system and contributes to the knowledge of the behavior of similar systems, which are anticipated to be a significant source of gravitational waves in the future. Moreover, our investigation adds to the extensive collection of binary star systems that are a crucial tool for understanding the formation and evolution of white dwarf stars. Lastly, our research shines a light on the need for more efficient and less costly observational strategies that can gather precise data on the system's behavior over time, which is essential for making accurate predictions about the system's future behavior and detection by gravitational wave observatories. An overview of our study's findings and proposed plan of action to enhance the understanding of this binary star system and numerous others is also presented. Furthermore, our research paves the way for a study that will closely monitor the system until the exact time when the secondary component emerges as the dominant star, which is anticipated to occur within the next 80 years. Global averaging techniques, such as average pooling and global average pooling in neural networks, are frequently employed to reduce the dimensionality of internal representations. However, they can be viewed as oversimplified solutions that fail to consider the complex distributions of the input data. In order to develop more effective global averaging operators, we propose adapting the principle of optimal transport, which aims to balance dimensionality reduction with fidelity to the original distribution. This leads to the introduction of a new family of global pooling operators for neural networks, which can be designed to mimic real-world data distributions more accurately. Our method can also be seen as a form of data-driven preprocessing that enables the development of more informed global averaging operators, thereby resulting in improved performance outcomes. The proposed pooling operators demonstrate superior performance compared to conventional and recent average pooling methods in both self-supervised and supervised learning applications, particularly on challenging image classification tasks. Additionally, they can be employed in a variety of other optimization techniques and global averaging methods with even greater effectiveness. Additionally, we establish the distinctiveness of a flat general rotation surface through a set of specific differential conditions. Furthermore, a formal method is devised to calculate the Christoffel symbols for these surfaces. Lastly, an example is provided to further illustrate and demonstrate the concepts presented. Leveraging these findings, we aim to broaden the scope of the existing symmetry of a 1-type Gaussian map on a flat general rotation surface, effectively enhancing our understanding of these maps. The study also raises a newly framed inquiry regarding the complete symmetry of the 1-type Gaussian map on such surfaces, which we aim to exhaustively address in a future research publication. The primary contributions of this research stem from introducing a novel metric on the rotation axis, a specific expression for the Gaussian map, and a formal calculation of the Christoffel symbols. Interestingly, we observed that a flat general rotation surface possesses a 1-type Gaussian map if and only if it exhibits a harmonic Gaussian map, thereby revealing the equivalence between these two phenomena. To further enhance our findings, we constructed an example of a flat general rotation surface with a 1-type Gaussian map that cannot be categorized as a spherical, gyration surface. The study offers a new perspective on the existing theories of a 1-type Gaussian map and a harmonic Gaussian map on a flat general rotation surface. Moreover, we presented an example to illustrate the distinct characteristics of a 1-type Gaussian map on a flat general rotation surface, thereby broadening the scope of its symmetry. The examples provided serve to augment the existing literature on a 1-type Gaussian map and a harmonic Gaussian map for general rotation surfaces. The study presents a fresh approach to understanding these maps, which holds potential for extension to other maps.
