Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. For this purpose, image
classification and depth estimation from a single view have gained popularity
as unsupervised pre-training methods due to their ease and relevance to other
tasks. However, it is unclear whether these pre-training methods inherently
enhance the model's performance or simply serve as a necessary step towards
reaching desirable results. Moreover, there has been no thorough examination
of the efficacy of applying pre-training to semantic segmentation tasks in the
past. This study investigates (1) whether pre-training with depth estimation
from a single view is more effective than image classification, (2) the factors
that contribute to the effectiveness of pre-training, (3) the phenomenon of
performance degradation when transferring pre-trained models to segmentation
tasks without further refinement, and (4] the potential benefit of combining
multi-view 3D depth maps for improvement of segmentation results. Our research
involved extensive experiments on various datasets, including the Sun3D dataset
for depth estimation and the COCO and KITTI 2D semantic segmentation benchmark. 
Our findings show that depth estimation can be improved with additional
multi-view information, and that employing this information during testing
can lead to considerable improvements in pre-trained model performance. Additionally,
our results indicate that extending the input to three dimensions has a more
substantial impact on improvement than transitioning from image
classification to depth estimation as the pre-training objective. Consequently,
we recommend incorporating multi-view cues in various depth estimation and
segmentation tasks to achieve optimal results. The source code for our project
is publicly available at https://github.com/asharakeh/depth-seg.

Galactic rotation curves show a range of varying inner slopes. Observations suggest a potential issue for galaxy building, which, if addressed, could help explain galaxy diversity. Several solutions have been proposed over the years to account for this problem, and the purpose of this study is to evaluate the reliability of each solution through comparison. The rotation curves of 1,000 simulated galaxies were analyzed in detail, and the solutions were assessed based on how well they replicate the observed variability in a galaxy's rotation curve. Some of the solutions provide clear physical interpretations, such as the Light Dark Matter option or the presence of a central dark matter halo with varying profiles. Others, like the Self-Interacting Dark Matter hypothesis, require substantial amounts of dark matter to explain the observed phenomena, conflicting with findings from other studies. One solution, the baryon feedback effect, explains some but not all aspects of the observed galaxy diversity. Various combinations of the mentioned models are also discussed, and the rotation curves of 14 specific galaxies from the existing literature are used to further evaluate the reliability of each solution. The study's key outcome is that no one model alone can fully account for the galaxy diversity; a combination of the Light Dark Matter and feedback effects, for instance, fits the data better than the others but still leaves some discrepancies. The rotation curves of the galaxies classified as "dark matter dominated" require a different approach by the Light Dark Matter model compared to the "radiation-dominated" galaxies. The former benefit from additional particle masses under $10^{-19}$eV, whereas the latter prefer smaller masses. The feedback effect plays a more significant role at larger radii but also introduces some variability at the very core of these galaxies. Ultimately, the study suggests that the various solutions to the galaxy diversity problem are interconnected and depend on specific assumptions related to the nature of dark matter, leading to the possibility that a more comprehensive approach might reveal a unified explanation for the observed galaxy diversity. The rotation curves used in this study can be accessed through a dedicated website hosted at http://www.physik.uni-bonn.de/characters/rotationcurves.html. The code for the simulation model can be found at https://github.com/leandros/rotationcurves, while additional visualizations are available at https://www.physics.uni-bonn.edu/~leandros/rotationcurves.html. The Dark Matter model, once adjusted to fit the observed galaxy diversity, can successfully replicate other observed phenomena, such as the Tully-Fisher relation. Yet, a key hurdle is overcome when different nations have disparate knowledge of each other's climate initiatives. Our research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by translating existing climate action data into a standardized knowledge base, which can then be queried to discover new climate partnerships and collaborations. Our method leverages a graph database to analyze and link climate action data from various countries, enabling users to discover relevant information through structured queries. We have applied this approach to support the effective mobilization of climate change mitigation efforts, as demonstrated by our analysis of relevant knowledge and potential cooperation opportunities between multiple countries. Long-term, our climate knowledge base can evolve to include predictive analytics, enabling even more effective climate partnerships and a greater chance of global climate change mitigation. Our work offers an innovative solution to addressing knowledge disparities, and its open-source source code can serve as a valuable resource for organizations seeking to expand their climate knowledge and mobilize new climate partnerships. Additionally, the climate knowledge base can facilitate applications beyond climate policy, such as supply chain management and cultural exchange, as well as a wide range of other domain areas. Furthermore, the climate knowledge base can be extended to encompass non-governmental entities, such as corporations and civil society organizations, to further enhance its utility and relevance. Finally, the climate knowledge base can be utilized for identifying and establishing strategic climate partnerships through a tailored recommendation process. Our technique, called SymNNU, employs a two-part approach that utilizes pre-trained transformers for universal event recognition and subsequent refinement via mask-filled span prediction.
By focusing on neglected information, SymNNU uncovers underdocumented symptoms, demonstrating high accuracy in extracting symptoms from unstructured clinical data, particularly for rare diseases and diverse demographics.

Our experimental findings indicate that SymNNU consistently outperforms current methods in extracting symptoms from unstructured clinical data, particularly for rare diseases and diverse demographics, suggesting a more effective approach to universal symptom extraction. A newly developed technique known as Deep Reinforcement Learning holds significant promise in resolving various complexities associated with autonomous driving. Despite recent breakthroughs, more research is needed to tackle real-world challenges such as safety and scalability. To address these issues, a novel architecture is presented that allows for training an autonomous vehicle navigation system using a vast synthetic dataset. By integrating the vehicle's state with a dynamically generated reference system, a consistent coordinate framework is achieved, facilitating the learning process. A substantial synthetic dataset is generated using a 3D simulation environment, with diverse scenarios including traffic signals, lane changes, and other interactions. By applying a policy-based Deep Reinforcement Learning approach, an autonomous vehicle module is developed that effectively navigates and follows roads, lanes, and signs. In recent years, cloud-based personal assistant services have gained immense popularity, largely due to their convenience and seamless access on various devices. However, these services pose significant security risks, encompassing the potential for eavesdropping, data interception, and data manipulation. Furthermore, concerns arise due to the extensive data collections these services engage in. To address the need for secure and data protection-aware personal assistant services, we developed Pando, a cloud-based personal assistant system designed for browser usage. Pando incorporates a novel approach to computing, wherein a client-side web application employs a proxy server to facilitate a divide-between between the user's device and the cloud. This architecture enables us to implement a range of security and data protection functionalities. For instance, we utilized SSL/TLS for encrypting both the user-cloud and proxy-cloud connections, while a locally-running JavaScript engine on the user's device ensures that the personal assistant remains data-bound within the local system. Our evaluation of Pando's security and data protection capabilities reveals a satisfactory level of efficacy in several commonly-encountered personal assistant scenarios. If adequately integrated into widely-used web browsers, we believe Pando has the potential to significantly impact the landscape of personal assistant services in a positive, security-aware manner. Our investigation also discovered that even seemingly basic personal assistant services involve intricate aspects of computation, significant data collections, and multi-level web proxy systems. As such, these services fall within the realm of cloud-based computing. Our analysis further uncovers that a personal assistant program can be viewed as a specific type of multi-agent system, with various agents collaborating to accomplish a shared goal, and with Pando's proxy-based design facilitating an effective implementation of this concept. Additionally, we utilized a system-based approach to specify and evaluate the data protection capabilities and limitations of Pando, and through successive iterations, we refined the system to address these shortcomings. Ultimately, we have come to realize that a personal assistant service is inherently dependent on the interplay between its computational and data-related aspects, and as such, a comprehensive evaluation of these components is essential to ensure a secure and reliable system. Our work with Pando has given us valuable insights into the complex interplay between web applications and their underlying infrastructure, and through our investigation, we unveiled the intricate proxy-based design of modern personal assistant services, revealing how these services rely on cloud-based computing for secure and data protection-aware operations. Our analysis also demonstrates the extensive data collections engaged in by these services, and we have effectively mitigated these risks through our design and evaluation of Pando,

In federated learning, multiple clients collaborate on model development by sharing
client-specific model iterations, typically trained on private datasets. Despite
client-side data privacy protections, models remain vulnerable to exploitation by
unintended parties due to exposure. To address this issue, we introduce Flatee, a
novel framework that integrates federated learning with heterogeneous Trusted Execution
Environments (TEEs). By housing models within separate TEEs, each representing a
distinct client, Flatee ensures both data and model privacy by isolating the
training process from untrusted entities, including the server. This modification
introduces new challenges: (1) normalized model updates, ensuring consistent
development across disparate TEEs, and (2) delayed updates due to TEE boundary
communications, potentially inducing stragglers. To overcome these obstacles, Flatee
centers on an efficient all-reduce algorithm, specifically tailored for multi-client,
multi-TEE scenarios, that maintains model convergence and reduces tail latencies.
Evaluation experiments demonstrate that Flatee supports stable and efficient
federated learning operations within various commercial TEE implementations. This
evaluation validates the potential of Flatee to provide an effective safeguard for
private federated learning environments, even in presence of existing vulnerabilities. 
Finally, this research highlights the complexity of implementing robust federated
learning across multi-client, multi-TEE settings and motivates the exploration of
federated learning within more comprehensive TEE environments. The Flatee source
code is publicly available at github.com/mimofee/flatee. The evaluation dataset is
available at doi:10.6082/FOSS-2023-federated-learning, encompassing various federated
learning applications, trained across both virtual and physical TEE environments. 
This dataset can also be accessed through this link: bit.ly/3nYkTCR. Additionally, the
adversarial evaluation dataset is available at github.com/mimofee/adversarial-eval.

This paper introduces a novel method for automating system call policies across containerized applications, eliminating the need for manual intervention. We have developed a dynamic approach to automatically generate system call policies for individual application components and integrate them into a security-rich kernel environment. This results in a secure and trusted system call framework, which we call Timeloops. As an optional addition, we can also utilize an intelligent system to detect potential security threats in real-time, based on system call patterns. The efficacy of our solution was tested through a simulation-based evaluation of a chat application, demonstrating that Timeloops can effectively protect against attacks with minimal performance impact, even in high-traffic scenarios. Furthermore, the integration of our system call framework with Kubernetes reveals opportunities for automatic system call policy generation and enforcement, thereby enhancing the security of containerized applications. Long-form speech generation through techniques like speech synthesis or speech augmentation necessitate significant amounts of training data, which can be costly to obtain. Current approaches rely on masked speech training, where a portion of the input speech is masked and the model predicts its masked section. Notwithstanding its efficacy, this method poses challenges of its own, chief among them being the potential degradation of speech quality as masks are applied uniformly across long segments of speech. To mitigate this issue, our proposed model, MaskedSpeech, utilizes a masking strategy that is sensitive to the context of speech. Through an examination of the acoustic properties of speech, we deduce that masks should be applied at natural speech breakpoints rather than being placed randomly. To this end, our model incorporates a breaker network that identifies optimal breakpoints for masking. Experimental results indicate improved speech quality when using the breaker network to select masks, which is further substantiated by an analysis of the human evaluation of the generated speech. Code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/orion88/MaskedSpeech.

The proposed method represents an unordered treatment by a series of binary variables and simplifies the calculation of the compliance probability into a linear prediction model. The key advantage of this approach is its ability to utilize large datasets that are categorized rather than continuous, thus providing estimates with reduced variance. The effectiveness of this method is validated through an application to the fields of study in the UK and the US, which yields compatible results: an increase of 5-6 percentage points in the return on investment for subjects studied overnight. The US data reveals a substantial 10 percentage-point increase in returns on investment for arts and humanities fields. To advance our understanding of the kernel of matter, high-precision experiments requiring antineutrons, antiquarks, and specific hidden-charm states are planned. We introduce a production reaction that can provide these necessary particles in sufficient quantities. This reaction involves colliding J/psi mesons with an energy target, yielding a wide range of products including antineutrons, antiquarks, and other essential particles. To achieve this, a beam of J/psi mesons can be directed at an atomic nucleus or a virtual energy contour created by an X-ray free-electron laser. Analyzing the final-state interactions resulting from the breakup of the J/psi meson in a nucleus via relativistic quantum mechanics confirms our prediction's validity. This method is capable of producing numerous antineutrons and other particles and has the potential to serve as a long-duration, high-intensity beam for next-generation high-precision experiments in nuclear and particle physics. A feasible experimental setup for producing this beam in existing facilities or future initiatives such as the ESR in Hamburg, Germany is described. Additionally, we outline how this research can lead to breakthroughs in understanding semiconductor structure, rare nuclear decay, and matter-antimatter symmetry. This work presents a reliable solution to meet the intense beam requirements of future high-precision experiments, resolving concerns previously expressed in the field. Crucially, this research will enable the development of a long-duration, high-intensity beam of antineutrons and other essential particles necessary for high-precision studies in nuclear physics, cosmology, and particle physics. To facilitate this research, we propose constructing an international research beamline for future high-precision experiments at facilities such as the ESR in Hamburg, Germany or a future linac in Shanghai, China. This research will present the first-ever long-duration, high-intensity beam of antineutrons, antiquarks, and other essential particles, yielding a tremendous return on investment for high-precision experiments in nuclear and particle physics, cosmology, and semiconductor research. Most of a multiple star system's final mass is accumulated during the first few million years of its existence, specifically through the disc accretion of low-mass components. In this process, interactions between low-mass companions and surrounding discs are frequent and their outcomes are crucial for understanding how binary and multiple star systems develop. We investigated the accretion rates of low-mass components within triple systems by simulating the interactions between these objects and the discs they reside in. Notably, our model considers the effects of any already present binary components on the accretion process. In our simulations, mass accumulation is largely influenced by the orbital characteristics of the objects, specifically by eccentricities and distances from the primary star's influence. Additionally, our results indicate that eccentricities of around 0.5 are typical for wide-range (10-10,000 astronomical units) low-mass components, with their rates of mass accumulation also heavily dependent on these orbital parameters. In cases of highly eccentric systems (eccentricities above 0.7) that extend far into the protoplanetary disc (up to 10,000 astronomical units), their central star's mass is primarily obtained through accretion from the disc. Furthermore, our results indicate that outer limits of mass accretion in these systems are directly related to the mass of the central star (as predicted by the theory of mass conservation), with mid-range (100-1000 astronomical units) systems however exhibiting super-Solar mass accumulation rates. In these mid-range systems, the object's mass accumulation speeds up as the binary's orbital distance increases beyond approximately 100 astronomical units, with their rates of mass accumulation eventually matching those of isolated low-mass components. In case of any existing binary components within the system, their presence typically reduces accretion rates, with the object's mass accumulation speeds up as the binary's orbital distance increases beyond approximately 100 astronomical units. In addition to these findings, the object's mass also plays a role in its accretion rates, with higher masses resulting in faster accretion. Finally, the object's orbital speed in these systems typically ranges from 0.01 to 10 km per second, with its masses below approximately 0.3 times the mass of our Sun (\odot) experiencing the object's accretion process being dominated by the object's motion, while those above this mass (\odot) experiencing the object's accretion process being dominated by the object's motion only in highly eccentric systems. Our research focuses on inherently flat spacetime models in a lattice, which are naturally occurring in a theory involving a gauge field with monopoles, and we investigate the expansion of a cosmological universe in this lattice framework. Similar to the quantum Hall effect, this lattice structure arises from a non-trivial topological property, and it leads to a universe with a lattice-like spatial geometry. We examined the lattice scaling factor, and found that it follows a power-law dependence on time, with an exponent that is a weighted average of the lattice constants, effectively acting as a scaled cosmological constant. Furthermore, the lattice's spatial periodicity implies a quantum nature, and we investigated the possibility of a quantized expansion rate, yielding a lattice-based spectrum of scalar field fluctuations. Ultimately, the monopole-induced lattice interactions preclude the existence of de Sitter or other types of expanding universes, and we must consider additional mechanisms, such as a dark energy component, to explain observed cosmological trends. These findings were further substantiated by examining the interplay between lattice modulations and the expected monopole-induced interactions, and we found that the latter overwhelmingly dominates the former, thereby necessitating a dark energy explanation for the present-day cosmological evolution. Lastly, although the lattice framework lacks scale invariance, we observed that the distribution of lattice spacings, weighted by their occupation probability, approximates a fractal distribution over a broad range and generates a power-law spectrum, thereby providing a potential explanation for the observed scaling behavior in the universe's spacetime structure. This research can serve as a natural, gauge theory-based implementation of the fractal universe concept. Additionally, we noted that the lattice cosmology may be viewed as an analogue to the modulated FRW model, and we highlighted the efficacy of the static lattice structure in capturing the universe's long-wavelength dynamics, effectively reducing the complexity of the monopole-driven interactions to a single, effective component. Finally, we concluded that the lattice universe is inherently no-scale, and we necessitate a mechanism, such as a dark energy component, to explain the observed cosmological evolution. This research presents a novel variational image segmentation model, derived from the Chambolle and Pock (CP) optimal transport algorithm. The proposed model integrates image segmentation and restoration capabilities, with a unique image representation technique ensuring a coherent whole. By reformulating the total variation minimization as a CP algorithm optimization, we obtained a simplified image segmentation model with edge preservation properties. Furthermore, we demonstrated that this new model can be reduced to the celebrated Mumford-Shah model under specific conditions. Through a series of experimental examples, the advantages of the proposed method over existing state-of-the-art techniques were effectively demonstrated. The results showcase that the novel method successfully achieves seamless integration of segmentation and restoration tasks. The proposed model exhibits robust edge preservation, and its extension to real-world image segmentation applications yielded satisfactory results. The code for this approach is openly accessible via GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/tiepeng1992/image-segmentation. The research data is available via DOI: https://doi.org/10.6086/M122-22.001.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at its center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black holes to explore the potential for ultra-light bosons, induced by black hole superradiance, to influence heavy quasars' spin characteristics. A comprehensive study was conducted with AGNs from the 12th Complete Bright Quasar Catalog, combining observations from various AGN luminosity stages, to establish whether superradiance's impact on black hole spins can be observed in the galaxy's evolution. Our investigation reveals that heavy quasars may have acquired most of their angular momentum not from superradiance, but from other processes occurring during the galaxy's formation. Therefore, if superradiance is responsible for regulating spin buildup, it is likely to influence a wide range of black hole masses across the galaxy's evolution. However, if superradiance is the primary driver of spin buildup, it may primarily affect a specific range of black hole masses. Further research is needed to refine the connection between superradiance and black hole spins, potentially shedding light on the phenomenon's significance in the formation of galactic nuclei.  The associated material, such as data and figures, can be found at https://doi.org/10.6084/m1.fao.2021.12.003.

Clyde, a flexible neural network emulator, seamlessly integrates with Brian, an established framework for simulating neural networks. We built upon this integration by creating an adapter, called Brian2Loihi, which enables efficient conversion of Brian simulations into hardware-compatible code for the Loihi chip. This Loihi-compatible code can then be directly downloaded onto the chip, allowing for a seamless simulation experience across software and hardware platforms. We tested the Loihi emulation process by simulating a diverse set of neural networks, ranging from basic to complex, which confirmed the effectiveness of our implementation. Furthermore, we discovered that the Loihi emulation was remarkably fast, with a notable speedup compared to traditional computer simulations. Interestingly, the speedup ratio exceeded the expectations based on the Loihi chip's specifications, which demonstrates the utility of this implementation in real-world applications. We envision this adaptation to be a valuable resource for researchers exploring the possibilities of hardware-assisted neural network computation. To ensure transparency and reproducibility, we openly provide the source code associated with this project on the Neurosim Toolbox repository. We kindly invite fellow researchers to utilize and further develop this resource. Additionally, we describe the general approach of "reverse engineering" existing simulators to create adapters, which can be applied to other simulators as well, such as NeuronCube, SpinyFlow, Nmodl, FINESSE, and MANA. This comprehensive information is presented in a publicly accessible document, which can be found here: https://neurosim-breizh.readthedocs.io/en/latest/breizh_flow.html#adapter_reverse_engineering. We believe this information will be beneficial to the entire research community as a valuable knowledge base. Furthermore, we developed a novel, flexible, and high-performance adapter for the Spark-SNAP hardware, which is described in the related paper titled "High-speed emulators for spiking neural networks using the C and Cy: frameworks," and is freely accessible through the arXiv platform (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.04519). We've analyzed a wealth of data from the Milky Way's second youngest cluster, Westerlund 2, in order to uncover its mass spectrum of the largest stars within it. Our investigation combines the powers of photometry and interferometric precision, thanks to the access we have to the VorONOID database and the study by Goodwin et al. (2017), respectively. It's worth noting that the resulting mass spectrum we've derived, which spans from roughly 10 to 30 times the mass of our sun, exhibits a smooth, consistent pattern devoid of gaps, thus supporting the idea that massive star formation undergoes a single continuous process. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the rate at which massive stars are formed in Westerlund 2 is significantly higher compared to others in the cluster. The outcomes of our investigation, which reveal a mass range for the cluster's massive star formation, may hold significant implications for the theoretical models of star formation. Additionally, our work highlights the need for a more comprehensive, expansive study of the cluster's early star formation phase. In search of clearer evidence, we suggest observing the cluster during a future interstellar cloud passage, which could reveal additional, younger star formation. Such a development would likely lead to groundbreaking discoveries, thus potentially altering our present understanding of the cluster's early star formation. Lastly, our analysis of the mass spectrum reveals that the cluster's metal content may already be close to the standard values seen in the rest of the galaxy, which could indicate that the cluster is relatively old, albeit still in its main star formation phase. The observed absence of very massive stars in the mass spectrum could imply that such stars may have a shorter lifespan compared to smaller stars, which could lead to their early extinction through supernovae explosions. The outcome of such massive star explosions might then give rise to a starless corridor at lower masses, which would need to be factored in for accurate future mass spectrum analyses. The findings of our investigation, which reveal a relatively uniform mass spectrum, thus corroborate the view that the cluster is relatively young and monolithic in its star formation. Consequently, the massive star extinctions might soon continue to include the remaining cluster stars, which could then lead to a profound environmental transformation. Moreover, our analysis emphasizes the role of early star formation feeding in the massive star formation in cluster environments, which could eventually give rise to dense, star-studded regions akin to globular clusters. The discovery of a relatively uniform mass spectrum might also have far-reaching implications for the theoretical models of star formation

The novel LSTM-based scheme serves as a channel estimator and aids in enhancing the accuracy of Acquire Channel (AC) procedures. Performance evaluations using a Real-time 802.11p simulator indicate that the proposed scheme excels in high-mobility scenarios when compared to existing channel estimation methods. Furthermore, the proposed LSTM-based scheme demonstrated superior resilience to interference and a maximum 56% improvement in performance in comparison to a single LSTM neuron. Consequently, this proposed scheme is deemed suitable for use in ITS applications requiring channel estimation, such as Geolocation and Mobility Assistance Services. The Universal Approximation Theorem states that any continuous function can be approximated by a feedforward neural network. However, finding the optimal neural network weights and architecture remains a challenging task. Despite the theorem's generality, the proof is flawed as it requires infinitely large networks. In reality, achieving precise infinitesimal error demands an excessively large number of neurons, rendering computation impractical. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel method for constructing near-optimal neural networks without manually adjusting architecture or weights. Leveraging the theorem's implications, we develop a unique learning algorithm for the parameters of each layer of the neural network. The proposed approach allows for the realization of an optimal or near-optimal solution in an unbiased manner. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the size of the neural network is substantially smaller than those derived from conventional optimizations, essentially reducing the 'overfitting' issue and enabling the approximation of intricate functions with high precision. The developed framework comprises three key components: an iterative training method, a robust transfer of weights, and an efficient pruning technique for dimensionality reduction of the neural network. Through extensive experiments, we show that the proposed structure outperforms leading state-of-the-art methods, achieving notable enhancements in classification and regression tasks. Specifically, we recorded a 15.5% and 12.3% improvement in accuracy for ResNet50 and AlexNet, respectively, while also achieving a 20.3% improvement in the mean squared error for UCI regression challenges. The proposed method is a groundbreaking improvement over existing neural network design algorithms, providing a practical solution to the historically intractable problem of optimizing neural network architecture and weights. This work further substantiates the efficacy of deep neural networks for a wide array of tasks, confirming the advantages of robust, well-designed neural networks over their shallow counterparts. The source code of this project has been made publicly available at https://github.com/plgunderson/Neural-Network-Structure-Optimization. Additionally, the pre-trained models can be accessed via request to the author. However, these models exhibit a common issue of generating highly detailed but repetitive outputs. In the context of medical imaging, this means generated anatomical representations may lack the complexity needed to effectively visualize local functional illustrations. This challenge is further compounded by the generative model's reliance on periodic activations (like in Switch), which produces repetitive generated content. In response, we introduce modulated periodic activations (MPA) that allow a generative model to generate diverse outputs within a limited computational budget. To facilitate the learning of local functional illustrations, we adopt a generalizable visualization approach called part-orientation invariant training (POIT). Utilizing POIT, the model learns to generate outputs that remain effective even when the ground-truth partial visual information is absent, thus enabling local functional illustration synthesis. Our approach is supported by comprehensive experiments, with our MPA-POIT model demonstrating superior performance over existing methods on the task of generating local functional illustrations in 3D MRI volumes. Furthermore, our model showcases unparalleled efficiency and effectiveness across a range of applications, expanding the possible range of generative models that can effectively learn local functional illustrations. Ultimately, the MPA-POIT model yields a range of novel benefits, such as enhanced generalizability and the ability to perform tasks beyond part-based synthesis, such as generating partial visual information and performing tasks without requiring a complete reference. Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning models remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a simplified representation of deep learning architectures by mapping them to geometric structures comprising generalized solenoids and orthogonal sets of vectors. This simplified framework enables us to derive a formula for the regularization effect of regularization techniques and model reductions, thereby providing a more accurate estimation of their effectiveness. Furthermore, our analysis leads to the development of a self-optimizing training method that autonomously adjusts the model's complexity to optimize performance, thereby eliminating the need for manual parameter tuning. By generalizing our geometric approach, we can apply the concepts of solenoids and vector bundles to the study of neural networks through a deeper, more fundamental understanding of the underlying mathematical structures. In a companion study, we leverage this enhanced understanding to explore the topological and algebraic properties of deep learning models (see arXiv:2207.15911). By reversing the traditional approach of deep learning theory, we derive our results from the targeted geometric and algebraic structures, thereby providing a novel, comprehensive framework for deep learning theory. Additionally, our analysis reveals an unexpected connection between deep learning models and the well-known Weil's theorem, thereby contributing to the broader realm of machine learning and algebraic topology. Lastly, our study includes an exploration of the implicit semigroup operations inherent to deep learning models, thereby opening up avenues for further generalizations and applications of the underlying theoretical structures. As such, this work is a collection of individual research findings, each grounded in the shared geometric and algebraic understanding of deep learning models. These results include novel applications of group theory, algebraic topology, and solenoid theory, along with an unexpected reinterpretation of the Weil's theorem through the lens of deep learning models. A major obstacle in using neural networks to solve sign-problem plagued systems such as the Hubbard model is the tendency for the network to drift towards an undesirable imaginary solution in the course of training. We introduce a novel type of neural network designed to withstand this sign issue, as sign issue-related errors can significantly hinder its performance. By constructing the network so that its responses remain legitimate even when dealing with challenging approximations, we ensure it can accurately handle heavy degeneracy and thermal fluctuations. Furthermore, our novel network architecture allows it to efficiently tackle high-temperature phases, a challenging task for many existing algorithms. Through rigorous testing of our method, we have successfully obtained precise results for the Hubbard model that rival those of exact algebraic calculations, thereby establishing a strong benchmark for future comparisons. As a result, our approach opens up new avenues for solving other complex systems that have hitherto been intractable. The newly developed code for this work is freely available and can be accessed at https://github.com/Arjun-Ojha/MCQNN.

In a composite Higgs model, where $SU(6)/Sp(6)$ is used, the flavor symmetry is identified as an $U(1)$ subgroup of $Sp(6)$. Here, the complex scalar field's', acting as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson, plays the role of a flavon, which bears a flavor charge. Upon the VEV of the flavon, $U(1)_F$ flavor symmetry is broken. This break results in the emergence of a small parameter and consequently generates a hierarchy between the masses of top and bottom quarks. A flavon lighter than the Higgs boson can naturally account for the observed top-quark mass and its ratio without violating the Planck scale. Furthermore, its presence allows for a fit to the observed $R_D/\Gamma_D$ anomaly, which suggests the existence of additional light bosons. A fit to the observed $R_D/\Gamma_D$ anomaly indicates the existence of at least one light boson below approximately 1 GeV. This model offers potential signs of flavor-resonance production in future lepton colliders and the capability to be tested via flavor-changing neutral-current processes in collider experiments. Additionally, it predicts the modification of lepton decays due to the interaction with the flavon and the Higgs boson. A summary of the deviations in various low-energy processes is provided. Lastly, it is noted that although this model can explain the observed $R_D/\Gamma_D$ anomaly, it may not be able to exclusively account for the observed CP-violation in semileptonic decays of neutral kaons without introducing additional complexity. Therefore, it is necessary to test the predictions of this model in various experiments to confirm its validity as a physical theory. On the other hand, even if this model fails to exclusively account for the observed anomalies, it remains a part of a broader theoretical framework that might be a part of a more general theory of composite Higgs models. As such, it is necessary to test the predictions of this model in order to determine whether it is a viable part of a more general theoretical framework. On the other hand, it is possible that the anomalies could be indicators of a more intricate physics connection between heavy scales and the flavon or Higgs boson through their interaction with the flavor symmetry, which would require a reevaluation of the mechanism of anomaly mediation in the context of this model. Therefore, it is necessary to perform thorough tests of the predictions of this model in order to determine its validity

Recent simulations involving the binary creation from collapsing molecular clouds showed promising results, but required further investigation due to the unusual characteristics of the cores involved. These cores, which did not match the typical values for mass and angular momentum, contained massive, extended disks that led to the creation of more massive binaries than typically observed. To address these issues, we recast the binary creation process using cores with masses of 1.00 $\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$ and angular momenta ten times higher, while maintaining constant other parameters. These modifications result in cores that more closely resemble those typically found in the study of molecular clouds. A series of simulations involving the core's collapse were conducted, with and without the effect of turbulence, which led to the creation of binary systems in both cases. These binaries had a mean total mass of 0.47 $\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$ and a mean spatial separation of 14 astronomical units. When compared to observational data, the resulting binary system's properties showed a close match, demonstrating that binary creation via core fragmentation can effectively produce the wide range of binary systems observed in molecular clouds. Furthermore, the technique was found to be effective in determining the system's ejection velocity and direction, which in this case was found to be primarily perpendicular to the core's initial angular momentum axis. These findings support the idea that binary creation via core fragmentation plays a significant role in shaping the final binary system's properties and angular momentum distribution in the star-forming process. Additionally, the technique's ability to reproduce observational data highlights its potential for precision calculations of binary system properties based on core characteristics prior to star formation. Such an ability has the potential to significantly advance our understanding of the star-formation process by linking initial core properties to the final binary system's properties and behavior. Finally, the technique's inability to reproduce binary systems more massive than 3 times the mass of the sun under realistic core conditions raises questions about the feasibility of the binary creation process in the formation of low-mass stars. If binary creation via core fragmentation is unable to produce binary systems in the mass range of 3 $\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$ or less, it raises questions about how turbulence affects core properties and the role of binary creation in the star-formation process. To address these questions and effectively model the binary creation process, a greater understanding of the core's properties and the effect of turbulence are needed. This paper reexplores the connection between finite model theory and algebraic proof systems, focusing on CPT (Choiceless Polynomial Time) and its contrast with PTime. A key element in differentiating these theories involves introducing fake variables to replicate choice operations in a program. This can complicate model-theoretic interpretations, but it's mitigated when it's possible to pinpoint a limited number of 'fake' variables that adequately capture the program's behavior. Building on this insight, it's shown that a specific CPT query, involving distinguishing graphs with certain properties, requires a particular level of complexity (specifically, at least $\widetilde{\mathsf{P}}_{\log}$). Notably, this bound is within the same complexity bound as a corresponding proof system (the extended polynomial calculus, MPC$^+$). This finding suggests that certain CPT queries might need to involve an inherent level of logarithmic size in variables, but it's possible that a more refined theory could yield better results. More generally, it's conjectured that a system with only polynomial size variables would be insufficient for differentiating graphs in PTime. This conjecture aligns with a corresponding hypothesis regarding MPC$^2$, a more powerful proof system (infinitely many variables, but with additional structure). Finally, it's noted that differentiating graphs in PTime is likely an intractable problem, but it's possible it could be solved under certain restricted conditions (for example, using symmetric variables). Unconventional therapies such as homeopathy defy scientific scrutiny due to their research limitations and complexities. Despite these constraints, the public remains receptive to these treatments. We aim to understand the underlying framework of such therapies' legitimacy through analyzing the reasoning patterns of their proponents, specifically those on German homeopathy online forums. Our framework involves identifying the core arguments that can potentially justify the plausibility of these treatments, even in the absence of empirical evidence. By mapping the arguments, we found that the proonents primarily rely on evidencing high treatment satisfaction rates, citing numerous successful personal experiences, rather than empirical research evidence. These findings suggest a system of 'evidential justification' that legitimizes the use of these treatments, particularly through anecdotal evidence. Exploring the relationship between this form of justification and the broader social context may offer new insights into the nature of this type of justification. It also raises significant epistemological concerns that remain largely unsolved. Our research provides a comprehensive analysis of the social framework of unfalsifiable claims, offering a detailed characterization of the type of justification underlying these claims and its implications for our understanding of the interplay between justification practices and the social context in which they operate. Additionally, our study demonstrates the potential of functional research to illuminate the underlying structure of the subject matter even when operating within constrained conditions. Furthermore, we identified key epistemological problems associated with this type of justification, particularly its reliance on the preeminence of individual experiences over empirical research, the relevance of treatment satisfaction as a justification criterion, and the circularity of combining these two factors to justify the success of these treatments. Identifying social media incidents in real-time is crucial for timely detection, yet several existing methods are impractical for large-scale use due to high computational requirements.  We propose an efficient real-time incident detection framework that integrates SVD dimensionality reduction technique to minimize computational costs, combining this with an improved k-means algorithm that incorporates optimal seed selection via density estimation.  Experimental evaluation on extensive datasets reveals our method detects incidents more accurately and processes data at a faster rate compared to existing methods.  Furthermore, we introduce a novel incident tracking approach that estimates vehicle trajectories, effectively mitigating false incident detection rates.  Validation on a large-scale social media dataset confirms our method's effectiveness in tracking incidents, outperforming existing methods in accuracy and computational efficiency.  Notably, our approach reduces computational complexity from quadratic to constant, enabling real-time operation on mainstream hardware even with massive datasets.  Technically, we contribute two novel components - an efficient incident detection algorithm and a trajectory estimation method that generalizes to various tracking methods.  Systematically, we evaluate the performance of three existing tracking methods and showcase the applicability of our approach on social media and microwave oven-related incidents.  Mobilizing such a system in real-world settings, we suggest a scalable deployment strategy that effectively integrates our method with existing surveillance systems.  Ultimately, our method subverts common assumptions about efficiency, effectiveness, and complexity that have hitherto guided the development of incident detection algorithms.  Instead, we showcase that diminishing computational resources can coexist with improved accuracy in detecting social media incidents, thus presenting a counterintuitive solution.  Mathematicaly, we establish the computational complexity of our method as linear and confirm the countercity of our approach through hands-on experimentation.  Additionally, we introduce a novel metric for evaluating incident tracking algorithms, extending the relevance of our contribution beyond detection to tracking.  Conceptually, we envision a future where efficient incident detection algorithms not only minimize computational costs but also diminish societal expenses by detecting incidents early in the process.  Thus, we effectively convert the societal asymptote of incident detection to a linear cost model through our method, presenting a visionary approach to detect social media incidents.  Finally, digitally, we encode the innovative approach of our experimentally validated algorithm using Java programming, showcasing the applicability of our method through interactive web visualization and dataset availability.  Notably, the source codes for our algorithm and visualization are publicly accessible on a CS platform, enabling reproducibility of our results.  Ultimately, we envision our method will revolutionize the development of incident detection

Recent research has demonstrated that machine learning models are susceptible to
adversarial attacks, yet many tests to verify their resilience are limited to
relatively simple scenarios. This study establishes a framework to assess the
adversarial resistance of Bayesian neural networks when dealing with more
complicated real-world applications. By creating a straightforward method to
verify resistance, this work shows that NLP models developed for binary
classification tasks can remain resilient to attacks. Conversely, this research
finds that such models are often unsuccessful in more complex scenarios, and
suggests that there might be an inherent trade-off between a model's
adversarial resistance and its accuracy. As such, this study delves into the
relationship between performance and resistance, and reveals that there could
be an optimal balance point that depends on the specific application at hand. 
Furthermore, this research provides code for verifying the resistance of various
models, including frequency-based ones, and demonstrates the benefits of
utilizing an alternative form of attack that takes into account the specific
characteristics of the target model. Ultimately, this study emerges as a
first effort to thoroughly examine the relationship between performance and
resistance, and showcases the potential for frequentist methods to further
the understanding of Bayesian neural networks' robustness.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in many countries, including China, where a strict lockdown was enforced to curb the spread. Despite these efforts, mysterious pneumonia cases persisted, fueling public fear and prompting officials to announce their investigation. This investigation was met with skepticism from some netizens, who spread rumors claiming the outbreak was a bio-terror attack facilitated by the US. As the pandemic worsened, health workers were allegedly infected and killed, further propelling online rumor circulation. However, our analysis reveals that these rumors showed early signs of decline on the Chinese micro-blogging platform Weibo. We examined the spatiotemporal patterns, propagation mechanisms, and influence of these rumors from February to April 2020. Our results show that virus-related rumors exhibited distinct spatial distributions, peaking during critical pandemic periods and reaching their lowest in mid-March. Our analysis also uncovers the primary nodes driving rumor dissemination and estimates their impact, revealing that most rumors enjoyed minimal spread and died quickly. Notably, our findings suggest that rumor propagation enjoys some government support, a conclusion consistent with official responses. Our study offers data-driven insights into online rumor behavior and spreads during the pandemic, which may contribute to the development of computational models for rumor quashing and influence measurement. The code and datasets for this research are openly available at https://github.com/ChenTaiyang123/Spread_of_rumor_in_China_during_the_pandemic.

This study investigates the effects of spectral dimensionality reduction techniques on hyperspectral image classification. Five methods were tested – principal component analysis, wavelet transform, discrete Fourier transform, discrete cosine transform, and non-negative matrix factorization – to compress remote sensing data while maintaining its utility for classification purposes. The techniques were applied to various datasets, including artificial data, real world hyperspectral images, and a large dataset generated by the CSU-40 simulator. The spectral reduction methods were evaluated using accuracy, pixel purity, homogeneity, and compatibility measures, and were compared to a baseline compression approach using nearest neighbor resampling. The results show that wavelet, Fourier, and cosine transforms are highly effective in reducing dimensions while maintaining high compression rates, and that wavelet and Fourier transforms offer strong performance in terms of compatibility and pixel purity. Furthermore, the best spectral reduction methods outperformed the baseline compression approach in terms of accuracy, pixel purity, homogeneity, and compatibility in some cases, but performed worse in others. The effectiveness of the techniques was found to be dependent on the dataset in question, and the parameter settings used (e.g. number of principal components, wavelet levels, etc.). Nonetheless, this study provides a comprehensive comparison of the effects of spectral reduction methods on hyperspectral image classification, and highlights the potential for these techniques to complement existing compression methods in remote sensing applications. In order to make these models accessible, researchers have developed various techniques to significantly reduce their size, while still being able to accurately generate text. This study focuses on understanding how existing size-reduction methods affect the performance of the compressed models, by examining which specific parts of the model's internal workings are affected by the compression process. We've developed a new approach to efficiently test these hypotheses and evaluated several established models and compression methods, uncovering key insights that can guide the development of more effective compression techniques in the future. Interestingly, our work also revealed that some compressed models can be equally effective as the original models in tasks such as language translation and question-answering, despite being significantly smaller in size. However, their ability to generate coherent text is still impacted by their reduced size. We've made our code, datasets, and other resources used in this study available for other researchers to build upon. A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and precise calculation of crucial chemical shift indicators in proteins, thereby determining the spatial arrangements of proteins. ProCS is calibrated with the results of high-accuracy quantum mechanical calculations, achieving remarkable agreement in predicting the amide proton chemical shifts of a small protein with a minimal error margin of 0.25 ppm (high correlation coefficient of 0.94). ProCS is now compatible with the PHAISTOS protein simulation program and used to determine the most plausible protein conformation by analyzing a simulated double double resonance NMR experiment. ProCS's predictive accuracy for protein structure refinement is also demonstrated using the residues of gaudium in solution, revealing discrepancies in some terminal dihedral angles (average error of 0.7 degrees) and showing potential for resolving smaller angular distortions in proteins. The development of ProCS is expected to significantly contribute to the refinement of protein structures. ProCS's source code is open-access at https://github.com/comp-rs/procs and ready for use in conjunction with the Materials Science Toolbox. The choice of loss function in deep learning is widely viewed as a key decision with limited exploration, under the assumption that some loss functions are inherently superior to others. In this context, our research investigates how different loss functions affect performance in image classification tasks. Through thorough experimentation using ResNet-50, we evaluate eight loss functions on four datasets: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and Tiny ImageNet. Our findings indicate that certain loss functions deliver superior results on image classification tasks, contradicting the common belief that some loss functions are inherently better than others. Moreover, our analysis highlights the significance of hyperparameter selection, advising against the automatic adoption of established loss functions without thorough optimization. Ultimately, our study underscores the importance of rigorous research into deep learning architectures and optimizers, and encourages more nuanced exploration of the role of hyperparameters, including hyperparameter optimization, in the pursuit of better performance in computer vision applications. Additionally, our paper contributes baseline performance estimates for the employed datasets and loss functions, and their accompanying code is available on GitHub for reproducibility.

In a novel type of superconductor featuring paired electrons with both spin and orbital components, we simulate how light influences these pairs within a specially aligned (nematic) state of matter. Under varying light intensities, a distinctive zero-field magnetic response emerges, characterized by an intensification of magnetic susceptibility in direct proportion to the light's power. Below a certain threshold light intensity, the pairs of electrons behave like conventional spins, whereas at higher intensities, they exhibit unique properties. Additionally, we propose a method to measure the paramagnetic response in a specially designed experiment using a light-powered magnetometer. Our research lays a foundational understanding of how light interacts with triplet-cooper-pair-based excitations within the established nematic N=2 superconductor model. Furthermore, we have identified potential avenues to explore unconventional light-electron interactions in novel superconducting materials possessing paired electrons with triplets. These novel materials are anticipated to be free of spin-triplet excitations, but may exhibit similar light-electron interactions as observed in the nematic N=2 superconductor. Consequently, the pairs of electrons may behave in a similar manner, exhibiting a paramagnetic response to light in these novel superconductors as well. However, the interplay between orbital and spin components of these pairs of electrons will likely present a significant challenge in differentiating between conventional and unconventional paramagnetic responses. Conversely, we have identified the potential for an unconventional paramagnetic response to be suppressed, presenting new avenues for research to understand unconventional light-electron interactions in novel superconductors. These novel superconductors possess paired electrons with triplet components but lack spin-triplet excitations, presenting novel phenomena that may be observed through differential light interactions. These research findings may be applied to explore novel ground states in novel superconductors, as well as other novel material systems where unconventional light-electron interactions may be present. Lastly, we have recognized the potential for an unconventional light-electron interaction in novel superconductors, as these materials may be free of triplet excitations but still exhibit novel interactions under varying light intensities. These novel interactions may be differentiated from those observed in the nematic N=2 superconductor by understanding how light interacts with the pairs of electrons in these materials. Conversely, we have identified the potential for novel ground states in these materials to be triggered by unconventional light-electron interactions, as these may enable novel research applications. We introduce a new research area in adversarial machine learning by exploring a minimax game where a learner and an adversary challenge each other in a battle of wits.  The learner seeks to minimize the impact of the adversary's interference, while the adversary aims to maximize his disruptive impact, making the task as difficult as possible for the learner.  From this adversarial mindset, we derive algorithms and theoretical frameworks that incorporate robustness and generalization as key considerations.  Our research provides empirical and theoretical evidence that enhanced adversarial training results in better performance, particularly when it comes to maintaining stability during testing and achieving improved generalization, while also reducing the impact of malicious interference.  Additionally, we investigate the properties of our method through the lens of theoretical convergence, showcasing that our approach is capable of achieving a learnable outcome under the right conditions.  Our work launches a new line of inquiry in adversarial machine learning, and the reader is invited to join us in this research endeavor, as well as to consider alternative approaches to this minimax problem.  We also provide code access to our research through this link: https://github.com/fwendong/Adversarial-Theoretical-Analysis.  Also, the reader is referred to the reference [1] for more information on the adversarial training method, while references [2]-[6] provide further context on related topics of computer science, as well as robust and adversarial machine learning.  Lastly, the reader is referred to reference [7] for more information on the geometric interpretation of our method, as well as reference [8] for the related work on computer science that inspired our research. This demonstrates a deep semantic connection between proofs, replacing the need to analyze proof coherence through cut-elimination. This notion of harmony can also be applied to other forms of structures in Ludics through a process called glorification, but the relationship between harmonization and glorification remains unclear. This paper reveals a new definition for harmony in Ludics that subsumes both glorification and harmony, establishing a key equivalence between harmonization and a form of termination for infinite structures. This new framework provides a general method for determining harmony in Ludics, resolving an previously open problem. Our approach to harmonization also offers a constructive method for recognizing why a given structure is harmonic. This paper further develops a proof normalization technique for extracting a harmony from an original proof, and verifies that this procedure is indeed a normalization for infinite structures, thereby confirming a key result originally found in Proof-Networks. Furthermore, our work reveals a new understanding of the relationship between Proof-Networks and Computational Ludics, allowing us to apply the results from Ludics back to Proof-Networks. A key consequence of our findings is that Proof-Networks and Computational Ludics become equivalent interaction theories. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to efficiently mark boundaries within visually organized data clusters, significantly reducing the required annotations. Our approach leverages both visual and semantic connections among these clusters to enhance their separation, after which we apply a straightforward and efficient ranking process to identify optimal actions. Through both theoretical justifications and practical evaluations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in efficiently leveraging human labels for complex reinforcement learning tasks, achieving nearly the same level of performance as traditional comparative approaches while significantly cutting down the required annotations. Moreover, we show our results are near optimal. We show that a topological space can be represented as a Smyth space if and only if it has a compatible compatible order when subjected to a refinement process. This refinement process, inspired by Scott information and stable functions, can also be used to define a compatible order for any Smyth space, resulting in a form of core-compactness. This core-compact structure possesses its own own reflection and relation-preserving version, which are both useful in the theory of ordered structures. Moreover, this core-compact structure is equivalent to a specific type of Scott information, known as SI*, which has been previously introduced in the literature. This SI* can also be extended to provide a rigorous definition for a broad class of monotonous continuous functions, including those which are continuous in the Scott topology, thereby providing a form of core-compactness for any Smyth space. This core-compact structure possesses several significant properties, including the existence of a form of Scott open sets, a compatible order that is both refined and refining, and a correspondence between Scott information and the cis-fibred categories associated with the space's open sets, which can also be used to define a form of core-compactness for any Smyth space through the cis-fibred categories' own core-compact structure. Moreover, this core-compact structure can be used to provide a form of Scott continuity for any continuous function that is also stable, and a corresponding form of core-compactness for any Smyth space, resulting from the extension of Scott information to SI*, can also be used to provide a form of core-compactness for any Smyth space. This verified price range ensures that prices within it result in optimal gains for both the auction system and its participants. Our mathematical protocol was validated through a numerical experiment, where we simulated a market with knowledge-deficient bidders and askers, and found that prices within it converged to the market's equilibrium value. Furthermore, we analyzed and validated the code used for the simulation, which simulates a double-sided auction environment to investigate price setting mechanisms. Our research provides a theoretical and practical framework for the design and evaluation of double-sided auctions that guarantee fair and stable price settings. In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, hidden system dynamics, and noisy measurements.  Despite the numerous advancements in subspace-based modeling techniques, the issue of extracting informative insights from noisy data still persists when applying these methods to flow data.  This work introduces an innovative approach, Linear and Nonlinear Clarify Optimization (LANDO), which combines kernel regression with a low-dimensionality constraint to develop a sparsity-based filter for dynamic mode decompositions.  By utilizing kernel learning, LANDO captures non-linear patterns in the data, thus enhancing the accuracy of dynamic mode decompositions.  Through the incorporation of a constrained sparse penalty in a variational framework, LANDO obtains an optimal kernel function that achieves a low-dimensional representation of the data, thereby yielding a refined solution for dynamic mode decompositions.  Several numerical examples, featuring various benchmark datasets as well as a study on turbulent flow, demonstrate the efficacy of LANDO in extracting meaningful insights from noisy data, with enhancements observed in both linear and non-linear settings.  Furthermore, the issue of variable seeking is addressed, where the kernel width is shown to have a direct influence on the performance of the model, thereby facilitating the identification of an optimal kernel width that maximizes the accuracy of dynamic mode decompositions.  Unlike current meta-dynamical mode decomptions, LANDO obtains an explicit representation of the kernel function, thereby resulting in improved performance when applied to low-quality data.  Based on these findings, the issue of seeking variables is addressed, where the kernel width is shown to have a direct influence on the performance of the model, thereby facilitating the identification of an optimal kernel width that maximizes the accuracy of dynamic mode decompositions.  Additionally, the non-linearity parameter in LANDO is shown to capture low-frequency patterns, and can thus be regarded as an explicit filter for non-linear components in the data, thus enhancing the issue of variable seeking in dynamical mode decompositions.  This work, therefore, provides an explicit representation of the issues encountered in dynamic mode decompositions and kernel regression, and reconciles the apparent contradictions between these techniques, thereby providing an insightful understanding of their functioning.  Furthermore, the numerical examples presented in this study were generated using synthetic data; these examples demonstrate the robustness of LANDO under various levels of noise, thereby confirming the technique's efficacy in extracting meaningful insights from noisy data, such as turbulent flows.  The optimization problems in LANDO were solved using the Adam optimizer, which is a gradient descent method

Chess players employ a range of strategies known as openings, which are formally defined as a sequence of moves leading to a specific position on the chessboard. Research into chess openings has been hindered by the lack of comprehensive and precise information regarding their implementation. This study seeks to quantify the level of detail in openings by analyzing data from the chess.com online community, focusing on the most prevalent openings. Additionally, we examine the similarities between different openings, discovering a hierarchical relationship in which certain openings serve as building blocks for more complex ones. Our results also reveal discrepancies between the most commonly used openings and those considered optimal by chess experts, highlighting the value of incorporating various perspectives from the chess community to understand openings. Furthermore, a neural network is employed to generate novel openings that adhere to established patterns, thereby enhancing the variety of strategies known so far. Finally, a chess opening library containing over 16 million openings is made available, enabling further exploration and analysis. This study presents a novel approach to studying chess, and its findings can be applied to the investigation of other complex and intricate systems. A comprehensive dataset is made available at: https://github.com/jmgomza/Chess-Openings/tree/master/data-packages. Also, an interactive website at: https://chess-openings.net. Please refer to the full paper (arXiv:2109.09016) for a detailed description of the methods employed and the results obtained. This work has been finalized and the data has been released just before the introduction of Stockfish 12, one of the leading chess engines, which in turn was inspired by the findings presented here. Despite being published in arXiv eight months prior to the release of Stockfish 12, our work provides an initial, broad, and more accessible view of the chess landscape that complements the more technical insights offered by the improved engine. The latter, in turn, has given rise to a new wave of interest in the intricate world of chess, as exemplified by the creation of Chessbox, a modern version of the chess database Leiden. This new tool, based on the data released here, has gained popularity among players of all levels, and has been adopted by the top chess players in the world, and has also been made available through our website at: https://chess-openings.net/chessbox. Three-dimensional (3D) model retrieval techniques are usually designed for users with advanced computer skills. To make 3D model retrieval more accessible to novices, we have developed an innovative drawing-based model retrieval approach that enables 3D shape retrieval through free-hand drawings in a three-dimensional virtual environment. This unique approach involves two distinct phases. Firstly, novice users create simple drawings to learn the underlying search query. This is achieved by analyzing the overall shape features from freely created lines in a 3D VR drawing environment. Secondly, these learned shape features are utilized to identify similar 3D models in a retrieval database. Our experimental findings indicate that, despite initial difficulties in generating suitable queries, users with basic computer skills can effectively employ our drawing-based approach to retrieve relevant 3D models. To facilitate widespread adoption, we also provide access to our drawing-based retrieval protocol, as well as a related database of 3D models known as Air Dataset (ADSD). The Air Dataset currently contains 50,000 3D CAD models and can be accessed through our dedicated website at https://airsd.mining-3d.org/. This comprehensive drawing-based retrieval methodology, along with the associated data resources, have the potential to greatly enhance the accessibility of 3D model retrieval for numerous types of users, including students, professionals, and researchers. Additionally, our approach can serve as a valuable educational tool to introduce basic 3D modeling and computer programming skills to individuals with limited computer backgrounds. Lastly, our drawing-based retrieval approach can provide valuable insights to developers in the field of computer programming, as well as designers and engineers working with 3D modeling software, to improve the overall user experience and efficiency. Freedrawing, a virtual reality (3D) drawing tool developed by our team, is an integral component of this drawing-based retrieval approach. It enables users to create 3D shape features by combining various line styles, such as points, lines, and polygons, in a user-friendly and accessible virtual environment. In other words, the order of consideration is from outcome to muscle patterns to inertial stabilization. In this study, we examined the reverse order of consideration, starting with the stabilization of inertial loads, then proceeding to the description of optimal muscle patterns, and finally aiming to enhance motor performance through outcome feedback. Our findings revealed significant discrepancies between predicted and actual movement outcomes, coupled with notable differences between predicted and actual muscle activation patterns. Furthermore, the experimental outcomes were compared to the predicted patterns, and we demonstrated that the EEEF hypothesis can be utilized to reverse-engineer an effective motor behavior by analyzing the relationship between movement outcomes, muscle patterns, and inertial loads. Similarly, the predicted muscle activation patterns also demonstrated a strong agreement with the actual experimental results. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Existing models successfully complete goal-based navigation tasks by utilizing diverse image features and memory mechanisms to track navigation history.
However, most navigation datasets contain objectives that can be easily identified using common image features, leading navigation models to overlook the information in their memory, as the goals are often readily available in the image.
To address this issue, we introduce a new task that requires agents to select relevant memories that contain information not visible from the starting point or the goal.
Our proposed model, MemoNav, outperforms existing models by effectively utilizing both the starting point and the goal, as well as the agent's navigation history to complete the task. Additionally, we develop a new metric to evaluate memory utilization and find that existing models are poorly adapted to this new task. Our research revealed that, for a certain class of CFTs, the OPE and Milne methods yield consistent results. However, significant differences exist between these approaches and the CFT methods employed by example CFTs, such as the $BC_d$ family. To better understand the OPE, we developed a novel approach for directly computing primary field decay rates. Furthermore, we explored how primary field decay rates are affected by degeneracy. Lastly, we investigated the behavior of primary field decay rates in the superconformal algebra and the consequences for operator growth, including the finding that primary field contributions become less significant as time progresses. Overall, our research addresses various questions and provides insight into the complex field structures of CFTs, ultimately shedding light on the fundamental nature of operator growth.
