This paper examines the distinctness problem for meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a projective variety. We define and explore two types of distinctness, namely rational and algebraic distinctness, along with their respective implications. We establish a significant result regarding the maximum dimension of a set containing mappings that are only rationally distinct. Furthermore, we prove a corresponding result for mappings that are algebraically distinct, demonstrating convergence to a degree of mapping. The concept of algebraic distinctness can be viewed as a variation of the classical Chow theorem. We also investigate the relationship between rational and algebraic distinctness, showing that the latter implies the former but not necessarily vice versa. The introduction of a measure-related concept for mappings that are rationally distinct reveals connections to the Chow theorem and the Green-Tao conjecture. We aim to further develop this concept and rectify the analogue of the Chow theorem for meromorphic mappings, addressing a longstanding unsolved problem. This research also addresses the analogue of the Chow theorem for dominoes, showcasing a solution under specified boundary conditions. The concept of algebraic distinctness can be extended to the case of mappings from a non-Kähler manifold, offering a unifying framework that reconciles existing results for Kähler and non-Kähler manifolds. Finally, we establish a result concerning the algebraic distinctness of meromorphic mappings from a Steiner surface to a projective variety, demonstrating its implications and showcasing its variation when applied to the non-Kähler manifold case. We develop a new algorithm to calculate the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system, which is a critical component for solving parametric polynomial systems. The algorithm utilizes signature-based codimension bounds and a new signature-filtering technique to efficiently reduce the codimension of the nondegenerate locus, ultimately enabling us to decompose it into simpler components. Each of these components can be further analyzed through a variant of the nondegenerate locus, which we refer to as a minimal nondegenerate occurrence. Additionally, the algorithm includes an implementation of a new minimal model computation strategy via signature-filtering, which can be used to establish minimal nondegenerate occurrences and provide a clearer understanding of the structure of the nondegenerate locus. The algorithm is now available as the package `NondegenerateLocus` for the Mathematica computer algebra system. Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess over hadronic contributions in $|y|<2.2$ and $|η|<2.2$, the observed $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess can be attributed to a nearly isotropic yield of inverse photon nature. The amount of photons at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ is marginally below the estimated amount based on quark-gluon plasma (QGP) calculations for medium-induced losses. By comparing Cu$+$Cu and Au$+$Au collisions at 200 GeV, we find that photonic signatures show a slight decrease from two larger systems. Hence, we infer that the photonic signatures of the QGP in smaller systems do not deviate from those predicted by QGP calculations, thereby offering grounds for the disappearance of QGP at the end of the rapid thermalization phase. Furthermore, we find that photonic signatures from small systems follow a trend intermediate to those of gluon and quark jets, thereby reinforcing analogous findings in smaller systems and lower energy collisions. Lastly, we estimate the photon v2 to be at the order of -0.05 (with uncertainties) for $2<|η|<3$ and $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$. Hence, we infer that the photonic signatures are vulnerable to side-by-side interactions in the course of their formation. Moreover, we find that photonic signatures can serve as sensitive indicators of anisotropic phases of matter at low momentum, even after the rapid thermalization phase. Finally, we infer that photons at low momentum can still offer valuable insights into the properties of the QGP, even after their emission from the quark-gluon phase of matter. Moreover, we find that QGP calculations at low momentum ($p_T$ < 5 GeV/$c$) predict a higher $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess than QGP calculations at high $p_T$ (up to 20 GeV/$c$), thereby illustrating the diversity of photonic signatures that emerge within distinct QGP scenarios. Moreover, we find that the differences in photonic signatures between two QGP scenarios at low and high $p_T$ could be attributed to differences in terms involving the square of the gluon polarization

The Turan tetrahedron problem sought the smallest excess in a tetrahedron-free graph of a specified size, with all vertices having a connection to at least three other vertices. This issue has been addressed for any $n$ with $n\geq 12$, and the findings confirm that the known lower and upper limits are equal, thereby solving the problem for all relevant $n$. The proof involves demonstrating that any given set of at most two edges in a tetrahedron-free graph cannot both have their endpoints connected to a third point and be close to each other without violating tetrahedron-free constraints, thus allowing the construction of a tetrahedron-free graph with nearly maximal density for any given $n$. Additionally, an algorithm is developed that identifies a set of approximately nearly-dense tetrahedrons in a tetrahedron-free graph, which are then demonstrated to be sparse enough to validate the constructed upper limit, thus confirming the original problem's solution. An independent examination of this process and its implications in a different context yields a similar finding, with the result that any tetrahedron-free graph on at most 12 vertices can be represented as a union of at most four tetrahedrons, which can be densely connected to each other without violating the constraints of a tetrahedron-free graph. Furthermore, it is proven that any tetrahedron-free graph on at least 13 vertices must contain at least five such tetrahedrons, as well as an upper limit on the ratio of its vertex density to edge density, which can be applied to various other sparse graph types with similar results, including a confirmation of a previously proposed problem's solution for a different $\b$ value. Lastly, it is confirmed that any tetrahedron-free graph on at least 14 vertices must contain at least six such tetrahedrons. The proof involves an iterative process that allows a vertex and its connected points to add new edges in a way that maintains a tetrahedron-free graph, which can then be applied to various other sparse graph types with similar results. Furthermore, an upper limit on the ratio of a tetrahedron-free graph's vertex density to edge density is confirmed, which holds not only for the originally considered $\b=2$ case, but also for any $\b$ in the range $1\leq \b <2$. The multivariate interpolation operator is a vital tool that combines data smoothing and interpolation techniques. Researchers have recently proposed a novel transcendental interpolation method, which builds upon existing radial basis function (RBF) schemes by incorporating derivative information to achieve more accurate results. This new approach led to the development of a positive definite interpolation operator, which preserves data shape while providing higher order accuracy. We have modified this operator to create a quasi-interpolation method that requires less computation and preserves data shape, despite not being positive definite. The proposed method can handle noisy data and demonstrates higher order accuracy, making it an effective tool for data smoothing and interpolation applications. The theoretical accuracy of the method was validated by conducting convergence analysis, and our results are further supported by a series of numerical experiments. The study confirms that the method achieves convergence orders of at least $C^{2k+1}$ for interpolation and $C^{2k}$ for differentiation, where $k$ represents the degree of the interpolation spline. These orders are in line with the known convergence orders for traditional RBF quasi-interpolation methods, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach. The study provides new insights into the development of shape-preserving interpolation methods and establishes a new standard for future research. The proposed method has numerous practical applications, including data analysis, image processing, and the approximation of field functions. Furthermore, the study confirms the method's ability to handle noisy data, which is a critical feature for real-world applications. The series of numerical experiments conducted to validate the method's performance in various scenarios, including thin plate splines, demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving high levels of accuracy even in the presence of noise. The study reveals that the method's error values are comparable to or lower than those obtained with other interpolation methods, showcasing its superiority in real-world data analysis applications. The confirmation of the method's convergence orders and error bounds in numerical experiments underscores the accuracy and precision of our approach, which outperforms existing interpolation methods in real-data applications. The study provides a new standard for the development of shape-preserving interpolation methods, and our results have the potential to influence future research in the field. The proposed method has a wide range of applications, including data smoothing, interpolation, and derivative approximation, and can be extended to translate RBF techniques into real-world problems, such as data smoothing and image processing. The novel RBF method developed in the study, which preserves data shape and achieves high orders of accuracy even in the presence of noise, has the potential to improve these tasks. As a result, real-time data on road conditions is limited, leading to inaccurate predictions of traffic patterns. This paper seeks to rectify this issue by developing an automated system for collecting road condition data through the analysis of meteorological patterns and traffic behavior. A multi-class dataset has been established to define weather patterns based on traffic behavior and it is used to evaluate the performance of Convolutional Neural Networks. This method not only saves computational resources but also enhances the accuracy of the network by 10% by optimizing the size of the training dataset. The implementation of this autonomous system would enable the collection of road condition data in real-time, enabling traffic managers to make more informed decisions. We identify four key areas of interaction: science assessing climate change impacts, institutional responses, and the economic consequences, which can further lead to the establishment of new standards. We provide a comprehensive overview of these interactions and conduct a detailed analysis of the role of science-based information. To this end, we develop a dynamic model that accounts for feedback among these interactions, and employ the use of fuzzy sets and fuzzy operators, specifically the Max-Min operator, to incorporate uncertainty inherent in these processes. We utilize fuzzy metrics to measure the stability of our model. We proceed to investigate how climate change information exchanges with other social standards in an institutional context. We introduce fuzzy metrics to gauge the interactions and apply the Max-Min operator, and draw inspiration from decision-making theories such as VIKOR and TOPSIS to develop a standard evaluation metric. Our approach integrates adaptability and robustness criteria into the assessment. We undertake a numerical study to illustrate our method and analyze the effectiveness of our metric for interacting standards. To model the interactions, we adopt a dynamic system of fuzzy difference equations, and employ resonant Lyapunov functions to establish stability properties directly from these equations, and utilize a technique from model predictive control to establish conditions under minimal control. We apply our metric in a case study of institutional standards for the impact of climate change on the economy, and extend it by incorporating stability properties directly into the assessment, and utilize a max-min optimization problem to obtain a perfect standard. Soft grippers are gaining popularity due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling them poses significant challenges, primarily rooted in nonlinearity and non-trivial nonlinarity-related issues. To tackle these problems, researchers have turned to simplified models and reduced-order approaches. However, these models often lack sufficient representation of the original system's complexities. To address this, we propose an online control system that integrates a simplified model generated through the Koopman operator theory. This novel approach enables the creation of an reduced-order model without prior knowledge of the original system's dynamics, thus offering more accurate representations. Integrating simulation and control functions, our system allows online tracking of the gripper's finger positions. To test its efficacy, we conducted multiple experiments using a three-fingered soft gripper under various control schemes, including a linear quadratic control designed for the reduced-order model and a novel, adaptive grip-control method. Results from these experiments demonstrate the substantial reduction of errors and the improvement of tracking performance when utilizing the proposed online control system. The associated code can be accessed via https://github.com/robotics-koopman/online_control_soft_gripper. Developed originally for organic organic chemistry, the Organic Gradient Descent method has been successfully applied to the synthesis of organic chemicals. In this paper, we broaden the scope of Organic Gradient Descent by incorporating a novel exploration strategy. In our enhanced version, each bond breakage probability is determined by a randomized factor, facilitating the creation of diverse reaction paths. This modification enables the discovery of more synthetic routes, notably allowing for the generation of chiral molecules through stereospecific reaction pathways. Furthermore, our updated algorithm demonstrates improved efficiency in synthesizing complex molecules, given sufficient data. Our findings reveal a significant enhancement in the number of feasible synthetic pathways, alongside an improved yield rate for challenging molecule constructions. In particular, the Organic Gradient Descent method with our proposed modifications successfully generated 93% of chiral molecules in its searches, given the presence of a relevant database, while also achieving a notable rise in the success rate of synthetic molecule constructions from 95.5% to 98.5%. In contrast to previous versions of Organic Gradient Descent, our enhanced algorithm facilitated the simulation of synthetic pathways for complex biological compounds such as steroids and terpenes, thereby marking a significant expansion of its applicability to distinct reaction domains. Notably, our updated results show a notable alignment with real-world synthetic practices in both the diversity of reaction paths and the percentages of feasible synthetic pathways. To validate its efficacy further, our enhanced Organic Gradient Descent method was used in the simulation of an artificial syntheses library for an anti-cancer drug, thereby resulting in multiple novel, clinically relevant synthetic pathways that weren't previously part of the initial drug synthesis library. In essence, our updated Organic Gradient Descent algorithm, characterized by its efficient exploration of reaction spaces through randomized bond breakage probabilities, demonstrates improved versatility and synthetic efficiency over its predecessor. Additionally, our enhanced version stimulates the discovery of innovative synthetic strategies for complex molecule constructions, thereby representing an indispensable tool in the development of synthetic chemistry. In particular, our updated results may contribute to advancements in the design of synthetic libraries for medication discovery by uncovering novel, reduced-cost pathways to target molecules. Furthermore, our enhanced Organic Gradient Descent method may serve as a valuable prototype for the development of novel bio-inspired optimization algorithms, thereby promoting transitions between inspiration and implementation more effectively. Lastly, our updated results demonstrate the applicability of Organic Gradient Descent in domains beyond organic chemistry, thereby suggesting its potential extension to the synthesis of inorganic compounds through analogous reaction mechanisms. High-energy emissions from ancient radio sources are potentially powered by a distinct electromagnetic phenomenon known as rapid variability. However, researchers believe that this emission is largely a legacy of lower-z sources, whereas younger sources are more likely to exhibit lower energy emissions. Our recent discovery of a z = 4.575 radio source, named J2102+6015, is an exceptional case. This high-redshift source not only exhibits extremely low energy emissions but also displays prominent jet features similar to those typically found in lower-z sources. Our study provides the first detailed look at this enigmatic source through both its host galaxy's optical emission and its multi-frequency radio spectra. Our analysis of its spectral energy distribution reveals a relatively low mass for the host galaxy (~10^10 M_⊙). Furthermore, our data combined with a detailed modeling of the jet's structure, reveal a total radio luminosity of (~10^25) Jy kpc^(-1), a large opening angle, and suggest that J2102+6015 may be in an early stage of its evolution. Our study using the SDSS DR9 spectrum of the brightest galaxy at the center of J2102+6015, however, uncovers notable emission lines that are likely powered by a compact active galactic nucleus. Our analysis of J2102+6015 not only surpasses, but also exceeds the criteria set forth in the FR2 subclass definition, which includes lower-z sources with similar low energy emissions. J2102+6015's extraordinary characteristics make it an exceptional example of a z > 4 radio source. This source may potentially resolve long-standing uncertainties surrounding the coexistence of low energy emissions and high-redshift radio jets. Moreover, its exceptional properties may challenge our existing understanding of the lifespan and evolutionary trajectory of giant radio sources. Our study of J2102+6015, which exhibits low energy emissions at z = 4.575, raises an intriguing hypothesis that giant radio sources may be experiencing a 'youthful' phase characterized by both high-redshift and variable low-energy emissions. This 'youthful' phase could be a critical period in the evolution of these sources. Moreover, our study suggests that J2102+6015 may be an ideal candidate for observing the activation of its jet, given its exceptionally low energy emissions and high-redshift properties. Our data also reveal a significant decrease in the luminosity of its radio core, which may indicate ongoing jet activation or suppression. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple information sources like clinical text, images, and medical history for a more comprehensive prognosis.
 
The proposed framework, consisting of an image feature extractor, a clinical text encoder, and a multi-learnable prognostic module, demonstrates superior performance on a large lung cancer dataset by achieving significantly higher accuracy in predicting patient survival times compared to other methods, including textual and multi-modal approaches. Moreover, the study highlights the importance of incorporating multiple information sources for lung cancer prognosis through thorough experimental analysis.
 
The findings of this research reveal that (i) incorporating multiple information sources yields better outcomes than single-information approaches, (ii) image information yields negative impacts on prediction performance, (iii) combining clinical text and medical history can lead to substantial performance enhancements, (iii) the prognostic module can effectively learn to predict lung cancer survival times from multi-modal information sources, and (iv) the prognostic module can also effectively utilize image information to improve prediction performance. This research is expected to contribute positively to multi-modal learning in cancer prognosis, and the associated code can be accessed via the link provided at the end of this document for reproduction of the results and further validation of the approaches.

A major challenge in reinforcement learning involves representing a state with sufficient detail to guide optimal action-taking. Natural language has been explored as a viable option to enhance representation learning and transfer knowledge across domains. Despite recent advancements in using natural language as state representation, it poses significant issues, notably lack of explicit structure and ambiguity, hindering practical application. This overview addresses these concerns by examining methods to incorporate natural language state representation, focusing on relevant techniques such as multi-modal learning, attention mechanisms, and neural network design. It also delves into key issues and offers potential directions for future research to tackle the inherent difficulties in using natural language as state representation. As a result, this summary provides a comprehensive understanding of the topic, making it an ideal starting point for new research initiatives. Introduction and related work provide a foundational understanding, while the core challenges and proposed solutions are highlighted. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new dataset by merging these resources to create a comprehensive
set of annotated data that can be utilized for training sentiment analysis models. An
LSTM-based framework was developed and tested on this combined dataset, yielding promising
outcomes. Our proposed model not only outperformed existing baseline models but also served as
a benchmark for comparing the effectiveness of various feature engineering methods for
binary sentiment classification. Additionally, our study showcases the potential of using
LSTM-based models for handling text-based sentiment analysis tasks. Our open-source code
and the gathered dataset are both accessible for reproduction and further exploration. 
Keywords: Text Sentiment Analysis, LSTM, Twitter, Sentiment Databases, Dataset Construction, Benchmark, Benchmarking, Benchmark Dataset, Benchmarking Dataset.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for extensive user involvement.  To address this issue, our proposed
approach centers on assigning a role to users to guide the development of a
meaningful conversation.  Specifically, our system compiles user inputs into a
standardized format,  applies a language model to produce responses, and
automatically determines response categories to facilitate a coherent
conversation flow.  Furthermore, to mitigate the adversarial effects of user
input, our system incorporates a module that identifies and filters harmful
content.  Evaluation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in
maintaining a healthy conversation flow and enhancing overall conversation
quality.  Notably, our system achieved a content safety rating of 4.17, well
above the average of 2.81 achieved by human developers,  specifically, our
system outperformed human developers in overall conversation quality by 0.56,
indicating a substantial 79% relative improvement.  Code and model artifacts are
publicly available at https://github.com/jaydenpan99/Role-Specified-Open-Domain
-Dialogue-System.  This study was supported by China under Grant

To overcome this limitation, a new framework integrates a massive open online encyclopedia with a semantic signaling game to establish a common ground for collaborative communication. A vast knowledge database, which encompasses detailed entry descriptions and interconnected relationships, serves as a shared understanding platform. To facilitate emergent communication, a signaling game design is employed, which generates temporal social contexts enabling agents to discover and agree on novel conceptual links among the offered information. To effectively navigate this signaling game, a neuro-symbolic causal reasoning agent is designed, which combines the efficacy of symbolic reasoning with the flexibility of machine learning. This new agent modularly integrates sequential learning with symbolic causal entanglement, yielding an emergent language capability, thereby enabling it to discover latent causal connections among the signaling game's temporal context, offered information, and recipient's queries. Through the utilization of causal graphs for knowledge compaction and the encoding of latent causal variables, the proposed approach surpasses state-of-the-art models in knowledge grounding, as evaluated on the widely adopted FG-KG dataset. Moreover, the developed agent successfully discovers new knowledge categories, extracts related entity embeddings from the knowledge database, and agrees on novel conceptual links with other agents through the signaling game, thereby facilitating emergent semantic exchanges in dynamic collaborative scenarios. The widespread adoption of interactive systems has created an opportunity for a new type of recommender system - session-based recommendation. The goal of these systems is to predict the next item a user will choose, based on their current session history of selected items. Current approaches to developing such systems are either focused on modeling the characteristics of selected items or on predicting future item selections by analyzing the user's current session. Nevertheless, they both overlook the essential role of understanding how selected items behave in a user's ongoing session. In an effort to address this gap, we introduce a new method called CSR, which utilizes item embeddings that change over the course of a session and captures the dynamic nature of user interactions. The CSR method consists of two main components: it uses a supervised learning module to develop item embeddings based on how selected items behave throughout a user's session, and a collaborative filtering module that generates recommended items based on the user's current session. The effectiveness of our approach is evident from our extensive empirical analysis, which includes eight real-world datasets, reveals that CSR consistently outperforms ten other established methods in terms of precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC. Moreover, we found CSR to be scalable and efficient, with a time complexity of O(n) and a space complexity of O(1), allowing it to easily integrate with existing recommender systems and perform well even in large datasets. The proposed session-oriented recommender system, along with its accompanying code, is now available online for the convenience of the research community. Moreover, we conducted a thorough set of experiments to examine how the components of CSR contribute to its performance and found that its candidate rank embedding module is pivotal to its success. We further demonstrated the theoretical underpinnings of CSR through the development of an analytical model, which confirms the essence of our method and reveals it to be a representation learning problem. Ultimately, we found CSR to be a versatile approach, with applications in various domains beyond just session-based recommendation, such as enhancing the quality of click-through datasets and improving the accuracy of future item predictions. We consider a non-self-adjoint Dirac operator on a compact, flat riemannian manifold with a zonal symmetry, equivalently an infinite strip in R^2, equipped with a metric that is symmetric under reflections in the boundaries. The operator is extended by a finite-band elliptic approximation, which we prove to be elliptic and bounded in the Hs space for any s less than or equal to 1/2. The approximation exhibits a compact resolvent for any band width and finite-band energies are in the L^2 space, rendering them finite. Additionally, we show that these energies are continuous with respect to band width. Following this, we establish a link to a related operator on an infinite strip in R^2 and demonstrate that its finite-band energies are equivalent to those of an unbounded tridiagonal operator, which yields a new interpretation of the latter's spectrum. Finally, we briefly discuss the connection of these findings to the boundness of the resolvent of the original non-self-adjoint Dirac operator. The latter's conclusion is contingent upon resolving a positive injectivity radius conjecture. The operators we study can be seen as perturbed versions of a bounded Laplacian on an infinite strip in R^2. The results we obtain hold equally for several variants of the operators we consider, whose characteristics are described in the main text of the article. The operators in question include Dirac, Laplace and Witten type operators. adoption. In an effort to overcome these challenges, this research aims to

This study focuses on transferring knowledge from a black-box decision model, specifically those representing neural networks, without requiring explicit knowledge representation. Instead, knowledge is transferred by modifying the input, based on classification outcomes from the target model. A two-step approach is proposed to achieve this transfer, which involves developing a novel representation for the output space of the target model, and creating a function to generate counterfactual attributions for the input data. These attributions simulate the effect of unseen "knowledge-bearing" inputs on the output. By combining these components with a black-box model, a streamlined training process is achieved, eliminating the need for explicit knowledge to be tuned during training. Experimental findings on various datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this knowledge transfer method in a zero-shot setting. Notably, this approach performs similarly to methods requiring explicit knowledge for semantic segmentation and sentiment analysis tasks, while offering a more practical solution for domain experts. Code and dataset resources are publicly available at https://github.com/asharakeh/Zero-Shot-Knowledge-Transfer. Additional details are provided in the supplementary material, accessible through the following link: https://asharakeh.github.io/Zero-Shot-Knowledge-Transfer-supplement.html. ZSKT showcases promising results on low-resolution images, achieving comparable performance on the PASCAL VOC 2007 challenge, even when direct training from the dataset is prohibited (zero-shot from SBD). Importantly, this approach can be easily adopted by domain specialists, reducing the required data for training by approximately 75%. A detailed investigation of the theoretical and practical underpinnings of this approach is presented in an accompanying report, available at https://asharakeh.github.io/Zero-Shot-Knowledge-Transfer-supplement.html. Key concepts are also explained in the main paper and a companion video, also accessible through the aforementioned link. One distinct feature of Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer is its reliance on counterfactual reasoning, which is evaluated and validated through an in-depth analysis of its behavior, presented in the supplementary material. Additionally, the method is demonstrated to be effective even when faced with noisy data, thanks to its ability to identify and mitigate the influence of adverse examples, as shown in the accompanying supplement. PAC codes are a type of error-correcting code that can correct arbitrary errors, not just limited to syndromes, which enables them to correct errors in codes with an infinite minimum distance. This correction capability, however, comes at the cost of higher latency and computational complexity due to the need for iterative decoding and error correction. Unlike conventional block codes, PAC codes rely on infinite-dimensional code spaces, which typically result in higher encoding and decoding complexities and latencies. This study focuses on enhancing the metric used in PAC code decoding and proposes a new error correction approach called selective PAC (SPAC) codes, which aim to correct errors while minimizing computational overhead. The key differences between SPAC and PAC codes concern the metric used and the way errors are propagated during decoding. Unlike PAC codes, which iterate until the desired metric threshold is reached, SPAC codes only iterate a limited number of times and stop when errors cease to spread further. This study evaluates SPAC codes for binary and ternary channels and assesses their performance across various channel conditions, comparing their performance to PAC codes. The results indicate that SPAC codes can correct errors in codes with finite minimum distances efficiently and offer improved latency and computational complexity relative to PAC codes, while also outperforming PAC codes in terms of bit-wise, block-wise latency and computational complexity. Furthermore, SPAC codes excel in latency and computational complexity when the packet error rates are low. To reduce decoding complexity, this study proposes two simplification methods, sparse and truncated PAC codes, which can be considered as generalized versions of traditional block codes, with the latter exhibiting lower complexity than PAC codes. The study evaluates these simplified architectures and finds that they perform sub-optimally compared to SPAC codes but offer improved latency and computational complexity relative to PAC codes, particularly in terms of reduced state complexity and computational overhead. The findings indicate that SPAC codes can be regarded as hybrid versions of traditional block and PAC codes, which offer improved latency and computational complexity while maintaining performance comparable to PAC codes, making them a more practical alternative. Additionally, the study presents two other architectures based on PAC codes, PAC-GF and PAC-SD, which aim to reduce latency and computational complexity by leveraging Gaussian approximations and scale-down factor techniques, which can lead to a complete elimination of state complexity in some cases. The study evaluates these architectures and finds that they perform close to SPAC codes, with PAC-GF codes exhibiting lower latency and computational complexity than SPAC codes, particularly when there is no error, while PAC-SD codes display reduced computational complexity

In SRAM-based systems, especially those used in IoT and mobile applications, extracting truth from random number generators is a significant challenge. Typically, SRAM failure modes are exploited to generate randomness from bit flips in memory, but the underlying physics of SRAM reliability is poorly understood. This knowledge gap makes it difficult to intentionally induce sufficient errors for successful randomness extraction. To address this issue, we introduce TuRaN, a novel approach that produces high-quality random numbers by manipulating system voltage to cause SRAM failures in a controlled manner. TuRaN's underlying model, developed through electrical analysis, allows for precise adjustment of voltage levels that enable the optimal balance of randomness and robustness, a critical consideration for battery-powered devices. The trade-off between efficiency and security can be finely tuned, enabling TuRaN to generate up to 1.3 GB/s of random data on a state-of-the-art processor while consuming approximately 0.5 W of power, a performance that surpasses current leading methods by nearly an order of magnitude. The source code enables users to replicate our results and provides a flexible platform for integrating TuRaN into various applications, including IoT devices and mobile phones. The efficiency and effectiveness of TuRaN, combined with its open-source availability, make it an ideal solution for organizations seeking to implement robust and secure random number generation in real-world contexts. They involve complex mathematical expressions that require resolution either by using analytical methods or numerical tools.
While both options exist, the main focus of this publication is on employing a novel approach for Feynman integral evaluation.
This approach utilizes a causal graph representation to numerically evaluate Feynman integrals.
The method is evaluated through a set of examples, including planar and non-planar Feynman integrals.
The results indicate that this technique is highly effective, even for cases where other methods face difficulties.
The code implementing this approach is openly accessible on the GitHub platform at <https://github.com/Prophecy3d/CausalDifferentialEquations>.

This tool will enable the evaluation of Feynman integrals up to high loops and high energies. 
The integration tool will be released once completed, and at that time, this abstract will be updated with the relevant information. 
Until then, further details about this tool and its functionality can be found at <https://feynart.org/causaldepiction>.

The ability of large water clusters to act as a probe for fundamental chemical processes in the atmosphere comes with two key assumptions. Firstly, it presupposes that the hydration of surfectric compounds behaves similarly to the hydration of pure acids, and secondly, it assumes that the dynamic behavior of these clusters can be understood through classical mechanics. A recent study tested the validity of the latter assumption by examining the importance of quantum vibrations in sulphuric acid's (H2SO4) small water clusters, ranging from zero to eight water molecules. Utilizing high-level path-integral molecular dynamics simulations, researchers found that the sub-10 water H2SO4 cluster does not meet the requirements of its larger counterparts as the influence of zero-point motion increases notably at lower water content. As a result, it is suggested that the conventional classical mechanical approach may not be sufficient for understanding the thermodynamic properties of small H2SO4 clusters, and therefore, the utilization of such clusters in modeling fundamental chemical processes in atmospheric systems should be approached with caution. However, the potential discrepancy between quantum and classical descriptions diminishes as the cluster size grows, and thus, it is hypothesized that the classical mechanical approach may be more accurately applied to larger H2SO4 clusters. Moreover, it is noted that the special thermodynamic properties of H2SO4, marked by negative heat of hydration, differ from those of other substances whose heat of hydration is positive. Consequently, it is conjectured that the behavior of H2SO4 clusters may be distinct from that of other substances, and the influence of zero-point motion may also affect the hydration of other surfectric acids in a similar manner. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Technologies.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  The key obstacle to overcoming this challenge is capturing complex language nuances that are difficult to model using traditional machine learning approaches.  In this paper, we explore the efficacy of Transformer-based models in addressing this issue, specifically by investigating their capacity to capture subtle linguistic cues in the context of automated essay scoring.  The study compares various Transformer models, assessing their performance on tasks such as essay classification, text classification, sentiment analysis, and language modeling.  Notably, our results reveal that Transformer models consistently outperform long-established machine learning models in these tasks.  To further enhance their performance, we investigate data augmentation techniques such as BERT-tie and BERT-MLM, finding them to be effective in improving task accuracy.  The research contributes to the existing literature by advocating for the utilization of Transformer models in applications involving complex language understanding.  The associated code and model implementations are publicly accessible on GitHub and Hugging Face Datasets and Transformers platforms.  The dataset used in this study can be sourced from UCI's Machine Learning Repository.  The research has practical implications for applications like automated essay grading, language modeling, sentiment analysis, and text classification, as well as more general NLP tasks like machine translation, summarization, and question-answering. This paper introduces marginal dependence models, which enable the representation of non-trivial associations between random vectors in higher dimensions, without adhering to either a joint Gaussian distribution or a copula model. We establish that these models naturally encompass the SDDT and SKD distributions as special cases, and propose a new model known as the marginal skew t-productition distribution. Through the development of an efficient maximum likelihood-based estimation method, this research demonstrates that the parameters of these distributions can be estimated in relatively low computational time, and supports our findings with valuable theoretical results. Additionally, the paper showcases the effectiveness of these models in capturing complex relationships in real-world data, using both synthetic and actual datasets. A comprehensive R package, named 'MDM', has been developed to implement these models and associated estimation techniques, making them accessible to practitioners. This research has the potential to expand the scope of multivariate dependence modeling, and enhance the accuracy of predictions in high-dimensional data analysis. We develop a model where different social mobility opportunities arise for various groups of young individuals over time, and these opportunities vary depending on the skills of their parents.  As a result, the chances for a successful career increase when parents and children have similar skills in certain skill areas, but this is not the case for unrelated skill areas.  As each age group reaches the end of its working life, a new population takes their place, and a utility-maximizing social program aimed at improving the overall economic well-being of the current population distributes opportunities to different groups based on their income and the expected benefits of supporting lower-skilled group members, ultimately resulting in a mix of high-skilled and low-skilled individuals in each age group.  This mix is determined through a unique equilibrium known as a Nash Equilibrium that is reached independently of how the previous generation chose to distribute opportunities, and it is found to be unique and achievable.  In our model's solution, it is revealed that the skill diversity within an age group directly affects the opportunity assigned to a group with lower-skilled members through a non-linear relationship and that the opportunity assigned to a group is directly proportional to the group's income.  Furthermore, it is shown that the opportunity assigned to a group is inversely proportional to the group's relative marginal utility of support, and it is demonstrated that the skill area to which an opportunity is tied is determined by the group's income rather than the group's relative utility.  Additionally, a condition is established to determine whether a group is high-skilled or low-skilled based on their relative utility and the level of support other groups provide, and it is shown that the opportunity assigned to a group is directly proportional to the group's income when it is low-skilled and inversely proportional to the group's income when it is high-skilled.  Finally, it is proven that a group's assigned opportunity is inversely proportional to the group's relative skill level.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented in this paper.
Our objective is to develop a practical anonymity solution for a decentralized cryptocurrency, capable of supporting thousands of transactions per block and providing users with secure stealth addressing capabilities.
Due to its compatibility with DPoS, Delegated RingCT has the potential to be utilized by existing cryptocurrencies that require anonymity, such as Dcash (DCT). Additionally, its protocol can serve as the foundation for developing subsequent anonymity solutions with enhanced security post-Snowden. Currently, Delegated RingCT stands as one of the most secure anonymity solutions for cryptocurrencies to date. Furthermore, its developed technology holds potential for other decentralized applications requiring linkable ring signatures in the future. 
In comparison to RingCT, Delegated RingCT showcases enhanced computational efficiency at the transaction processing level, stemming from integrated signature and encryption mechanisms that suppress redundant computations.
Consequently, this results in faster transaction verification and better overall performance, while maintaining comparable levels of security and anonymity functionality. Moreover, our analysis reveals that Delegated RingCT can process transactions at an efficiency rate comparable to that of Bitcoin, bolstering its feasibility for widespread use in decentralized cryptocurrencies. In a financial context, the chief advantage of Delegated RingCT over RingCT lies in its faster transaction confirmation speeds by a factor of 20. In summary, Delegated RingCT presents an effective anonymity solution that strikes an optimal balance between security, efficiency, and stealth addressing capabilities for stealth transactions. In light of emerging cyber threats, Delegated RingCT stands as an effective solution, showcasing a substantial improvement in practicality over previous anonymity solutions for cryptocurrencies. In particular, its anonymity performance surpasses that of RingCT, integrating seamless DPoS compatibility into its design, resulting in a ruggedized anonymity solution. The security proof presented in this paper confirms that Delegated RingCT provides both computational and decisional anonymity security. Furthermore, our protocol demonstrates the ability to provide efficient linkable ring signatures without compromising anonymity security, thereby presenting a more practical solution for linkable ring signatures in future cryptographic applications. A recent innovation in quantum key distribution, employing partial randomization of carrier and decoy states, has improved resilience against collective attacks. Nevertheless, our research reveals a newly discovered weakness in the system where an all-in-ones attack can succeed, potentially threatening its reliability. To rectify this flaw, we introduce a modified protocol incorporating partial randomization of phases in both carrier and decoy states for the QKD system, effectively mitigating the all-in-ones attack and enhancing its security. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the efficacy of phase randomization in enhancing the security of quantum key distribution systems, recommending its adoption in future applications. Computational simulations are utilized to evaluate the reduced error rates resulting from both existing and modified protocols in the presence of an all-in-ones attack. Our studies indicate that, with phase randomization in both carrier and decoy states, reduced error rates can be accomplished at a comparable rate to an all-in-ones attack on a system without phase randomization. In essence, this modified protocol not only defends against an all-in-ones attack, but also achieves a comparable rate of reduced error rates, thereby enhancing the overall security of the QKD system. Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a state-of-the-art model when employed in-context learning tasks. We discovered that a pretraining corpus's quality has a direct impact on the model's ability to learn in-context, whereas its quantity has an inverse relationship - higher pretraining corpus sizes yield better results but at a diminishing rate. Additionally, we found that a pretraining corpus with real-world data yields better results than one composed entirely of written content. Our findings indicate that a pretraining corpus with a mix of textual and spoken content yields the most advantageous outcomes for in-context learning. We make our code and dataset available for the sake of replicability.

The processes governing the formation, fragmentation, and expansion of cold, dense gas within galaxy clusters are complex and involve various physical mechanisms that interact with each other. According to numerical simulations, the evolution of cold gas clumps is primarily shaped by a combination of radiative cooling, thermal conduction, and magnetic field instability. We have conducted a series of high-resolution simulations to examine how these processes evolve over time, particularly within the central regions of galaxy clusters. In the presence of both cooling and thermal conduction, the development of cold gas clumps resembles a "wave-like" pattern. However, when magnetic field instability is factored in, the cluster core begins to strip away at higher rates, leading to an increased mass loss of cold gas through a hotter, Conduction-Limited Radius. This effect is most pronounced at higher levels of magnetic field strength. We have developed a simplified model that effectively captures the impact of magnetic field instability on the dynamics of galaxy clusters, and this model is comparable to previous findings. Furthermore, our study highlights the significance of considering magnetic field instability in the context of galaxy cluster simulations, particularly when studying the cooling problem, as it leads to an increased mass loss of gas and thus strengthens the case for thermal conduction suppression. On the other hand, the cluster core strips away at higher rates due to magnetic field instability, which could potentially alleviate the cooling problem, depending on the underlying magnetic field strength. Our work also illustrates the dynamic nature of the Radioactive Inversely Rate (RIR), which may help to explain previous discrepancies between simulations of galaxy clusters, particularly regarding the core gas density and temperature distributions. RIR is sensitive to the cluster mass, its thermal energy relaxation time, and the magnetic field strength, all of which affect the dynamics and thermodynamics of galaxy clusters, resulting in varying mass-to-energy ratios that depend on the underlying magnetic field strength. The growing expectation for sustainable energy systems necessitates the integration of energy-efficient design principles into the planning of future cellular networks. In this study, we focus on the core network of a 5G wireless system and investigate the relevance of managing temperature in data centre cooling systems. Our initial findings reveal that dynamic compensation of server power by a flexible core network can lead to significant reductions in cooling energy. To exploit these opportunities, we develop scalable, autonomous management strategies for dynamic scaling of the core network. Two distinct approaches, based on the concepts of resource pools and container-based architectures, are presented along with a comprehensive evaluation of their cooling energy benefits. Our analysis demonstrates that these autonomous management strategies yield substantial cooling energy savings of up to 5% and can also quickly adapt to changing traffic demands, achieving speed-up ratios of 1.05-1.20. Furthermore, we illustrate that combining dynamic core network scaling with static large-scale core network design yields superior outcomes, characterized by enhanced system scalability and lower cooling energy consumption. Our numerical evaluations confirm that the core network management at a data centre level can significantly influence the overall scalability and energy efficiency of the core network. Consequently, integrating core network management into the broader 5G wireless system design is crucial for achieving optimal and sustainable energy efficiency. Moreover, the concepts presented in this study can be extended to other areas of 5G wireless systems, thereby promoting a more sustainable data-driven society. A critical challenge in building speech systems with minimal resources is identifying basic speech units and their sound combinations. Most approaches rely on written descriptions of these units, but since we're working with limited resources, we've developed a technique that uses acoustic models to select units that sound similar when combined. This strategy allows us to synthesize speech without first writing down the unit sounds. While the results, however, show that written transcriptions still yield better speech synthesis outcomes, the difference is minimal, and for the first time with limited resources, the quality of the synthesized speech approaches that of human-generated speech, according to mean opinion score metrics. To validate these findings, a subjective test was conducted. The code for this project is openly accessible at https://github.com/external-internal/VCS.

A novel multi-level optimization framework for motion planning is presented, addressing the interaction between a robot's wheel geometry and ground topography. To tackle this complex problem, our method divides the planning process into coupled sub-optimization stages, starting with an initial solution from a simplified model, then refining it utilizing data-driven representations of interactions. These coupled sub-optimizations are approached through a novel application of relaxed McCormick envelopes within two-level optimization techniques. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach via simulations of a robot navigating diverse environments, showcasing its generalizability and performance under various conditions. Key results indicate a substantial reduction in computational time, achieving solutions within a narrow error margin for all tested scenarios in approximately one to two hours. Further, the employed data-driven approach to modeling interactions enables robust performance despite minor deviations in wheel or ground topography characteristics. These characteristics, modeled as compact polynomial constraints, do not substantially affect the optimization outcome. Consequently, solutions obtained from our approach exhibit minimal sensitivity to variations in these parameters. To validate the adequacy of our model in capturing interaction effects, we performed a thorough analysis of its asymptotic convergence and achieved this through a novel application of a specific topological structure, ensuring efficient sum-to-one matrix transformations, thereby facilitating the use of the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers optimization method with guaranteed convergence. This theoretical underpinning of our approach further underscores the relatively low computational cost of our method, which enables it to efficiently solve the intricate coupled optimization problems. The integration of a robust optimization framework, enabling protection against uncertainties in interactions, did not deviate from the core methodology; instead, it complemented it by incorporating risk averseness, utilizing a Benders' framework that initially requires an informed guess for the optimal value of a coupled sub-optimization problem. This guess can be obtained through a preliminary iteration of the proposed methodology or the Benders' framework itself, thereby presenting an integrated solution to the problem at hand. The key concepts of our approach, coupled with data-driven modeling, relaxation, and optimization techniques, are thoroughly outlined to provide a clear understanding of the proposed motion planning framework, which we believe will serve as a useful tool for control evaluation in related research. We examine the physical principles underlying probabilistic conversions of quantum states using the quantum complementary uncertainty principle. We establish strict limitations on the physical processes transforming a quantum state $A$ into state $B$ with a certain success probability. These limitations indicate that a certain amount of uncertainty in state $B$ is inevitably introduced during the conversion process, even if the initial state $A$ and target state $B$ have minimal uncertainty in a shared quantum system. Our findings are substantiated through a detailed analysis of a specific physical scenario involving entanglement swapping between two qubits. We explore the possibility of surpassing these fundamental limitations by examining the physical processes achieving the maximum success probability in converting a quantum state $A$ into an equivalent state $B$. These processes, dubbed "optimal converting processes," possess unique characteristics, including being reversible and isotonically entangling. We also demonstrate that a specific type of optimal converting process can be used to generate a quantum state $B$ from a quantum state $A$ with certainty, provided that a certain success probability exceeding 100% is achieved in the conversion process, a condition known as the "overwhelming" probability. Our study provides a unified approach to understanding the relationship between quantum state conversions and thermodynamic systems, ultimately leading to a new interpretation of a prior finding in a different context by Luo, Zhang, and Zhang. Furthermore, our work enables a novel explanation for the zero-energy condition in two distinct physical processes: the black-hole holographic principle and quantum complementarity in pair-cat states. The latter involves an innovative analysis of the later process based on a novel approach to its interpretation, contrasting with a prior explanation by Zhang, Zhang, and Luo. Finally, our work rectifies an inductive generalization in a prior study by Zhang, Zhang, and Luo, establishing a new theory termed the "conversion uncertainty principle." The new principle encompasses the famous quantum complementary uncertainty principle as a fundamental instance. Moreover, the uncertainty principle has vast applications in diverse fields such as thermodynamics, spintronics, and quantum cryptography, extending beyond its applications in quantum information theory. Lastly, our work delves into the distinct physical processes achieving the maximum success probability in converting a quantum state $A$ into an equivalent state $B$ and identifies a specific type of such process: a category of optimal converting processes that possess a unique characteristic, namely that they cause less uncertainty in state $B$ than would be introduced by the minimum uncertainty principle, a distinction that could potentially lead to the development of more efficient quantum computers. In our research paper, we address the challenge of minimizing a weighted average of functions across a network of interconnected devices, with the added complication of data heterogeneity. To achieve this, we devise a robust decentralized training algorithm, DR-DSGD, which adapts the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent method by incorporating robustness to distributional changes via the Drift-Plus-Robust Variance regularizer. Our algorithm demonstrates better convergence in comparison to previous decentralized methods, with particular advantages in data-heterogeneous settings. By rigorously testing our algorithm on synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate its effectiveness and superior performance in practice. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of our algorithm's theoretical and empirical aspects, which substantiates its efficacy in a variety of scenarios. Specifically, our results indicate that DR-DSGD achieves faster convergence in distributed training applications, particularly when dealing with data heterogeneity. This research contributes a robust and efficient training method that can be applied to a broad range of decentralized applications, such as machine learning in blockchains and federated learning in mobile networks. Additionally, our experiments enable the exploration of new research avenues in decentralized training, which we hope will guide the development of more refined training methods in the future. Ultimately, our algorithm's parameter-free design enables users to easily scale our method to a large number of devices and networks, which further validates its potential for real-world applications. To formally state our research contributions: (i) we propose a novel decentralized training algorithm, DR-DSGD, which achieves distributional robustness in a network-trained model; (ii) we provide theoretical and empirical justifications for DR-DSGD's parameters, thereby establishing its efficiency and effectiveness; (iii) we perform extensive experiments to validate DR-DSGD's and analyze the influences of its parameters; and (iv) we design and tune DR-DSGD to achieve superior performance, thereby establishing a robust method for real-world decentralized training applications. We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established substantially contributes to the total entropy produced in collisions. In line with initial state energy theories such as EPS08, our data show that entropy generated before equilibrium is established makes up roughly 50-70% of the total entropy produced. This leads to a revision in our previously proposed relationship between average initial energy and particle multiplicity, and further showcases the utility of the hydrodynamic attractor concept in relativistic nuclear collisions.

This high-velocity jet component is thought to be primarily comprised of the protostellar jet, whereas the slower-moving component may be the result of the high-velocity jet interacting with surrounding material, forming a fan or cone shape. We investigate how light-matter interactions behave under transformations that change their state, preserving certain properties. In a theoretical model using tight-binding methods and based on electronic wavefunctions, we find a general condition that ensures light-matter interactions remain the same regardless of the state change. This condition has a straightforward application in simple models with localized orbitals and reduces to a known rule for a specific type of state change. Our findings are validated by applying them to a range of materials, including a 2D graphene sheet, a TMD layer, a silicon crystal, and a silicon phosphide crystal, and we observe that their electronic structures obtained through TB and first-principle calculations match closely. Furthermore, we confirm that the electronic transitions predicted by our TB model align with those obtained through more detailed calculations for the specific materials. In a final step, we demonstrate how our findings can be used to create and visualize electronic states with desired properties using an example. Our work lays the groundwork for developing innovative light-driven technologies. By establishing the underlying theoretical framework to describe light-matter interactions in a consistent and predictable way, we make the underlying mathematical concept of state transparency more approachable for materials scientists. Additionally, we propose a practical method for applying a specific mathematical concept to a broader class of tight-binding models based on localized orbitals. Finally, we identify potential practical applications of our theoretical model, such as controlling and inducing optical phenomena in materials. Our investigation into the preservation of light-matter interactions leads to a fundamental insight into the underlying physics, revealing a deeper connection between the electronic structures of materials and the characteristics of light that interact with them. In a broader context, our work represents a significant contribution to the broader field of contemporary condensed matter research, where researchers continuously seek to develop new theoretical frameworks that describe complex materials in terms of simple mathematical concepts. Our TB model, for example, reduces complex problems associated with light-matter interactions into manageable equations based on orbital interactions, thereby enabling the prediction of electronic states with desired properties and the preservation of light-matter interactions under specific state changes. Our work also represents an important application of the mathematical concept of unitary equivalence, which has far-reaching implications in diverse fields such as mathematics, physics, and computer science to the understanding of light-matter interactions. Lastly, our investigation into the preservation of light-matter interactions also leads to a significant practical application, as our TB model allows us to develop and create innovative light-driven technologies by harnessing the collective properties of electronic states, which have become a crucial factor in the development of next-generation energy technologies

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active perception approach is adopted, in which the observer strives to collect optimal information to confirm their hypotheses about the category in question. When observations are limited or compromised by interference, a reliable assessment of the category is sought through the evaluation of available information. Two new problems, optimal category perception and robust category perception, are defined and demonstrated with practical applications using simulated data in various scenarios. Future research will aim to incorporate real-world data and apply these algorithms in practical category-level perception scenarios. Code for the proposed methods is publicly available at https://github.com/fifo911/Category-Perception. 

Our approach to optimal category perception relies on the development of an optimal decision rule for confirming hypotheses based on observed data, demonstrating higher performance in detection and lower error in classification compared to existing methods. To address observation limitations and interference in real-world sensor data, a robust version of the optimal category perception algorithm is introduced. Evaluations of the algorithms were conducted across various categories using PASCAL VOC 2012 and KITTI dataset, yielding successful results in reliable category perception through the evaluation of available information despite potential distortions. 

Key applications of the proposed algorithms include reliable object pose estimation using sensor data, as demonstrated through the evaluation of category-level object pose using PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset, and a novel task of category-specific object recognition, where Keypoints on the chair category were used to distinguish chairs from other categories. Another application involved the use of the robust algorithm in vehicle detection near intersections, where prior knowledge of potential vehicles was utilized to enhance detection under limited and compromised conditions. Future research will aim to incorporate real-world data and enable practical category-level perception in a variety of situations. Code for the proposed methods is publicly available at https://github.com/fifo911/Category-Perception.

Additionally, two methods are presented to construct classical confidence squares for both parameters, yielding results in the form of lower bounds only. Furthermore, this paper examines the behavior of the proposed methods as the sample size increases, and suggests alternative approaches for larger data sets. The methods are demonstrated using R examples. The complete R code is provided in the supplementary materials. 

The main contributions of this paper are primarily focused on developing methods to construct classical confidence squares for the parameters of a Cauchy distribution, an effort in line with the original work of Stein (1935) Steins (1949). The proposed methods employ a quantitative assessment of the parameter square's coverage area, an approach inspired by the Chandra Pokarabelski theorem. The behavior of the square's boundary as the sample size increases is also systematically analyzed. The proposed methods exhibit desirable asymptotic properties, including smoothness and concentration. The confidence squares proposed in this paper can serve as a useful approach for targeting a range of parameters, including skewness, kurtosis, and other measures of asymmetry or distribution shape, in addition to the location and scale parameters of a Cauchy distribution. The Cauchy distribution's flexible shape has led to its widespread application across numerous disciplines. The location parameter $\gamma_1$ represents a parameter of interest in many fields, while the scale parameter $\gamma_2$ is often a source of additional variability. The proposed methods for constructing confidence squares can be useful in a variety of contexts, including targeting unknown means of independent samples in a normal distribution, or the standard deviations of mixed normal distributions.

A new statistical approach is developed for basket trials to determine the required sample size by strategically sharing information between subgroups within a single trial. This innovative method utilizes Bayesian statistics to calculate the necessary subject numbers while considering the potential clinical benefits of treating patients in multiple disease subgroups simultaneously. Our approach enhances traditional sample size calculations by allowing for direct and indirect learning within the trial, effectively combining data from each subgroup. By applying Bayesian principles, we develop formulas to assess sample size requirements for basket trials with overlapping subgroups, thereby maximizing the statistical power to detect significant treatment effects. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical examples and real-world applications. Furthermore, we outline potential challenges and limitations of this approach, highlighting the need for careful protocol design and Bayesian model specification to achieve optimal results. Keywords: Basket trials, Bayesian statistics, Sample size assessment, Subgroup borrowing, Clinical trials.

To meet the needs of industry and research for high-precision motion, we developed a linear parameter-varying (LPV) sequential loop tightening (SLT) technique. It combines the benefits of LPV and sequential approaches to enhance high-precision motion performance while reducing computational costs. The LPV model allows for an optimal, high-performance control design despite nonlinearities, and the sequential structure ensures efficient, parallel processing of calculations. The technique requires dividing the control law into connected segments and implementing an LPV controller for each segment using a common scheduling variable. A key feature of the technique is the ability to select various scaling factors for each segment through a dedicated algorithm, enabling us to minimize computational costs by reducing the number of calculations required. Furthermore, the technique enables the development of high-performance controllers for complex motion systems and reduces unnecessary calculations by limiting motion segment activation. The effectiveness of the LPV SLT technique was validated through simulations of a precision motion drive, resulting in a 300 times decrease in computational costs while maintaining an average error of less than 0.04% for high-precision motions. The LPV SLT technique is a versatile and efficient approach for developing high-performance controllers that combines benefits while minimizing computational costs. While a few keypoints alignment method, like DeepConcordance, excels in certain scenarios, it's not suited for complex tasks like facial surface alignment due to its limited flexibility. In contrast, learning-based approaches, like SGN and TSN, struggle with the computational demands of their direct 3D matching methods, especially when dealing with intricate objects and limited landmark data. Moreover, their focus on surface alignment, though necessary, isn't sufficient to ensure accurate matching of internal surfaces. In this paper, we introduce Partial Registration Network (PRN) - an efficient and versatile approach for aligning partial surfaces, even when data is limited and surfaces complex. Unlike previous methods, PRN treats alignment as a partial-to-partial surface matching problem, employing a self-supervised learning scheme that directly matches corresponding surface patches, thus bypassing expensive 3D surface alignment. Furthermore, PRN leverages a patch normal voting loss to exploit the generative model's ability to generate unlimited synthetic data, thereby enhancing alignment robustly. Through testing on the public LabeledFacePP dataset, we demonstrate PRN's superiority over existing methods, with performance enhanced by up to 15.4% in PCD, 11.8% in NM, and 8.7% in CDF 0.5. Additionally, we showcase PRN's versatility by successfully applying it to the tasks of facial surface alignment and partial 3D object matching, thereby underscoring its broad applicability. The code and model will be publicly available.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G induce an automorphism of the solenoid $\hat{G}$, the inverse limit of nilpotent quotients of G. For generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups, we determine when they satisfy this property, providing a computational tool that can be applied to diverse groups of this type. Our study focuses on the generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups $G_{m,n}$ and investigates whether all automorphisms $\varphi$ of $G_{m,n}$ induce an automorphism of the solenoid $\hat{G}_{m,n}$. A positive result is obtained for cases where $m=n$ or $m=n+1$, as well as for some additional scenarios with small values of $m$ and $n$. However, it is found that not all automorphisms of $G_{m,n}$ induce an automorphism of $\hat{G}_{m,n}$ for many other cases, including those with $m=n+2$ and $m=n+3$. Our research employs the concept of compasses, a specific type of algorithmic tool, to establish the $R_\infty$ property for $G_{m,n}$. It is demonstrated that any automorphism $\varphi$ of $G_{m,n}$ can be represented within a defined group action, while also defining the action of $\varphi$ on integers and investigating its effect on the solenoid $\hat{G}_{m,n}$. Our proof of the $R_\infty$ property for $G_{m,n}$ involves descriptive data and establishes a relation between $\varphi$ and another group action, while also providing additional insights into the properties of $G_{m,n}$. This research provides a new approach to studying generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups and their solenoids, while also contributing to the broader field of group dynamics. Our results have far-reaching applications and can be applied to diverse groups of this type, offering computational tools and insights that can expand our knowledge of group theory and its applications.
