Future high-energy colliders such as the VLHC, CLIC, and FCC-ee are expected to offer excellent opportunities for accurately pinpointing the higgs instability at approximately 125 GeV. To make an informed decision about which collider is best suited for this purpose, it's crucial to carefully assess the requirements and potential pitfalls in this study. Here, the focus is on the theoretical and experimental considerations that might restrict access to the instability, and I investigate the sensitivity of these benchmarks at the 5σ level over the phase space in proton-proton collisions. By comparing the sensitivity of the 27 and 100 TeV proton-proton colliders, and examining the optimal observables for pinning down the higgs instability at 125 GeV, I demonstrate that the 100 TeV proton-proton collider might be sufficiently capable of accurately determining the higgs self-coupling. Nevertheless, the 27 TeV energy may still be sufficient for this goal if the future electron-positron collider is utilized to supplement the measurement. Consequently, the decision to build either the 27 or 100 TeV proton-proton collider depends on additional factors and considerations. Ultimately, combining the strengths of these various experimental setups with the aid of the future electron-positron collider will offer an extremely reliable means of accurately establishing the SM instability. Furthermore, the study reveals that the essential requirements to study the higgs instability at 125 GeV can also be met with a low-energy electron-positron collider operating at 250 fs time scale due to the presence of virtual Higgs boson exchanges in the forward tagged kinematics. As a result, this alternative provides a viable means of accurately pinning down the higgs instability. Additionally, the study shows that the electron-proton collider has the capability to produce sufficient signal events for this goal, indicating that it might be a more suitable option for this purpose. Consequently, the study advocates for a more flexible approach to determining the higgs self-coupling by exploring the potential of the electron-proton collider at 26 TeV total centre-of-mass energy in producing sufficient signal events for this goal. In medical image segmentation, Pan-Carlini Approach has proven to be an efficient low-resource solution that requires only two labeled MRI scans. However, this method's performance relies heavily on the quality and similarity of the reference MRI scan to the target scan it's being compared against. Achieving comparable results for scans with significant differences is a significant challenge. To overcome this limitation, integrating multiple unlabeled modalities such as PET and CT scans into the training process could improve performance, specifically in PET-MRI fusion tasks. However, directly incorporating multiple modalities into the Pan-Carlini framework is problematic due to the need for similarity in the reference scan. To tackle this issue, we suggest dividing the modalities into separate tasks and applying the Pan-Carlini approach to each isolation. Nonetheless, this raises challenges of task uniqueness and separation. To address these concerns, we suggest Cycle-Division GAN, a novel approach that achieves instance segmentation on multiple modalities without the need for manually labeled datasets. We evaluate our approach through fusion tasks involving various pairs of PET-MRI and a CT modality, demonstrating its effectiveness in segmentation tasks. The code for this project is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/Chen-543121/Cyclic-Division-GAN. Additionally, the 3D visualizations can be accessed on GitHub at https://github.com/Chen-543121/CDGVisualizations. Predicting future actions of complex agents is a challenging task in multiple fields.  We address this challenge by developing a novel method which utilizes the capabilities of Recurrent Neural Networks to forecast agent movement.  A key component of our model involves feature extraction through a Radial Basis Function kernelized transformation of RNN encoded features.  In order to accurately forecast movements, we train our model to output a distribution of potential actions rather than a single outcome.  This approach results in our model generating a diverse set of distribution parameters, including location, velocity, and motion direction.  Through testing on a simulated environment, we demonstrate improved movement predictions utilizing sight and sound data from a common video game-like scenario.  Notably, our model achieves enhanced prediction accuracy by incorporating sight information over the use of sound alone.  The main advantages of our model include its flexibility, capability of learning diverse features, and provision of multiple movement possibilities.  While this model may not be suitable for high-speed high-dimensional systems due to computational complexity, it exhibits excellent performance in the tested scenario and provides a valuable contribution to the field of movement forecasting.  Code is publicly available at https://github.com/csujia/Kernelized-RNN.  Evaluation videos are posted at https://youtu.be/4s5jU0GdI1M and https://youtu.be/ajC2V3LTL9Q.  This work is based on an unpublished paper from 2018 and the authors would like to acknowledge the generous support of Yuchin Chung during that time.  We would also like to express our gratitude to David K. Wilson for his kind assistance in proofreading. We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons within the context of nearly G2-manifolds. A nearly G2-manifold can be viewed as a complex vector bundle equipped with a specific Hermitian metric, a connection, and an almost G2-structure that satisfies specific compatibility conditions. Our research focuses on how these components can be modified simultaneously under variation of the nearly G2-structure. In addition, we establish relationships between the deformation spaces of G2-instantons and those of related objects, such as connections and the almost G2-structure itself, within the context of quasi-morphisms of the group algebra of SO(7). A significant deformation anomaly is found, which implies that a specific condition of simplicity cannot be preserved through deformation. However, this anomaly can be resolved by introducing deformed versions of instantons, allowing for the preservation of simplicity. A direct result of this reasoning is the discovery that the space of deformation-analytic G2-instantons on a nearly G2-manifold is isomorphic to the space of connections, weighted by the first Chern class of the associated bundle. Our findings can also be extended to the domain of 7-dimensional nearly hyperholomorphic contact manifolds, which possess a distinct structure related to G2-manifolds. A key connection between these two domains is facilitated through the application of the Fefferman-Graham expansion technique. This technique allows us to gain a deeper understanding of the space of semi-regular points within the deformation theory of G2-instantons, which, in turn, enables the resolution of a long-standing conjecture regarding the space of regular points. This approach also opens up new avenues for research, such as the broadening of instanton theory to encompass a wider range of structures, including deformed and non-deformed versions of G2-manifolds, which would constitute an extension of the realm of hyperkaehler geometry. Furthermore, this research may contribute significantly to the development of a generalized Fefferman-Graham theorem, which would allow the reconstruction of a G2-manifold from its 8-dimensional distribution, armed with essential information regarding its obstructions. In addition, this work may provide a solution to the anomaly, which would enable the preservation of simplicity in the deformed version of G2-instantons, thus establishing a direct relationship between the space of deformation-analytic G2-instantons and the space of connections, weighted by the first Chern class of the associated bundle, for all nearly G2-manifolds.

A key finding is the existence of a countable set of p-core p'-sequences. Neural network-based point cloud models have shown exceptional performance in handling ambiguous and uncertain data due to their robustness in handling noise. However, their reliability is limited to a point and the entire network must be re-trained if a single erroneous data point is encountered. To address this flaw, a novel approach called Transformation-Unique Point Cloud (TPC) is proposed for enhancing the robustness of point cloud models through data smoothing. By integrating TPC into the existing model, it is possible to significantly lower the impact of isolated errors and significantly reduce the need for data pre-processing without compromising the model's original accuracy. The proposed method has been successfully tested on three challenging datasets (Synthetic, Semantic3D, and KITTI) with notable improvements in test accuracy after data smoothing, specifically up to 44.3% and 32.6% in the case of synthetic and real-world data, respectively, with no compromise on the model's original precision. The code for this research can be accessed at https://github.com/achiau/TCP_smoothing. This method relies on observing the neutral hydrogen signal, which we assume follows a particular pattern based on a model of galaxy distribution and the neutral hydrogen's average density across different scales. We then apply mathematical operations to determine how this signal is changed when the galaxy spectrum is analyzed using different patterns or models. We assume that a previous estimate of the neutral hydrogen's average density is known and use that information to make predictions about the resulting spectra. These predictions come in the form of altered signals and noise levels for different types of galaxy spectrum analysis. We also explore the effects of removing foreground signals from the data, which reveals that this process can introduce bias and noise. We further refine these predictions to account for the uneven distribution of galaxies in the universe and the resulting effects on the neutral hydrogen's signal. We then compare our predicted signals and noise levels to actual data from the DASHNyx experiment, which suggests that certain assumptions about the galaxy distribution and the neutral hydrogen's average density may need to be adjusted. We investigate the openness of the zero energy on the cubic almost Mathieu operator when it belongs to unpinned type B regimes. It's demonstrated that there are multiple modes of unpinned type B regimes, and an openness criterion is established to differentiate between modes of unpinned type B and pinned types. Additionally, it's found that the condition of freeness for certain tridiagonal matrices, specifically the WGM freeness condition, is satisfied for matrices whose elements follow specific statistical patterns. These findings are relevant to the study of modes of unpinned type B in systems of coupled Josephson junctions. Computational evidence suggests that modes of unpinned type B can lead to the emergence of non-f freeness (freeseness with non-zero eigenvalues) in the corresponding Hamiltonian, resulting in a different form of spectral distribution known as semi-free freeness, and potentially explaining the breakup of the unpinned type B regime into multiple modes. However, it's hypothesized that semi-free freeness can also arise from other types of spectral distributions, and that modes of unpinned type B may not necessarily exhibit semi-free freeness, and certain modes may fail to satisfy the openness criterion, instead pinning at zero energy, indicating that there may be a relationship between modes of unpinned type B, semi-free freeness, and pinned types at zero energy. It's further conjectured that modes of unpinned type B can be characterized by a specific spectral distribution, and that this distribution is equivalent to the WGM freeness condition, and that the openness criterion can also diagnose the presence of modes of unpinned type B in systems of coupled Josephson junctions. These results are not limited to the specific types of systems under investigation but offer a new approach for determining the openness at zero energy in systems of cubic almost Mathieu type, and potentially a broader class of systems. Finally, it's noted that the openness at zero energy can be diagnosed through both computational methods and the WGM freeness condition, and that future studies may prioritize testing these predictions in systems of coupled Josephson junctions using both numerical and experimental methods.

Initially introduced in 2001, the concept of observing timed properties leveraged timing information from real-time systems to enhance conventional temporal properties. To build upon this foundation, we revisit and expand this idea by exploring two key aspects. Firstly, we develop a symmetric definition, incorporating both systematic and observational approaches. Secondly, we demonstrate that observing timed properties with both deadlines and deadlines with tolerances can be reduced to a single equivalent framework, which we call the observing timer framework. This new framework allows us to define a single logical operator, observed-next-within, to describe the behavior. Based on this new framework, we identify the tolerable tolerances for any set of timing constraints and establish the relationship between observing properties and traditional real-time logic. Furthermore, we present a model-checking algorithm for verifying timing properties in discrete-time systems, implemented in an accompanying software library. The library also includes a tool for generating PASTA (prefix-and-suffix analysis temporal-axioms) temporal axioms, describing a system's behavior, from TIM (timed-invariant-model) models. Ultimately, we present practical case studies to validate our findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of our observing-timing approach in understanding real-time systems. This approach has potential applications in safety-critical systems, where timing information is crucial in verifying essential system functions. The GRAVITY instrument, featured in the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, employs a laboratory-designed telescope that assembles eight closely related beams originating from the Very Large Telescope. The telescope's aperture is minimal, measuring just 0.8 meters in diameter, which poses significant constraints on the optical system's performance. The realm of diffraction limitations and optical imperfections poses challenges for high optical quality, necessitating the optimization of numerous technical aspects. The presentation outlines and validates the parameters characterizing the GRAVITY telescope's image quality, magnification, and field of view, in addition to discussing the efficiency of the GRAVITY telescope in gathering light. The success of GRAVITY in achieving a 0.02 microsecond time delay precision for 300 h combinations, as well as its remarkable 10^-9 amplitude precision in differential visibilities, has paved the way for the pioneering achievement of reaching 100 microsecond time resolution with angular resolutions better than 7 milli-arcseconds, a feat that was accomplished in 2019. The presentation provides an overview of the instrument's outstanding capabilities that resulted from the intricate telescope design, the impressive optical quality of the GRAVITY telescope, and the exceptional environmental stability of the laboratory-designed telescope under operation at the Very Large Telescope. The presentation illustrates the remarkable achievements of the GRAVITY telescope in a regime far beyond the diffraction limit of the telescope components, enabling novel applications such as the reconstruction of complex images and the observation of short duration astrophysical phenomena at unprecedented angular resolutions. The overview provides details on the current status and the future prospects of the GRAVITY instrument, as well as its involvement in various scientific projects such as the observation of the disk surroundings of a gravitational wave source, the analysis of the photosphere and outer atmosphere of the planet host star Proxima Centauri, and the phase-gradients based disentangling of the binary system Gamma Orionis. The ambitious targets of achieving time resolution beyond 10 seconds at a spatial resolution of about 100 milli-arcseconds are presented together with the adopted strategy of achieving these parameters by means of the sampling of phase method. The presentation closes by highlighting the remarkable stability of the GRAVITY telescope, where the entire technical infrastructure continues to enable unprecedented precision measurements over long periods of time, as has been demonstrated in the 300 h long combination of 2019, and continues to empower novel astrophysical research at a resolution surpassing the diffraction limit of the telescope components by several orders of magnitude. Solving the constraints of the Hamiltonian and momentum equations for numerical relativity is a challenging task in solving the initial conditions for the Bianchi types IX models. Given that these constraints are non-linear and involve higher than first-order derivatives of the spatial metric and gravitational field, it becomes extremely difficult to solve them in a logical sequence. In order to overcome this obstacle, we introduce a novel approach called the Conjugate Time Kinematics method (CTK) that effectively decouples the Hamiltonian constraint from the other higher-order equations, allowing us to solve the problem in a more practical manner. This breakthrough enables us to generate a full set of conjugate momentum variables, thereby revolutionizing the research of numerical relativity by providing a more accessible approach to solving the metric evolution equations. As such, we present a newly constructed set of conjugate kinematic variables, dubbed the Conjugate Kinematic Repository (CKR), which serves as a fundamental component for implementing the Filling-in-the-Solutions method (FIS). CTK proves to be an ideal choice for implementing the FIS approach, thereby resulting in a more efficient implementation compared to other methods. This research presents two novel solutions designed to satisfy the constraints of the Hamiltonian and momentum equations, which we refer to as Solution Sets I and Solution Sets II. Solution Sets I employs two conjugate mean curvature functions, thereby simplifying the Hamiltonian constraint, while Solution Sets II introduces an additional unknown function, thereby completely eliminating the Hamiltonian constraint. Notably, the CTK method proves to be an efficient and effective choice for solving the momentum equations, thereby allowing us to recover the conjugate momentum variables, known as Solution Sets III, which can be obtained by taking the time derivative of the CKR variables. This research showcases that the CTK method offers a flexible and effective approach for solving the conjugate momentum variables. This finding enables us to revisit the FIS method and reveal that certain previously hypothesized solutions actually reside within the Solution Sets I and Solution Sets II solutions. This research further extends the FIS method by introducing two novel solution families, thereby enhancing the theoretical framework of numerical relativity. This goal requires highly accurate 1% oscillation-related calculations, primarily dependent on the photomultiplier tube's linear energy response. A 1% error in this response will limit the experiment's accuracy, thus necessitating the mass and energy-related characteristics of the PMTs need to be carefully assessed. A comprehensive evaluation of twenty-inch photomultiplier tubes for use in the JUNO experiment involved examining the internal structure of the PMTs. The final step in this process involved selecting 20 PMTs with the most suitable characteristics. However, the uncertainty associated with the chosen tubes' properties necessitated a investigation into the environmental impact of the DOP PMTs during the testing procedure. This study provides an overview of the final 20 selected tubes' characteristics and discusses the possible effects of the surrounding water's refractive index change. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued quantities like velocity or momentum. Furthermore, a corresponding finite element method exists for solving the transport equation of a scalar quantity. We introduce a novel, second-order accurate method that resolves the transport of vector fields like momentum across quadrilateral elements. The proposed scheme incorporates an averaging approach for interpolating the transported vector field on each edge of a face shared by multiple elements. This technique can be computationally costly if not enough local data is available, but we show that it can also be implemented using only nearby elements with shared faces, thereby reducing computational expenses. The scheme's efficiency and performance are validated through several numerical experiments. Moreover, we demonstrate that a simplified variant of the scheme, requiring computation on a coarser grid, is nearly as accurate and can be an attractive alternative for coarse-grid corrections in more complex schemes. The latter idea is particularly relevant in the context of variable-coefficient Helmholtz decomposition, a technique we also apply to enhance the model's numerical simulations. Specifically, our corrections improve the already high accuracy of the variable-coefficient linear transport operator, thereby achieving a nearly exponential decrease in errors. The entire framework is implemented in DUNE and made publicly available under an open-source license. The DUNE implementation details can be found in an accompanying GitHub Gist. Finally, we show that similar concepts can also be extended to approximate advected tensor fields. In the context of differential problems, the overall error associated with approximating a solution via numerical methods can be broken down into two distinct components: the discretization error, which arises from the step-size, and the approximation error inherent to the solution itself. We introduce a novel family of continuous-stage Runge-Kutta estimators, which not only provide a more comprehensive understanding of the error but also enable the identification of the inherent approximation error. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis demonstrates that these estimators can achieve the same convergence rate as the traditional Runge-Kutta method, while also providing a more refined bound on the error, specifically the inherent approximation error. The findings of our research are corroborated through both theoretical and numerical examinations. The latter reveals that the newly proposed estimators can offer significant improvements in convergence rate and precision, particularly in low-dimensional dynamical systems. The implementation of our approach is facilitated by an open-source software framework. The code is meticulously documented, with clear explanations of the estimator calibration process and relevant numerical experiments are conducted to showcase its effectiveness. The software package is freely accessible at the following repository: https://github.com/Juandrog/CSRK. This research presents a fresh perspective on runge-kutta estimators, highlighting their potential utility in numerical analysis and providing a valuable contribution to the field. The study also delves into theoretical aspects, with complementary material available online, along with numerical evaluations that showcase the benefits of these new estimators. The influence of our findings is likely to extend beyond theoretical analysis, with possible applications in science and engineering. This paper introduces a novel approach called regional critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing multiple GPUs to train a deep neural network. By segmenting the network into layers and assigning them to separate GPUs, we develop innovative strategies to coordinate the learning process. Notably, we propose a regional critic, a neural network that assigns optimal gradient signals to each regional layer, leveraging both direct and indirect gradient information shared across GPUs. Our method requires no conventional back-propagation computations, thereby eliminating the need for inter-GPU data transfer during back-propagation. Our approach can also be combined with other model-parallel training methods, such as data-parallel training, to further generalize the method. Experimental results demonstrate that regional critic training achieves comparable performance to traditional data-parallel training methods, while also providing a framework to explore new hardware architectures for neural networks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jahanbin regional_critic_training.

Cybersecurity in IoT is a major concern due to increasing cyber threats, and IoT devices are frequent targets. To mitigate this issue, anomaly-based network security systems have been implemented in recent years, detecting malicious network traffic by identifying unusual patterns, including DoS attacks, which account for the majority of IoT-related threats. However, detecting DoS attacks efficiently is still an area of improvement, mainly due to the massive traffic volumes involved, making it challenging to extract distinctive features from network data. To address this limitation, a novel Naive Bayes classifier-based encoder, NBcoded, has been proposed to simplify network traffic, extracting compact features that distinguish between malicious and benign traffic, thereby enhancing the accuracy of anomaly detection for resource-constrained devices. Additionally, an NBcoded-based detector is proposed to detect DoS attacks in real-time, yielding superior performance compared to existing approaches, including GRNN, SVM, and CNN, with the bonus of requiring minimal hardware resources for implementation. To validate the effectiveness of NBcoded, experiments were conducted using the TON dataset, which is known for its traffic volume volatility, mimicking real-world scenarios, and demonstrating the versatility of the model. Finally, the implementation details of the NBcoded model are provided to facilitate its adoption in practical applications. We discuss recent advancements in a physical inference approach known as Discovery Science, which involves uncovering underlying physics laws through data analysis. This is distinct from the traditional physics methodology where experimental results are analyzed to confirm existing theories. Discovery Science uses statistical and machine learning techniques to identify universal patterns in data and propose new physical laws that account for observed discrepancies. Two case studies involving gravitational screening and local time variation of fundamental constants demonstrate the efficacy of this method in generating novel, experimentally verified predictions. These predictions provide valuable insights for refining existing physics models and resolving long-standing inconsistencies between data and their assumed linear variations. The boson peak is distinguished from other acoustic phonon modes by its local origin, specific higher-frequency components, and complex dynamics, all of which are influenced by the density of states. The central issues surrounding the boson peak involve its long-standing debate on the continuum or mode representation, in addition to its intricate connections with other glassy phenomena, such as the pseudogap in electrons. Our research focuses on the impact of introducing novel electron-phonon coupling mechanisms, including the flexural mode coupling mechanism, on valley physics in two-dimensional materials. To investigate this, we develop a 2D valley quantum pseudo potential based on a smooth, curved surface and derive analytical expressions for the valley-dependent quantum potential and effective mass. We demonstrate that the effective mass exhibits a valley-dependent sign change when the novel electron-phonon coupling mechanism is dominant. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the valley distribution of the electron density can be intentionally manipulated by adjusting the phonon mode mixture, ultimately leading to the emergence of valley-specific effective mass properties. This understanding can guide the development of 2D valley materials with adjustable effective mass properties, thereby expanding the material property control repertoire. When the novel electron-phonon coupling mechanism is not considered, the effective mass exhibits the typical characteristics of a parabolic shape, regardless of the valley index. A research paper proposes an innovative design for a millimeter-wave patch antenna that can operate within a broad frequency range ($$126.6\sim 134.8$$ GHz) while maintaining a relatively large beamwidth of $$54^{\circ}$$, making it suitable for applications in integrated wireless transceivers. Additionally, the antenna showcased an operational stability over a wide angular range ($$\pm 30^{\circ}$$/) with minimal gain fluctuations. The antenna's observed gain, beamwidth, and input impedance were measured as follows: a gain of approximately $$3.3\sim 4.3$$ dB, a beamwidth of about $$54^{\circ}$$, and an input impedance that remained relatively stable within a $$100\pm 2$$ $$\Omega$$ range. The data presented in this research paper will be valuable to experts designing millimeter-wave antennas with broad bandwidth and large beamwidths. Quantum metrology uses entangled quantum states to enhance precision beyond classical limits. This research investigates improved measurement accuracy in two-cavity systems where the number of photons in the cavities is counted. A comprehensive analytical solution is developed for the probability distribution of photon numbers in both cavities, yielding an optimal entanglement gauge measurement field that maximizes accuracy. Comparing this approach to traditional generalized quantum gauge measurements, reveals better performance, however, this benefit decreases as the number of photons increases due to the limitations imposed by photon number conservation. A possible experiment setup utilizing two cavities is proposed for implementing this measurement scheme. Furthermore, this research extends the concept of quantum metrology to the investigation of temporal correlations of photon emission. These correlations offer a clear signature of the entangled quantum state and could serve as the detection criterion for quantum metrology, thereby separating it from classical behavior. The research also discusses potential errors in detection and suggests methods for confirming the entanglement of photon states. These includes the execution of Fidelities between the intended entangled states and those actually produced, as well as the simulation of quantum states and their projections onto specific Hilbert spaces. Furthermore, this research offers an innovative approach for analyzing complex quantum systems through their transition probabilities, thereby providing deeper insights into their behavior. This includes the recognition of conserved quantities in these systems, thereby simplifying the calculation of transition probabilities and revealing inherent patterns in the probability distribution of photon numbers. This understanding could be applied to various research areas such as atomic and subatomic physics for analyzing the possible decay paths of unstable systems and their probability distributions, thus extending the concept of quantum metrology to universal precision measurement. Lastly, this research discusses the possibility of implementing quantum metrology in a wide range of applications through its connection to the broader field of precision measurement. These include quantum communication applications and the development of precise quantum clocks, thereby facilitating the transfer of quantum metrology ideas to these and other relevant fields. The research also presents an alternative perspective for understanding quantum metrology through its generalization to distinct areas of research. Achieving the formation of intricate, three-dimensional structures in tissues remains an intricate challenge within optical trapping techniques. Although phase-only holographic systems have demonstrated potential in forming complex structures, their infidelity in dealing with tissues due to nonlinearity limits their applications. To overcome this, a novel approach combines a phase-only holographic system with a feedback control mechanism, making it suitable for the formation of intricate 3D volumes in tissues with optimal precision. The proposed system, a phase-only holographic control system (POHCS), relies on an iterative algorithm that adjusts the holographic pattern in line with the current wavefront's aberration, thereby maintaining minimal distortion. By implementing a thin-layer approach, POHCS facilitates the precise control of forming multiple complex structures simultaneously within a three-dimensional volume. Our study demonstrates POHCS' effectiveness by generating a variety of structures, such as a V-shaped trimer and a V mandala, within a 200-micron range of a tissue phantom. The POHCS system, with its versatile and adaptive properties, has the potential to form intricate tissues in biological tissues. The source code for the POHCS model is available at https://github.com/zhengdajie/POHCS. POHCS has been patented with registration number 2021103055263.0. This work has been submitted to Journal of the Optical Society of America A.

A monolithic large-tech demonstrator, CLICTD, is set to be a key component of the International Linear Collider and is now being developed at the Helmholtz Desy school in Hamburg, using the small collection-electrode design. This design boasts high precision and efficient tracking capabilities, as well as the ability to handle extremely high radiation environments. To optimize its performance, researchers used Monte Carlo simulations to analyze different sensor thicknesses and substrate materials. Sensors made from high-resistance Czochralski-grown CzSi exhibited the best results, with 95% of tracks less than 130mm from the sensor's surface and 5% within the innermost 5mm. Changing the sensor thickness affected the hit reconstruction's angular resolution, with thicker sensors performing better. Using the ILDBeamline test beam facility, researchers confirmed these findings and verified the CLICTD's performance with actual particles, finding its hit efficiency and track quality in line with expectations. This successful R&D will contribute to developing the CLICTD technology, ensuring it meets the ILC's stringent requirements and serves as a prototype for future detector development in particle physics. This work will be presented at the 14th International Workshop on Advanced Accelerator Physics in November 2022. Following this, the CLICTD's technical development will participate in a topical review on monolithic and small collection technologies in January 2023. Advanced telescopes strive to counter the impairments caused by atmospheric distortion,  making wavefront sensing a crucial component in search for extraterrestrial life.  Recent breakthroughs in artificial intelligence and machine learning have led us to  explore self-coherent adaptive optics (SCAO) as a promising approach to achieve  high precision low-order sensing in turbulent environments.  This innovative method  employs fast focal plane detectors to directly exploit the inherent coherence of laser  light, eliminating the need for expensive and bulky laser design.  For the first time,  we have successfully implemented this concept on the Santa Cruz AO testbed using  a fast photodiode array as part of a demonstration.  Our experimental findings  demonstrate the capability of SCAO in achieving low error frames, high frame rates,  and achieving a 95% convergence rate to a fixed target in an intense turbulent environment.  These remarkable results make SCAO an attractive technology for future  astronomical telescopes seeking to efficiently achieve high precision low-order sensing.  Our code and data are publicly available for the benefit of the AO community.

Due to the finite time required for particle collisions, using a single time step can result in an oversized time interval, leading to inaccurate solutions. Our new method tackles this challenge by breaking down the larger time interval into multiple smaller sub-intervals for explicit numerical calculations. A revised integration coefficient is developed to account for particle collisions within these sub-intervals, enabling explicit calculations. This approach can easily incorporate traditional collision models and is adaptable to various flow conditions, as demonstrated through simulations of different scenarios, such as Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids. Furthermore, our method broadens the applicability of previous studies on collision time and particle dynamics, facilitating more accurate modeling of complex geological and geophysics phenomena. Extensive validation against theoretical models confirms the method's accuracy under diverse conditions, and our approach enables precise modeling of particle dynamics for a wider range of flow regimes. A comprehensive comparison with the current state-of-the-art method, IPSA, reveals that our new method surpasses IPSA in accuracy and performance, particularly in complex simulations of multiparticle collisions. Investigating the source of emitted radiation is crucial in understanding the paradox between quantum mechanics and general relativity. In the Unruh process, which is essentially a Hawking process, we uncover the non-perturbative, microscopic mechanism driving real particle emission. When charge and hole couple to the vacuum fields, they precipitously transition from a low-energy, non-invariant state to a high-energy, adaptive state. This transformative shift gives rise to a cloud of particle pairs, predominantly containing high-energy photons. In contrast to perturbative theories, the cloud forms at a characteristic radius, approximately equal to the de Sitter horizon radius, and is replete with photons having energies above the local Unruh temperature. The emitted photons derive primarily from the cloud's entanglement with the vacuum states of the fields, rather than from the adaptive state itself. Consequently, the adaptive state, which is inherently non-invariant, gives rise to particles lacking wave functions with global spatial overlap. This article presents comprehensive results for the entire set of non-negative integer solutions to the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$. It demonstrates that valid solutions exist for $n$ equal to or greater than $2$, with additional non-negative integer solutions limited to $n$ equal to $1$. Furthermore, solutions are confined to the range $a,b\le 7^{n-2}$. Notably, it's established that solutions with $a=b$ are prohibited, and numerous examples of solutions for given values of $n$ are provided. An explicit upper limit for the maximum value of $b$ in solutions for a given $n$ is also formulated. Lastly, several theoretical questions are posed in pursuit of further enhancement of these findings. Prior to this research, solutions had only been documented for $n=1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8$, with the present work extending these known solutions and addressing several previously overlooked queries. An interesting aspect of this research arises from the realisation that $k(k+1)^2=7^n$ has solutions for $n\ge 2$. Additionally, many upper bounds for the solutions were previously conjectured by Quan and Wang but were later proven too restrictive in this research. An improved upper bound of $b\le 7^{n-1}$ was finally formulated. An intriguing question remains as to the precise range of the solutions; while it's confirmed that $a,b\le 7^{n-2}$, the maximum possible value of $b$ when $a$ is fixed or vice versa remains uncertain. An unknown range of the solutions for two key cases when $n$ is an multiple of $4$ and when it's not, also remained unsolved and left theory based. An interesting comparison can also be drawn between the given equation and the well known Diophantine equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7k$, which remains unsolved. An intriguing instance of the solution of $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ is also brought up where both a and b are perfect squares. An extensive study into the solutions for the case of $a=b$ was also conducted but it remained confined to solutions that could be decoded and remained the largest known solutions for this case. An extensive research into the solutions for the case of $k=a$ was also conducted but it remained confined to solutions that could be decoded and remained the largest known solutions for this case.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve crash consistency at algorithmic levels, thereby enhancing system reliability and reducing the need for extensive checkpointing and snapshotting. However, the complex nature of algorithms complicates implementation of crash consistency, especially when multiple stages are involved. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel framework that utilizes a virtualized approach to streamline the process of crafting fault-tolerant algorithms. By segmenting algorithms into basic units and reconfiguring them according to memory availability during recovery, our proposed method allows for the integration of multiple algorithms and enhances the performance of fault-tolerant algorithms by up to 3 times and parallel algorithms by up to 2 times compared to conventional techniques. The advantages of our approach include its flexibility, the ability to perform algorithmic-level error correction, and the integration of multiple algorithms through a shared framework. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the efficacy of our method by applying it to the development of a fault-tolerant FFT algorithm, thereby showcasing the potential benefits of our approach. The algorithm-directed approach we have developed promises to significantly enhance the fault tolerance of real-world algorithms and contribute substantially to the advancement of high-performance computing systems. The proposed framework and algorithm code are publicly accessible through GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/yl1129/FXTCVMSIM. The documentation for our framework, including installation instructions, can be found at: https://yl1129.github.io/FXTCVMSIM/index.html. The documentation also includes a step-by-step guide on implementing the crash consistency for FFT algorithm directly from the link: https://yl1129.github.io/FXTCVMSIM/patterns/FFTCVMSIM.html. The test code for evaluating the performance of our approach can be accessed through the following link: https://yl1129.github.io/FXTCVMSIM/testcases/FFTtest.html. The test code includes a detailed guide on setting up the compiler, the model, the driver, the stream manager, and the error injector, among other essential components of our approach. The compiler used in our experiment is GCC version 4.9.4 and the model is based on NVMM, available at: https://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=2827435. The error injector is also available at the same link as the model. The stream manager, the driver, and the compensation unit are custom-designed software components specifically for our approach

To understand how asteroids or other near-Earth objects (NEOs) behave dynamically, researchers must accurately forecast their future trajectories. A statistical model known as the Flux-driven Three-Body Problem has been developed to accurately predict the long-term paths of NEAs in a simplified astronomical setting. This model relies on probabilistic calculations that consider various resonances and non-gravitational forces acting on NEAs, such as ablation caused by sunlight. Abolation can significantly impact an NEO's motion, particularly in the Sun's gravitational influence. As a crucial test of this model's accuracy under different environmental conditions, this study investigates its predictions for NEAs orbiting within specific regions of the main asteroid belt, taking into account various resonances and the effects of ablation, including a scenario where ablation's impact is maximized. Our analysis focuses on the accuracy of long-term predictions for NEAs within certain boundaries and the likelihood of resonant capture under different environmental conditions. Our results indicate that the Flux-driven Three-Body Problem model generates accurate long-term predictions for a statistical population of NEAs in a specific region of the main asteroid belt, accounting for both gravitational and non-gravitational effects. Additionally, this study explores the influence of ablation on the prediction of orbital cross-sections and the likelihood of asteroid capture within specific resonances, revealing a complex interplay between ablation and gravitational influences that can lead to asteroid capture within particular regions of the main asteroid belt. Based on these findings, we estimate that a substantial percentage of the population of NEAs in our sample may be captured by the 7:4 resonance, with or without considering ablation. Our study also indicates that the effects of ablation on the prediction of long-period dynamics for NEAs in our sample may become more pronounced under certain conditions, such as strong sunlight exposure, in addition to its well-documented impact in the vicinity of the Earth. As a consequence, the Flux-driven Three-Body Problem model must accurately account for both gravitational and non-gravitational effects in order to generate precise long-term predictions for a statistical population of NEAs. When numerous test cases for a software system are run in parallel, the time taken to identify these test cases becomes a bottleneck, hindering overall performance. A new method is proposed to address this limitation by parallelizing the determination of test cases through Singular Value Decomposition, employing multiple processors or cores to expedite the process. This approach leverages SVD's capability to efficiently identify test cases from a high volume of data across multiple software systems simultaneously. To optimize results, a modified SVD variant is applied, which enables parallel processing of sub-matrices independently to maximize throughput. To further improve efficiency, a data loading technique is employed, allowing parallelization of data loading and SVD computation operations. Experimental outcomes confirm that this approach yields substantial speed-up, outperforming the conventional SVD method by parallelizing the operation. The degree of speed-up achieved is found to be directly proportional to the number of processors or cores available. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, a series of empirical experiments were conducted using open-source software systems, including Linux and Firefox, as test subjects. The aim was to examine how the number of processors or cores affects the performance, in terms of speed-up, of the parallelized SVD method, across varying data sizes. To evaluate the reliability of this approach, metrics such as speed-up and efficiency were used to assess the process. The results demonstrate that the parallelized SVD method achieves a consistent and substantial speed-up, even with large data sizes. Moreover, the approach exhibits good efficiency when using an optimal number of processors or cores. To showcase the capabilities of this approach, a video presentation is included. The video illustrates the execution of the parallelized SVD method on a graph, demonstrating how the operation is distributed across multiple processors or cores to maximize performance. The proposed parallelized SVD method is an effective solution for accelerating the determination of test cases in software systems, even at large scales, by leveraging the processing capabilities of multiple processors or cores, thus yielding substantial speed-up and good efficiency. The study provides valuable insights into performance by examining speed-up and efficiency metrics, using real test subjects, varied data sizes, and an optimal number of processors or cores. The key contributions of this work are: (a) the proposed approach successfully parallelizes the determination of test cases through SVD, resulting in efficient resource utilization; (b) the study offers a practical solution to a long-standing limitation in software engineering, addressing the bottleneck of test case determination in software systems; (c) the work provides relevant software tools, including a video

Suicidal thoughts are a severe indicator of mental disorder and require urgent attention. To address this critical issue, we developed an advanced predictive system that can identify individuals who are more likely to have suicidal thoughts. Unlike existing models, our system uniquely integrates three distinct data sources - Electronic Health Records, social media, and text messages - making it an essential research topic in the field of Mental Health and Suicidal Prediction. To effectively combine these disparate data sources, we employed a state-of-the-art deep sequential model that leverages the hidden representations of multiple modality sources. The proposed model consists of three components: a BiLSTM module for capturing longitudinal patterns in individual data, a CNN module for analyzing temporal relationships, and a Fusion module that integrates the feature representations from the three modality sources. Through extensive experimental evaluation on a large-scale dataset, we were able to demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed model, alongside qualitative analysis and diagnostic metrics. Furthermore, we were able to successfully validate our model on a real-world dataset, highlighting its practical utility and applications. The source code of our model has been made available for the research community at https://github.com/abhinayamishra/DeepSuicidalTweets. In addition to the code repository, we have also made available the associated dataset for Suicidal Prediction research at https://valohai.com/store/datasets/electronic-health-records-suicidal-records. This publicly accessible dataset showcases its value through 10-fold cross-validation, while also illustrating the challenges associated with its implementation. Interestingly, our model was able to surpass its 10-fold cross-validation performance on the actual dataset, while consistently achieving comparable results on related tasks. In essence, our proposed model has been strategically designed to effectively tackle the complexities of mental health and suicidal prediction, while also Intrinsic Motivation to consistently outperform itself over time. The research findings of this study align with the goals of the National Strategy for Suicide Prevention by emphasizing the importance of accurate classification in mental health, while also showcasing the significant impact of social media and text messages on suicidal prediction. The findings also validate the widely-held belief that individual data provides more accurate predictions of suicidal thoughts than group data. To address the associated technical challenges, our model employs a data-driven 'Memory Mechanism' that helps integrate individual data from various sources while modulating the influence of group data. The proposed model has been successfully validated on a large-scale dataset of Electronic Health Records, social media, and text messages, while demonstrating comparable performance to existing machine learning models,

Between October 2022 and February 2023, nine observations were conducted, spanning an energy range from 2-10 keV. The X-ray polarization levels from a central region were measured as 5 to 9 percent. The polarization vector's direction is found to be aligned with the X-ray brightness peak's radiation direction. The measured polarizations are consistent with the two-component non-thermal model of synchrotron radiation. This query sparked a prolonged investigation, with researchers eventually proving the existence of such an arithmetic progression for numbers up to the power of n+1, where n is a sufficiently large number. This finding verifies the stronger conjecture proposed by Ruzsa and Tamari.

In this research paper, we demonstrate that there exists an arithmetic progression of 10 distinct numbers in which the sum of the first 10 terms is 10 times a single number. This discovery confirms the weaker conjecture proposed by Erdos. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of an arithmetic progression composed of the numbers 1 through 9, in which the sum of the terms is 10 times a single number, thus extending an earlier finding of Erdos from an arithmetic progression of 9 distinct numbers to one of 10. The sound speed in dense stellar matter, particularly in dense matter related to compact stars, is extensively investigated.  In this research, we focus on the adiabatic sound speed in dense stellar matter consisting of nucleons, various types of hyperons, quarks, strange baryons, strange mesons, and other exotic constituents.  Our analysis reveals that, at low densities, the sound speed in neutron star matter does not significantly deviate from that in pure neutron matter, as the various components contribute minimally.  However, at higher densities, the sound speed in various phases of stellar matter, such as matter consisting of nucleons and hyperons or quarks, begins to differ from that in pure neutron matter.  Our findings also indicate that the adiambatic sound speed in various states of stellar matter can serve as an identifying feature in determining their respective equilibrium states.  This concept will be beneficial in extracting information about the state of matter within compact stars through their observed properties without prior knowledge of their composition.  Moreover, our work offers insights into the coexistence of different phases in compact stars, such as neutron-starne white dwarfs and quark stars, based on the sound speed's behavior at their respective equilibrium density.  Specifically, we observe that the sound speed in some states of stellar matter may exhibit a discontinuity at their equilibrium density, indicating a potentially first-order phase transition.  Furthermore, we note that the adiabatic sound speed in various types of stellar matter can be utilized to derive an adjective, thermodynamic invariant relation applicable to any type of stellar matter, and may also be useful in understanding the behavior of other areas of physics and astronomy, such as binary star systems and supernovae. We provide a rigorous semantics for the random lambda-calculus by translating it into higher-order probabilistic logic.  By establishing that this translation preserves the calculus's syntactic structure, we demonstrate the calculus's soundness.  Conversely, we show that any probabilistic logic formula can be transformed into an equivalent random lambda-calculus expression, revealing a strong connection between the two frameworks.  This translation is then utilized to prove that certain key properties of the calculus are universal, meaning they cannot be contradicted.  Specifically, we prove that there are an infinite number of distinct normal orderings, a infinite number of distinct normal forms, and a infinite number of equivalence classes among these normal forms.  Furthermore, we show that these counts are not dependent on a specific sequence and therefore hold universally.  In addition to these results, we establish that the calculus supports efficient probabilistic inference.  Efficient inference allows for an efficient distance metric to be defined on equivalence classes of normal forms, leading to which a proof of convergence for a metricized version of the calculus is achieved.  Finally, we show that the calculus contains a natural embedding of the probabilistic predicate logic of Moss and Ong, and thus contains an infinite number of distinct equivalence classes, an fact that was previously proven independently by Ahrens and Maitreenut.  Moss and Ong's probabilistic logic, in turn, contains an efficient embedding of the probabilistic lambda calculus introduced by Abramsky and Fox.  The connection between the calculus and Moss and Ong's probabilistic logic also allows for a analysis of the calculus's expressiveness relative to its weaker variants, and reveals a previously previously observed fact that the calculus contains an efficient embedding of the probabilistic lambda calculus introduced by Abramsky and Fox.  The strong connections between the random lambda calculus and other probabilistic logic frameworks reveal that the universal properties of the calculus are a reflection of deeper mathematical truths.  These same strong connections also suggest a number of future research directions.  Furthermore, the proof strategy used to establish the efficient inference capability of the calculus, and the metricized version of the calculus, is similar to a strategy recently employed by Feruglio, Feruglio-Nusimov, and Ong in their analysis of the probabilistic predicate calculus. Several local authorities face challenges in deploying advanced, deep learning-based solutions for road damage detection due to a lack of adequate resources, including access to high-quality training data and sophisticated computational capabilities. Additionally, many organizations struggle to adopt new technologies because traditional methods can yield satisfactory results in their specific environment. Despite these possibilities, very few successful implementations of road damage detection through deep learning have been reported, especially in multiple country settings. This paper aims to address this gap by developing an efficient, computationally simple, and effective road damage detection method that can be applied to various environments. This goal is achieved through a transfer learning approach that utilizes pre-trained, widely applicable models to facilitate adaptation to new, domain-specific datasets with minimal adjustments. A key innovation of this paper involves a new dataset compilation of 19,000+ images from four different countries (UK, Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa) that can be utilized as a pre-training data source for enhanced model adaptability. The proposed solution focuses on detecting various types of road damage through a multi-class classification framework, with an ultimate aim of achieving 90% accuracy with minimal modifications. This approach achieves high levels of accuracy with reduced computational requirements by leveraging pre-trained models (initially trained on a separate dataset), with performance evaluated across three different scenarios using the compiled dataset, with results showing high levels of accuracy with minimal computational requirements. Notably, the proposed solution achieves 88.69% accuracy with a small number of adjustments and 90% accuracy with more comprehensive fine-tuning, outperforming a baseline model by a significant margin across all evaluation scenarios. The compiled dataset and associated code are publicly available for further research and development. Several future research directions are also identified and suggested. Overall, this paper contributes a transfer learning-based solution for effective road damage detection across multiple environments with minimal modifications, with potential applications extending beyond this domain to various other issues. Our results show that a very strong magnetic field - exceeding 1000 Gauss - is able to prevent the star's surrounding matter from fragmenting, effectively isolating the star and preventing matter from reaching its surface. This dynamic maintains a disk that is highly turbulent but stable, preventing the star's surrounding matter from fragmenting due to its intense gravitational pull. This research investigates the mental health impact of court-ordered therapy for individuals convicted of crimes. Using a detailed dataset that tracks the medical and psychiatric treatment of convicted individuals in a certain US state between 2010 and 2015, we examine how requiring therapy affects mental health outcomes. Specifically, we analyze the effect of court-ordered treatment on the use of prescription medications for common mental health disorders. Our results indicate that individuals who underwent court-ordered treatment had lower prescription rates for antidepressants, antianxiety medications, and stimulants before the treatment period ended. However, this reduction in prescription medications is temporary, as prescription rates return to their pre-treatment levels soon after. Interestingly, individuals who received court-ordered treatment showed an increased use of prescription medications for mood disorders and decreased use of medications for antianxiety one to two years following the treatment period. Moreover, court-ordered treatment is associated with an increased risk of suicide, particularly when treatment lasts longer than average. Overall, our study finds mixed results, highlighting both the potential benefits and limitations of court-ordered treatment for improving mental health outcomes among convicted individuals. It is essential to note that the duration of treatment has a significant impact on mental health outcomes, prompting further research into the most effective treatment durations and the potential long-term effects of court-ordered treatment. Additionally, our results suggest the importance of incorporating therapy that targets various mental health disorders to complement existing treatment approaches. Furthermore, our study underscores the need to address the potential increase in the risk of suicide associated with court-ordered treatment, particularly among those who receive longer treatment durations, by targeting high-risk individuals more effectively. To achieve this, mental health professionals may employ pre-treatment risk assessments to identify individuals who are most likely to benefit from therapy and develop customized treatment plans that address their unique needs. Current approaches to automatic speech recognition and machine translation are often hindered by limited training data, leading to subpar performance in real-world scenarios. By training on these artificial examples, the model is enabled to learn from its own training data, thereby improving its accuracy on tasks including Librispeech ASR and Multi-OMRON translation.  Two variants of the method are employed: one automatically selects the most beneficial transformations through statistical analysis, or by utilizing an already existing transformation strategy; while another manual option allows human evaluators to make the decision.  This research highlights the effectiveness of a low-effort, statistically-driven data augmentation approach that yields improved accuracy without requiring significant human input.  By automating the process, even greater gains in performance could be achieved. Through further analysis, the technique is found to particularly effective at enhancing robustness to noisy signals in cases where clean examples are scarce. We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint, tied to a quadratic and integral cost function. This result draws upon the ability to establish the existence of solutions to a related non-linear parabolic equation with restrictions on the boundary. In addition, it leverages the use of an implicit function theorem, which in turn relies upon regularity of the transport equation in a mean field game. Notably, our approach simplifies previous demonstrations of mild solution existence in similar contexts. Furthermore, under additional assumptions regarding regular paths and Lipschitz costs, we demonstrate the convergence of approximate controls, leading to a'mild solution' in the classical sense. This note presents a condensed version of the author's doctoral thesis, with'mild solutions' defined as solutions derived from an implicit function theorem and'regular paths' being solutions to a transport equation. The thesis itself offers a thorough review of relevant publications, while this note focuses on key technical contributions. 

\textit{Note:} This note assumes a basic knowledge of mean field games, including the key concepts and results, as well as the technical tools required for the explicit and implicit function theorems.

However, our results contradict these earlier conclusions.  As with earlier research, our data show that there are many localized star clusters; yet, unlike earlier research, we found no evidence to support the existence of stellar filaments in the Milky Way. For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as completely compatible or not, which is impractical given the inherent ambiguities of human perception. In reality, items that don't fully match can still be wearable. To address this, we introduce Visitor, a pipeline that extracts key semantic features from image pairs and learns a compatibility score through a self-supervised contrastive training method. Visitor leverages a combination of transformer-based multiview encoding for outfit items and graph attention for modeling item relationships within outfits. By capturing rich contextual information among items, Visitor outperforms existing models and aligns more closely with human judgment. Additionally, we release the FashionNet dataset for visual compatibility, containing meticulously annotated fashion items along with their visual context. Denoted as VICTOR, our proposed method relies on Visitor's feature extractor to generate vector representations of outfit items, which are then analyzed through a variety of experiments using the VICTOR model. Key evaluations include a detailed comparison of our model to state-of-the-art approaches, an assessment of its robustness to labeling inaccuracies, and demonstrations of its practical utility in the healthcare and fashion industries. To conclude, we showcase VICTOR's performance on a range of real-world challenges. Importantly, the model's code, dataset, and model weights are openly available for public reference. To our knowledge, this is the first publicly accessible fashion visual compatibility toolkit. It was trained on the FashionNet dataset containing 200,000 annotated outfits, ensuring high reliability of its outputs. To verify this, we present human evaluation results showing that VICTOR's performance surpasses other approaches by a substantial margin. A crucial application of our model involves visual impact assessment for mental health analyses, where a healthy range of visual impact scores can be identified through human evaluation of the model's outputs. To address this challenge, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the testing process and propose a testing mechanism using lower-resolution images to alleviate the memory burden without compromising the model's performance. The intersection of quantum theory and black-body radiation, known as quantum light, drives the development of modern optical technology and quantum computing. A crucial component in the quantum light resource theory is the description of electromagnetic states. Despite being well-defined, these states pose challenges due to infinite dimensional complexity and the inherent non-Hermitian nature of radiative processes. To address these issues, a new theoretical framework, known as generalized nonclassical illumination theory (GNIT), is introduced. GNIT is an adaptation of non-Hermitian quantum mechanics and non-Hermitian quantum information theories, incorporating a specialized inner product that filters out incoherent radiation. This leads to a formulation of quantum processes and maps that are now coherent, thereby resolving issues related to incoherent transformation and scattering processes. Additionally, GNIT enables a comprehensive categorization of optical systems, including lasers, spontaneous emission, and superradiance, through a novel distinction between pure and mixed states. A key concept in the resource theory is the resource metric, defined as the likelihood of finding a photon within a given interval. This enables the identification of resource states and the development of optimal conversion processes. Furthermore, GNIT is versatile enough to be applied to other areas, such as non-Hermitian quantum field theory, by extending the paradigm to higher dimensions and its potential applications are discussed. Finally, GNIT is compared to an alternative theoretical framework, known as non-Hermitian quantum light theory, and the distinction between these two approaches is elucidated. This introductory review is expected to pave the way for further research in the field of GNIT. A comprehensive list of references is included for the benefit of the reader. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronization issues become a significant challenge. Internal device gradients may become outdated due to the delay in communication, leading to inferior performance or even convergence failure. To resolve this, researchers have proposed asynchronous aggregation techniques, but current implementations are limited in that they only allow updating model parameters while channels remain open. We present an alternative framework where the model can be updated freely between aggregation cycles, without incurring additional communication costs. Our approach is built around a novel buffered asynchronous aggregation algorithm, which distributes gradient updates across the channel lifetime and aggregates them only when communication resumes. This framework offers more flexible gradient collection and reduces communication costs, with a model update latency equivalent to a single transaction. In our experiments, this framework achieved comparable performance with traditional synchronization methods, with added benefits of lower communication costs and end-device latency. Furthermore, we observed that the gradient collection process can be optimized to exploit the capabilities of specific channels, enabling a fine-grained control over when to transmit and update the model. We demonstrated this by developing an adaptive mechanism, which dynamically manages the gradient collection buffer based on channel conditions and adjusts the model update latency to match the channel latency. This adaptive version not only outperformed traditional synchronization methods but also achieved better performance compared to the standard framework, with added robustness and reliability. Our proposed framework provided a versatile solution for handling asynchronous communication in federated learning, with a model update latency and communication costs that were both close to the optimal values. By combining the framework with an efficient gradient collection strategy, we achieved a significant improvement in performance, with robustness and reliability that were superior to both the standard framework and the adaptive version. These results validated the potential of the proposed framework, which was designed to provide a general solution for the asynchronous communication problem in federated learning. To validate the generalization, we observed and analyzed the performance under various challenging scenarios, where the communication conditions changed suddenly due to a network disruption. Our results showed that the proposed framework performed consistently better than the comparative methods, with a noticeable improvement in performance as the communication latency increased. Moreover, this framework provided a more stable performance compared to the adaptive version, which only performed well under specific latency conditions. To further validate the efficacy of the proposed framework, we observed and analyzed the distribution of gradients within the framework, and how it compared to the benchmark synchronous method. Our results showed that the gradient distribution within the framework was identical to the benchmark synchronous method, which required significantly fewer communication transactions to achieve the same performance. In this context, we investigate how the Swampland program constraints the properties of such dark matter in our Universe. Notably, the requirements for dark energy - specifically that the Universe's current acceleration continues forever, as dictated by the horizon, imposes stringent conditions. The constraints on the primordial black hole mass are more stringent when considering the Swampland bounds on the gravitational potential's behavior at short distances, rather than the conventional assumption that general relativity holds at large scales. The implications of our findings are that the fraction of dark matter comprised by primordial black holes cannot exceed $10^{-10}$, and the radius of these black holes must be less than $1.3 \times 10^{22}$ meters. Thus, while the hypothesis that dark matter is comprised by these black holes is appealing due to its simplicity, our analysis reveals that the constraints on its realisation are quite severe. The presence of proteins within these rafts significantly alters their physical properties by creating holes and irregularities in the raft's surface as proteins bury their tails in the raft, causing the surrounding lipid molecules to congregate and create depressions. These surface defects eventually spread into the raft's deeper layers, influencing the protein's local movement and other surrounding proteins. The extent of these defects is determined by the size of the embedded protein and the surrounding proteins' affinity for the raft. A higher number of surrounding proteins binding to the raft leads to smaller defects and slower protein movement, whereas larger embedded proteins producing more prominent defects may lead to faster local movement due to reduced steric constraints. The dynamics between embedded proteins within raft platforms are further complicated by the emergence of new defects as one protein leaves the raft, causing another to take its place and alter the raft's surrounding environment. This replacement process is heavily dependent on the embedded protein's size, requiring larger proteins to overcome higher energy barriers due to increased steric constraints. This research investigates the effects of anisotropic strain on the electronic properties of GaN by matching its lattice to that of various III-N-As and III-M-Sn compounds. Due to the varying crystal structures of these materials, finding a perfect match is challenging, leading to inevitable strain. To better understand the influence of this strain, the research calculates its impact on the electronic properties of GaN. Interestingly, the results show that anisotropic strain significantly affects the hole conductivity compared to isotropic strain. Additionally, the study finds that matching the lattice to ZnGeN2 enhances the hole conductivity by two orders, while matching it to MgSiN2 has a minor positive effect. Crucially, the research identifies the key factors that contribute to these improvements, suggesting that improving the hole conductivity could be achieved by substituting certain elements in the III column of the compound. The findings contribute valuable insights to the design of p-type GalnAs/Naln/GaN nanostructures for use in photonic devices. Furthermore, the study reveals multiple combinations of elements in the III column that could improve the electronic properties of a given material, offering an extensive database of reference materials for III-N-As and III-M-Sn. The study uses a machine-learning-based algorithm to make these predictions, confirming that the algorithm's findings can be verified theoretically. Consequently, we successfully demonstrated the navigation of an autonomous marine robot through a complex and dangerous underwater environment, exemplified by a replica of the Titanic shipyard. Nevertheless, the development of TG-aware KGE models has been hindered due to the increased complexity and scarcity of high-quality temporal datasets compared to static KGs. In the context of a heavy quark's disruption, we've developed a detailed analytical framework capable of withstanding both external electromagnetic and strong interactions. This novel approach can be applied both when heavy quarks are freely moving and when they're bound to other particles. One area where our research shines is in its generation of heavy quark dispersion relations across a diverse spectrum of magnetic fields, which helps to accurately identify changes in quark behavior in response to external electromagnetic forces. This breakthrough will greatly enhance the accuracy of quark's dissociation velocity measurements, ultimately fostering a deeper understanding of how complex interactions affect the quark's dissociation process. This work marks a significant advancement in the study of quark disruption, paving the way for further exploration into the phenomenon's inherent nature. Moreover, our research findings reveal notable similarities and differences between quarks and photons in their responses to external magnetic fields, which has profound implications for quantum field theory's self-consistent model of charged particles.
