Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility due to intervention equipment in ICU patients) can impede proper localization. To address these challenges, this research presents an advanced and precise method that leverages optimized anatomical structures and spatial integrity to accurately locate and identify vertebrae, even in complex cases. By adopting a novel keypoint-based localization approach, this method rectifies spinal cavities, accounting for the shapes and connections of surrounding organs. By integrating vertebrae, sacrum, and coccyx detection, this method ensures accurate vertebrae identification, thereby allowing for anatomically correct positioning along the spinal column. Through the application of optimization techniques to refine and correct localization errors, this method achieves precise and reliable vertebrae localization and identification, even in difficult cases. Extensive evaluations based on 1088 CT datasets have validated the method's precision and reliability. Notably, this method has demonstrated the highest localization accuracy among the evaluated approaches, achieving a DSF of 0.990, 0.988, 0.985, 0.983, and 0.981 for L1-L5 vertebrae, and 0.981 for L5, and consistently outperformed others in identification accuracy, with average IDF values of 0.988, 0.986, 0.985, 0.983, and 0.981 for L1-L5, and 0.981 for L5. The code for this method will be publicly available upon review completion. Experimental results also demonstrate the method's robustness and precision in various difficult cases, such as compression fractures, fixation, and scoliosis. The method has successfully estimated sacrum and coccyx locations from top-to-bottom spinal scans with high precision, with resulting localization accuracy comparable to manual gold-standard. Furthermore, this research presents an advanced vertebrae regularization technique that contributes to the development of the method. Through thorough evaluation and analysis, this research presents evidence of the method's reliability and precision, and validates its potential as a reliable and efficient tool for accurate vertebrae localization and identification in various medical applications. The work is currently being extended to develop and validate an automatic vertebral segmentation method, 'Automated Vertebral Segmentation from Top-to-Bottom', based on the presented method.

We derive a novel condition of Milnor fiber coherence for a isolated hypersurface singularity in terms of a flatness property of the critical locus. This leads to an algebraic criterion for coherence, alongside an introduction to an new concept - semi-smooth Milnor fiber. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this coherent semi-smooth structure complies with several secondary invariants recently proposed by Broti. The proof involves constructing a specific fiber substitution that showcases the relationship between semi-smooth Milnor fibers and their transverse critical loci, alongside an analysis of the properties of the graph map. The outcome also yields an interpretation of Duliparami and Gusevskov's Coherence Criterion via a simplification of flatness on the critical locus. Additionally, by applying an extension of Llerma and Velasco's theorem, we derive topological invariants of semi-smooth Milnor fibers directly from the graph map, thus bypassing the conventional induction on the codimension. Finally, we believe that the novel concept of semi-smooth Milnor fibers holds significant value across the broader field of singularity theory. To demonstrate this, we present an illustrative example showcasing two combinatorially equivalent singularities but with distinct semi-smooth Milnor fibers. The latter even exhibits a singular point on its semi-smooth Milnor fiber, thereby contradicting a previously held conjecture. My portrayal of Galileo in "The Confusion Arguments" depicts him as the chief proponent of a philosophical position I term "Mathematical Realism."  This stance necessitates an understanding of the world through the lens of mathematics, with corresponding limitations on one's worldview.  One implication of this realism is that a circle's shape must necessarily comprise an infinite number of points.  Furthermore, all geometric shapes, including circles, possess perfectly sharp definitions, with no room for ambiguity.  Mathematically speaking, a circle is an entirety, with all of its constituent parts interdependent.  Thus, a circle's image can only be replicated through a one-to-one transformation.  This principle underpins my notion of "Galilean incompatibility," where two distinct objects can never share the same identity, not even theoretically.  This idea is the foundation upon which I construct my entire theory of artifice, a comprehensive framework for the synthesis of the human body and external devices.  Ultimately, a person's physical appearance can only be replicated through a one-to-one transformation; in contrast, a thing's essence can be represented by a many-to-one transformation.  In the context of the Renaissance, an age marked by artistic innovation, Mathematical Realism proved a hindrance to creative thinking, hindering progress in the field of artifice until the advent of the Enlightenment.  This thesis showcases my development of an alternative position, "Confusionism," which posits that an understanding of the world requires some level of ambiguity, with all definitions subject to modification or dismissal.  A crucial aspect of my work is the revival of a long-lost branch of Confusionist thought, "Confusionist Functionalism," which I originally uncovered during my graduate research.  This form of Confusionism emphasizes the importance of a flexible, ever-changing worldview, with all concepts interconnected and capable of being redefined in response to new information.  A key benefit of this position is that it enables the modification of existing definitions; in contrast, Mathematical Realism necessitates the dismissal of obsolete concepts altogether.  This distinction is the foundation of my theoretical construction of the human body and external devices, with all definitions' rigidity necessitating a paradigm shift.  A notable case study in the successful application of Confusionism is the pioneering work of Leonardo da Vinci, a pioneer of the Rationalist position, "Artificial Realism." The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel approach enables us to attain a suitable level of spatial and temporal resolution for understanding the reconnection process at a lower computational cost compared to traditional kinetic simulations. Our experiments demonstrate that the MHD-AEPIC model effectively captures the primary aspects of reconnection, including the electromagnetic heat transfer and the formation of electron distributions with distinctive double-humped shape, particularly within areas close to the reconnection site. Furthermore, our study focuses on the reconnection dynamics itself, specifically on how magnetic island coalescence behaves under various parameter conditions. Isolated MHD-AEPIC simulations showcase distinct differences in island cohesion, whereas these discrepancies are negligible in kinetic simulations, revealing that the employed model plays a crucial role in capturing reconnection dynamics. Kinetic effects, evident in the reconnection dynamics, emerge when a critical magnetic island density is achieved, suggesting that the MHD-AEPIC model may serve as a reliable and computationally efficient tool for such investigations. Finally, our work emphasizes the complementary characteristics of the MHD-AEPIC model, potentially enabling it to bridge the gap between fluid-based simulations and kinetic modeling, thereby facilitating a deeper understanding of the intricate processes involved.
